*** FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST’S HAWAI‘I REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER ***

 Electronically Filed
 Supreme Court

 28-OCT-2026
 09:37 AM
 Dkt. 22 OP

 IN THE SUPREME COURT OF THE STATE OF HAWAIʻI

 ---o0o---
________________________________________________________________

 MARCUS L. KAWATACHI, in his official capacity as
 Executive Director of the Hawaiʻi Civil Rights Commission,
 ex relatione, ROBERT A. FAHN and BRENDA A. FAHN,
 Respondent/Plaintiff-Appellant,

 vs.

 THE PARRISH COLLECTION, LLC; THE PARRISH COLLECTION KAUAI;
 JONATHAN D. PARRISH and SIMONE McCAFFREY,
 Petitioners/Defendants-Appellees,

 and

 LINDA EVANS, as Trustee of the LAURA P. EVANS
 REVOCABLE TRUST DATED May 8, 2022,
 Respondent/Defendant-Appellee.
________________________________________________________________

 SCWC-XX-XXXXXXX

 CERTIORARI TO THE INTERMEDIATE COURT OF APPEALS
 (CAAP-XX-XXXXXXX; CASE NO. 5CCV-XX-XXXXXXX)

 OCTOBER 28, 2026

 DEVENS, C.J., McKENNA, EDDINS, AND GINOZA, JJ., AND
 CIRCUIT JUDGE DREWYER, ASSIGNED BY REASON OF VACANCY
 *** FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST’S HAWAI‘I REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER ***

 OPINION OF THE COURT BY McKENNA, J.

 I. Introduction

 During the COVID-19 pandemic, a tenant with a disability

requested that a landlord provide an accommodation waiving a

weekly cleanings provision in a rental agreement. The tenant

explained that, because of his disability, he faced an increased

risk of hospitalization or death if he contracted the virus. He

therefore did not want non-family members entering the property.

The landlord denied the request, saying that the accommodation

was neither reasonable nor necessary.

 The Circuit Court of the Fifth Circuit (“circuit court”)

granted summary judgment in favor of the landlord. The

Intermediate Court of Appeals (“ICA”) vacated this judgment and

ordered a remand. On certiorari, the landlord alleges the ICA

erred.

 The ICA did not err by vacating summary judgment. But in

this opinion, we provide guidance on how disability

accommodation requests are to be evaluated under Hawaiʻi’s fair

housing law. We also address an issue not addressed by the ICA.

Although parties are encouraged to engage in an interactive

process, under current law, there is no standalone liability if

there is a breakdown in engagement.

 2
 *** FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST’S HAWAI‘I REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER ***

 We therefore affirm the ICA’s December 17, 2025, judgment

on appeal and remand the case to the circuit court for further

proceedings consistent with this opinion.

 II. Background

A. Legal Background

 1. Formation of the HCRC

 The Hawaiʻi Civil Rights Commission (“HCRC”) was formed

through Act 219, Session Laws of Hawaiʻi 1988, which was codified

as HRS Chapter 368. 1998 Haw. Sess. Laws Act 219, § 1 at 1-3;

see HRS § 368-1 (2015). HCRC is authorized to provide “a

uniform procedure” for enforcing Hawaiʻi’s anti-discrimination

laws in the areas of employment (HRS Chapter 378), housing (HRS

Chapter 515), and public accommodations (HRS Chapter 489). HRS

§ 368-1 (2015); see HRS § 515-9.

 In enacting Chapter 368, the Hawaiʻi State Legislature (the

“Legislature”) found and declared, among other things, that

discrimination in housing is contrary to public policy. Chapter

368 also vests the HCRC with powers to “receive, investigate,

and conciliate complaints;” “hold hearings and make inquiries;”

“commence civil actions in circuit court to seek appropriate

relief;” “issue the right to sue to a complainant;” “order

appropriate legal and equitable relief or affirmative action;”

and “adopt rules.” HRS § 368-3(1)-(5), (9) (2015).

 3
 *** FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST’S HAWAI‘I REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER ***

 2. Hawaiʻi’s Fair Housing Law

 Hawaiʻi’s fair housing law is codified in the Hawaiʻi

Discrimination in Real Property Transactions Act, Hawaiʻi Revised

Statutes (“HRS”) §§ 515 et seq., and Hawaiʻi Administrative Rules

(“HAR”) §§ 12-46-301 et seq. Hawaiʻi’s fair housing law

protects against discrimination on the basis of race, sex

(including gender identity or expression), sexual orientation,

color, religion, marital status, familial status, ancestry,

disability, age, or human immunodeficiency virus infection

(“HIV”). HRS § 515-3(a) (Supp. 2023). Chapter 515 applies to

sales, leases, rentals, and other housing practices, see HRS §§

515-3(a)(1)-(11) and 515-5 (2018), and provides complainants

with substantive rights as well as potential legal and equitable

remedies. See HRS §§ 515-9 (2018) and 515-13 (2018).

 When Chapter 515 was initially promulgated in 1967, the

Legislature directed that it “shall be construed according to

the fair import of its terms and shall be liberally construed.”

HRS § 515-1 (2018).

 Then, in 1992, the Legislature passed Act 171, Session Laws

of Hawaiʻi 1992. The purpose section of Act 171 stated:

 SECTION 1. The purpose of this Act is to conform the Real
 Estate Transactions Law, which prohibits discrimination in
 matters related to housing and real estate, with the
 federal Fair Housing Amendments Act of 1988. The Department
 of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) has published notice
 that Hawaiʻi’s law is no longer substantially equivalent to
 federal law. HUD intends to decertify Hawaiʻi unless these
 amendments are enacted. Certification is necessary in order

 4
 *** FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST’S HAWAI‘I REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER ***

 for Hawaiʻi to receive federal funds for the investigation
 of housing discrimination cases.

1992 Haw. Sess. Laws Act 171 § 1 at 1 (“Act 171”).

 The HCRC administers Hawaiʻi’s fair housing law. To

maintain HCRC’s federal certification, HUD requires that “the

fair housing law that the agency administers provide[] rights,

procedures, remedies, and the availability of judicial review

that are substantially equivalent to those provided in the

federal Fair Housing Act.” 24 C.F.R. § 115.201(a) & (b); see

HRS Chapter 368. Act 171 was passed because Hawaiʻi’s fair

housing law was apparently not as protective as the 1988 federal

Fair Housing Amendments Act of 1988 (“FHAA”), especially with

respect to disability discrimination.

 3. HCRC’s Enforcement of Hawaiʻi’s Fair Housing Law

 As required by Act 171 of 1992, the HCRC promulgated HAR

§§ 12-46-301 et seq. to implement and conform Hawaiʻi’s fair

housing law to Title VIII of the Civil Rights Act of 1968, as

amended by the FHAA. HAR § 12-46-301; 42 U.S.C. §§ 3601-3619;

1992 Haw. Sess. Laws Act 171, § 1 at 1.

 HAR § 12-46-301 states in relevant part:

 The purpose of this subchapter is to implement laws
 prohibiting discrimination in real property transactions
 toward the goal of eliminating such discrimination and to
 implement changes made by Act 171, Session Laws of Hawaiʻi
 1992, to conform state law to Title VIII of the Civil
 Rights Act of 1968, as amended by the Fair Housing
 Amendments Act of 1988. Chapter 515, HRS, prohibits
 discriminatory practices by an owner, any person engaging
 in a real property or real estate transaction, or a real

 5
 *** FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST’S HAWAI‘I REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER ***

 estate broker or salesperson against another person because
 of a protected basis.

 4. Conformance with Federal Law

 Thus, both Act 171 and HAR § 12-46-301 require this court

to construe our fair housing law in conformance with federal law

for HCRC to remain qualified as a certified agency to receive

federal funds for investigation and enforcement work. Hence,

federal caselaw interpreting the FHAA guides this court’s

interpretation of Hawai‘i’s fair housing law.

B. Factual and Procedural Background

 1. Factual Background

 As the founder of the Parrish Collection Kauai, Jonathan

Parrish (collectively, “Parrish”) oversees the management and

operation of high-end vacation rental properties on Kauaʻi.

 In 2006, Robert A. Fahn (“Robert”) was diagnosed with heart

disease. In August 2020, Robert and Brenda A. Fahn (“Brenda”)

(together, the “Fahns”) moved from Colorado to Kauaʻi with their

family because Kauaʻi had relatively few COVID-19 cases.

 In August 2020, the Fahns and Parrish executed a rental

agreement for a rental property in Koloa. The rental agreement

contained a provision governing weekly cleanings of the

property:

 6
 *** FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST’S HAWAI‘I REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER ***

 4. Cleaning to be scheduled every week and completed by the
 Parrish Collection Housekeeping staff and paid for by the
 tenant. This will be done hourly at $40.00 per hour and the
 number of hours dependent on property condition.

(“Weekly Cleanings Provision”)

 Shortly after moving in, Brenda emailed a Parrish employee

that she did not want housekeeping staff entering the property

based on a negative COVID-19 test result. At the time, while

not expressly requesting an accommodation based on Robert’s

heart disease, Brenda explained that Robert “has a 5-6 [percent]

mortality rate and almost 20 [percent] hospital rate (because of

his age and conditions).” Brenda ended with, “I hope you

understand wanting to delay housekeeping.”

 But on November 16, Parrish informed the Fahns that they

failed to comply with the Weekly Cleanings Provision and that

they “cannot be selective” in granting Parrish access for

repairs but not for cleaning.

 Then, on November 23, the Fahns’ doctor sent Parrish a

letter expressly requesting an accommodation through suspension

of the Weekly Cleanings Provision because of Robert’s heart

disease. On November 24, Robert also sent Parrish a letter

formally requesting a waiver of the Weekly Cleanings Provision

based on his disability.

 On November 25, the Fahns’ mainland attorney emailed

Parrish a cease-and-desist letter, asserting that the Weekly

Cleanings Provision was unenforceable and a violation of the

 7
 *** FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST’S HAWAI‘I REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER ***

Fair Housing Act of 1968. The attorney alleged that Parrish

breached the rental agreement and committed fraud, and demanded

that Parrish: (1) stop enforcing the Weekly Cleaning Provision;

(2) reduce rent by fifty percent for September, October, and

November; (3) pay $5,000.00 in reasonable attorney’s fees; and

(4) pay $10,000.00 in general damages.

 That same day, Parrish rejected the demands and countered

that the request to simply not enforce the Weekly Cleanings

Provision was not reasonable. It suggested as an alternative

that the Fahns not be present in the property during the weekly

cleanings. Parrish indicated that it followed strict industry

protocols for its cleaning crew. It noted that all of employees

are screened daily, wear full personal equipment (including

masks and gloves), and use CDC-approved cleaning products. It

stated, “this is not a negotiation. Your clients have a binding

Lease. They will comply with the terms of that Lease or it will

be terminated.”

 On November 27, Parrish terminated the Fahns’ tenancy,

effective as of November 30 and filed a complaint for summary

possession on November 30.

 On December 31, the Fahns vacated the rental property.

Parrish retained $5,471.44 of the $6,000.00 security deposit to

clean, replace, and repair the property.

 8
 *** FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST’S HAWAI‘I REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER ***

 2. HCRC Proceedings

 In December 2020, the Fahns filed a complaint with the

HCRC, alleging that Parrish “unlawfully discriminated against

[them] on the basis of disability by failing to engage in the

interactive process and by failing to provide a reasonable

accommodation for [Robert]’s disabilities.”

 Following an investigation, the HCRC “found that there was

reasonable cause to believe that unlawful discriminatory

practices had occurred.” When conciliation efforts proved

unsuccessful, the parties received notices of the right to sue

in March 2023. The Fahns exercised their right to sue in April

2023.

 3. Circuit Court Proceedings

 In July 2023, the H

U.S. Bank N.A. v Iqbal 
 2026 NY Slip Op 06344 
 October 28, 2026 
 Appellate Division, Second Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 U.S. Bank National Association, etc., appellant, 
 v 
 Miriam Iqbal, et al., respondents, et al., defendants. 

 Supreme Court of the State of New York, Appellate Division, Second Judicial Department 
 Decided on October 28, 2026 
 2024-12871, (Index No. 700383/23) 
 Mark C. Dillon, J.P. 
 Paul Wooten 
 Lourdes M. Ventura 
 Lisa S. Ottley, JJ. 

 Hinshaw & Culbertson LLP, New York, NY (Ali Degan and Schuyler B. Kraus of counsel), for appellant. 
 Binakis Law, P.C., Astoria, NY (Patrick Binakis of counsel), for respondents. 

 [*1] 
 DECISION & ORDER 
 In an action to foreclose a mortgage, the plaintiff appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Queens County (Tracy Catapano-Fox, J.), entered August 14, 2023. The order, insofar as appealed from, denied those branches of the plaintiff's motion which were for summary judgment on the complaint insofar as asserted against the defendants Miriam Iqbal and A.K.M. Wohiduzzaman, to strike those defendants' answer, and for an order of reference. 
 ORDERED that the order is affirmed insofar as appealed from, with costs. 
 In December 2005, the defendants Miriam Iqbal and A.K.M. Wohiduzzaman (hereinafter together the defendants) executed a note in the principal sum of $612,000 in favor of Option One Mortgage Corporation. The note was secured by a mortgage on certain real property located in Briarwood. 
 In January 2011, the plaintiff commenced this action against the defendants, among others, to foreclose the mortgage. The defendants timely interposed an answer. Thereafter, the plaintiff moved, inter alia, for summary judgment on the complaint insofar as asserted against the defendants, to strike the defendants' answer, and for an order of reference. The defendants opposed the motion and cross-moved for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against them, arguing, among other things, that the plaintiff lacked standing. In an order entered August 14, 2023, the Supreme Court, inter alia, denied the plaintiff's motion on the ground that the plaintiff failed to submit admissible evidence establishing the defendants' default. The plaintiff appeals. We affirm, albeit on different grounds. 
 Contrary to the plaintiff's contention, the defendants did not waive the affirmative defense of lack of standing. RPAPL 1302-a provides that, notwithstanding the provisions of CPLR 3211(e), "any objection or defense based on the plaintiff's lack of standing in a foreclosure proceeding related to a home loan . . . shall not be waived if a defendant fails to raise the objection or defense in a responsive pleading or pre-answer motion to dismiss" ( see US Bank N.A. v Blake-Hovanec , 191 AD3d 821, 825 ; GMAC Mtge., LLC v Coombs , 191 AD3d 37, 46 ). 
 Generally, a plaintiff moving for summary judgment in a mortgage foreclosure action establishes its prima facie case through the production of the mortgage, the unpaid note, and evidence of default ( see Lakeview Loan Servicing, LLC v Swanson , 231 AD3d 801 , 802; HSBC Bank USA, NA v Thoppil , 227 AD3d 1056 , 1057). Where, as here, the plaintiff's standing has been placed into issue by the defendants, the plaintiff must also prove its standing in order to be entitled to relief ( see Lakeview Loan Servicing, LLC v Swanson , 231 AD3d at 802; Wells Fargo Bank, NA v Oziel , 196 AD3d 618, 621 ). A plaintiff has standing to maintain a mortgage foreclosure action where it is the holder or assignee of the underlying note at the time the action is commenced ( see Aurora Loan Servs., LLC v Taylor , 25 NY3d 355, 361-362 ; HSBC Bank USA, N.A. v Herod , 203 AD3d 805, 807 ). "Either a written assignment of the underlying note or the physical delivery of the note prior to the commencement of the foreclosure action is sufficient to transfer the obligation, and the mortgage passes with the debt as an inseparable incident" ( U.S. Bank, N.A. v Collymore , 68 AD3d 752, 754 ). 
 Here, the plaintiff failed to establish, prima facie, that it had standing to commence this action. In support of its motion, the plaintiff asserted that it was the holder of the note at the time the action was commenced. However, the plaintiff failed to present admissible evidence establishing that it was in possession of the note, which was endorsed in blank, at the time the action was commenced. The plaintiff relied upon an affidavit of Miguel Baque, a contract management coordinator employed by PHH Mortgage Corporation, the plaintiff's loan servicer. Baque averred, in relevant part, that the plaintiff received physical delivery of the original note on December 28, 2005, and maintained possession of the note when this action was commenced. Even if Baque's affidavit was sufficient to lay a proper foundation for the admission of his employer's business records, no records were submitted therewith that establish that the plaintiff was the holder of the note when this action was commenced, and Baque did not aver that he had personal knowledge of the physical delivery of the note. Thus, Baque's averment that the plaintiff had possession of the note prior to the commencement of this action was inadmissible hearsay and insufficient to establish, prima facie, the plaintiff's standing ( see Nationstar Mortgage, LLC v Guarino , 238 AD3d 885 , 887; OneWest Bank, FSB v Fraiser , 210 AD3d 994, 995-996 ). 
 The plaintiff's remaining contentions either are improperly raised for the first time on appeal or need not be reached in light of our determination. 
 Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly denied those branches of the plaintiff's motion which were for summary judgment on the complaint insofar as asserted against the defendants, to strike the defendants' answer, and for an order of reference. 
 DILLON, J.P., WOOTEN, VENTURA and OTTLEY, JJ., concur. 
 ENTER: 
 Darrell M. Joseph 
 Clerk of the Court

U.S. Bank Natl. Assn. v Alexander 
 2026 NY Slip Op 06341 
 October 28, 2026 
 Appellate Division, Second Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 U.S. Bank National Association, etc., respondent, 
 v 
 Lavern Alexander, appellant, et al., defendants. 

 Supreme Court of the State of New York, Appellate Division, Second Judicial Department 
 Decided on October 28, 2026 
 2022-07198, 2022-07199, 2023-04511, (Index No. 13781/12) 
 Francesca E. Connolly, J.P. 
 Brathwaite Nelson 
 Barry E. Warhit 
 James P. McCormack, JJ. 

 Mobilization for Justice, Inc., New York, NY (Yara Calcano of counsel), for appellant. 
 Friedman Vartolo LLP, Garden City, NY (Stephen J. Vargas of counsel), for respondent. 

 [*1] 
 DECISION & ORDER 
 In an action to foreclose a mortgage, the defendant Lavern Alexander appeals from (1) two orders of the Supreme Court, Kings County (Lawrence Knipel, J.), both dated May 31, 2022, and (2) an order and judgment of foreclosure and sale (one paper) of the same court dated February 1, 2023. The first order, insofar as appealed from, granted those branches of the plaintiff's motion which were for leave to enter a default judgment against the defendant Lavern Alexander and for an order of reference and denied the cross-motion of the defendant Lavern Alexander, in effect, pursuant to CPLR 3215(c) to dismiss the complaint insofar as asserted against her as abandoned. The second order, insofar as appealed from, granted the same relief to the plaintiff and referred the matter to a referee to compute the amount due to the plaintiff. The order and judgment of foreclosure and sale granted the plaintiff's motion to confirm a referee's report and for a judgment of foreclosure and sale, confirmed the referee's report, and directed the sale of the subject property. 
 ORDERED that the appeals from the orders are dismissed; and it is further, 
 ORDERED that the order and judgment of foreclosure and sale is reversed, on the law, the plaintiff's motion to confirm the referee's report and for a judgment of foreclosure and sale is denied, those branches of the plaintiff's motion which were for leave to enter a default judgment against the defendant Lavern Alexander and for an order of reference are denied, the cross-motion of the defendant Lavern Alexander, in effect, pursuant to CPLR 3215(c) to dismiss the complaint insofar as asserted against her as abandoned is granted, and the orders dated May 31, 2022, are modified accordingly; and it is further, 
 ORDERED that one bill of costs is awarded to the defendant Lavern Alexander. 
 In July 2012, OneWest Bank, FSB (hereinafter OneWest), commenced this action against the defendant Lavern Alexander (hereinafter the defendant), among others, to foreclose a mortgage. The defendant failed to appear or answer the complaint. In August 2016, the plaintiff, as OneWest's alleged successor in interest, moved, inter alia, for leave to enter a default judgment [*2] against the defendant and for an order of reference. The plaintiff subsequently withdrew the motion. In an order dated December 10, 2019, the Supreme Court granted the plaintiff's unopposed motion, among other things, to vacate an order directing dismissal of the action and to restore the action to the calendar. 
 Thereafter, in September 2021, the plaintiff moved, inter alia, for leave to enter a default judgment against the defendant and for an order of reference. In January 2022, the defendant cross-moved, in effect, pursuant to CPLR 3215(c) to dismiss the complaint insofar as asserted against her as abandoned. In an order dated May 31, 2022, the Supreme Court, among other things, granted those branches of the plaintiff's motion and denied the defendant's cross-motion. In a second order also dated May 31, 2022, the court, inter alia, granted the same relief to the plaintiff and referred the matter to a referee to compute the amount due to the plaintiff. 
 In November 2022, the plaintiff moved to confirm a referee's report and for a judgment of foreclosure and sale. In an order and judgment of foreclosure and sale, the Supreme Court granted the plaintiff's motion, confirmed the referee's report, and directed the sale of the property. The defendant appeals from the two orders dated May 31, 2022, and the order and judgment of foreclosure and sale. 
 The appeals from the orders dated May 31, 2022, must be dismissed because the right of direct appeal therefrom terminated with the entry of the order and judgment of foreclosure and sale ( see Matter of Aho , 39 NY2d 241, 248 ). The issues raised on the appeal from the orders are brought up for review and have been considered on the appeal from the order and judgment of foreclosure and sale ( see CPLR 5501[a][1]; Matter of Aho , 39 NY2d at 248 ). 
 "The language of CPLR 3215(c) is not, in the first instance, discretionary, but mandatory, inasmuch as courts 'shall' dismiss claims (CPLR 3215[c]) for which default judgments are not sought within the requisite one-year period, as those claims are then deemed abandoned" ( Chase Home Fin., LLC v Dasuja , 204 AD3d 638, 639 [internal quotation marks omitted]; see Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v Hart , 247 AD3d 846 , 847-848). "In a mortgage foreclosure action, a plaintiff satisfies the requirements of CPLR 3215(c) when, within one year of a defendant's default, the plaintiff takes the preliminary step toward obtaining a default judgment of foreclosure and sale by moving . . . for an order of reference pursuant to RPAPL 1321" ( U.S. Bank N.A. v Penate , 176 AD3d 758 , 760 [internal quotation marks omitted]; see Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v Bakarey , 198 AD3d 718, 721 ). "Failure to take proceedings for entry of judgment may be excused, however, upon a showing of sufficient cause" ( Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v Charles , 186 AD3d 454, 456 [internal quotation marks omitted]). "To establish sufficient cause, the party opposing dismissal must demonstrate that it had a reasonable excuse for the delay in taking proceedings for entry of a default judgment and that it has a potentially meritorious action" ( id. [internal quotation marks omitted]; see Chase Home Fin., LLC v Morris , 235 AD3d 827 , 829). 
 Here, the plaintiff failed to establish that it took proceedings toward the entry of a default judgment against the defendant within one year of the defendant's default ( see US Bank Trust N.A. v Meyer , 244 AD3d 900 , 902; Federal Natl. Mtge. Assn. v Dauphin , 195 AD3d 696 , 697). Further, the plaintiff's proffered excuses for its failure to take proceedings toward the entry of a default judgment against the defendant within one year of the defendant's default were conclusory, unsubstantiated, and failed to account for the plaintiff's lengthy delay ( see Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. v Wercberger , 244 AD3d 1029 , 1031; US Bank Trust N.A. v Meyer , 244 AD3d at 902). 
 Since the plaintiff failed to set forth a reasonable excuse for its failure to take proceedings toward the entry of a default judgment against the defendant within one year of the defendant's default, the issue of whether it demonstrated a meritorious cause of action need not be reached ( see Chase Home Fin., LLC v Morris , 235 AD3d at 829; Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v Bakarey , 198 AD3d at 722 ). 
 Accordingly, the Supreme Court should have denied those branches of the plaintiff's motion which were for leave to enter a default judgment against the defendant and for an order of [*3] reference and granted the defendant's cross-motion, in effect, pursuant to CPLR 3215(c) to dismiss the complaint insofar as asserted against her as abandoned. 
 The plaintiff's remaining contentions are either without merit or not properly before this Court. 
 CONNOLLY, J.P., BRATHWAITE NELSON, WARHIT and MCCORMACK, JJ., concur. 
 ENTER: 
 Darrell M. Joseph 
 Clerk of the Court

U.S. Bank Natl. Assn. v Diakhate 
 2026 NY Slip Op 06342 
 October 28, 2026 
 Appellate Division, Second Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 U.S. Bank National Association, etc., respondent, 
 v 
 Khadidatou Diakhate, etc., appellant, et al., defendants. 

 Supreme Court of the State of New York, Appellate Division, Second Judicial Department 
 Decided on October 28, 2026 
 2025-08026, (Index No. 520260/16) 
 Hector D. Lasalle, P.J. 
 Cheryl E. Chambers 
 Janice A. Taylor 
 Phillip Hom, JJ. 

 Michael Kennedy Karlson, New York, NY, for appellant. 
 Atlas | Solomon LLP, New York, NY (Jordan M. Smith of counsel), for respondent. 

 [*1] 
 DECISION & ORDER 
 In an action to foreclose a mortgage, the defendant Khadidatou Diakhate appeals from an order and judgment of foreclosure and sale (one paper) of the Supreme Court, Kings County (Cenceria P. Edwards, J.), dated May 27, 2025. The order and judgment of foreclosure and sale, upon an order of the same court (Noach Dear, J.) dated June 21, 2018, inter alia, granting those branches of the plaintiff's motion which were for summary judgment on the complaint insofar as asserted against that defendant, to strike that defendant's answer, and for an order of reference, granted the plaintiff's motion to confirm a referee's report and for a judgment of foreclosure and sale, confirmed the referee's report, and directed the sale of the subject property. 
 ORDERED that the order and judgment of foreclosure and sale is affirmed, with costs. 
 On November 16, 2006, Balla Moussa Sagnan (hereinafter the borrower) executed a note in the amount of $496,080 in favor of Mortgage Lenders Network USA, Inc. (hereinafter Mortgage Lenders). The note was secured by a mortgage on certain real property located in Brooklyn. The borrower died on December 16, 2009. 
 On November 16, 2016, the plaintiff, Mortgage Lenders's purported successor in interest, commenced this action to foreclose the mortgage against, among others, the defendant Khadidatou Diakhate, as administrator of the borrower's estate (hereinafter the defendant). The plaintiff attached a copy of the note to the complaint. In her answer, the defendant alleged that the plaintiff lacked standing and failed to send her a 90-day notice pursuant to RPAPL 1304. 
 In February 2018, the plaintiff moved, inter alia, for summary judgment on the complaint insofar as asserted against the defendant, to strike the defendant's answer, and for an order of reference. In an order dated June 21, 2018, the Supreme Court, among other things, granted those branches of the plaintiff's motion. 
 In October 2019, the plaintiff moved to confirm a referee's report and for a judgment of foreclosure and sale. In support of its motion, the plaintiff submitted the report of the referee, who concluded that the borrower's estate owed a total of $799,867.30 on the note as of December 26, 2018. The referee relied upon an affidavit of Tiffany Hollis, a vice president of Ocwen Loan [*2] Servicing, LLC (hereinafter Ocwen), the plaintiff's loan servicer, who averred that she was familiar with Ocwen's records and record-keeping practices. Hollis attached to her affidavit business records, dated December 26, 2018, reflecting the amount due on the loan as of that date. In an order and judgment of foreclosure and sale dated May 27, 2025, the Supreme Court granted the plaintiff's motion, confirmed the referee's report, and directed the sale of the property. The defendant appeals. 
 "Strict compliance with RPAPL 1304 notice to the borrower or borrowers is a condition precedent to the commencement of a foreclosure action" ( Citibank, N.A. v Conti-Scheurer , 172 AD3d 17 , 20; see Tri-State III, LLC v Litkowski , 239 AD3d 911 , 912). RPAPL 1304(1) provides, in relevant part, that "at least ninety days before a lender, an assignee or a mortgage loan servicer commences legal action against the borrower, . . . including mortgage foreclosure, such lender, assignee or mortgage loan servicer shall give notice to the borrower." Contrary to the defendant's contention, the defendant, who was not a borrower, was not entitled to notice pursuant to RPAPL 1304 ( see U.S. Bank N.A. v Lloyd-Lewis , 205 AD3d 838, 839 ; HSBC Bank USA, N.A. v Shah , 185 AD3d 794, 796 ). 
 Further, the fact that the original lender was involved in bankruptcy proceedings did not affect the plaintiff's standing to foreclose. A plaintiff has standing where it is the holder or assignee of the underlying note at the time the action is commenced ( see Aurora Loan Servs., LLC v Taylor , 25 NY3d 355, 361-362 ; U.S. Bank N.A. v Hadar , 206 AD3d 688 , 689). Here, the plaintiff established its standing by attaching a copy of the properly endorsed note to the complaint ( see U.S. Bank N.A. v Hadar , 206 AD3d at 689; Deutsche Bank Trust Co. Ams. v Garrison , 147 AD3d 725, 726 ). The defendant's contentions regarding the assignments of the mortgage are without merit. A mere assignment of mortgage is irrelevant to the issue of the plaintiff's standing to foreclose, as the mortgage is not the dispositive document of title ( see U.S. Bank Trust v McGlone , 201 AD3d 999, 1001 ). 
 "The report of a referee should be confirmed whenever the findings are substantially supported by the record, and the referee has clearly defined the issues and resolved matters of credibility" ( U.S. Bank N.A. v Jong Shin , 224 AD3d 933 , 936 [internal quotation marks omitted]). "The referee's findings and recommendations are advisory only and have no binding effect on the court, which remains the ultimate arbiter of the dispute" ( U.S. Bank N.A. v Winnie Realty Group, LLC , 237 AD3d 871 , 873 [internal quotation marks omitted]). 
 Moreover, "[t]here is no requirement that a plaintiff in a foreclosure action rely on any particular set of business records to establish a prima facie case, so long as the plaintiff satisfies the admissibility requirements of CPLR 4518(a), and the records themselves actually evince the facts for which they are relied upon" ( Citigroup v Kopelowitz , 147 AD3d 1014, 1015 ; see Bank of N.Y. Mellon v Robustello , 245 AD3d 875 , 877). Here, contrary to the defendant's contention, Hollis's affidavit provided a proper foundation for the admission of Ocwen's records. 
 The defendant's remaining contentions are without merit. 
 Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly granted the plaintiff's motion to confirm the referee's report and for a judgment of foreclosure and sale. 
 LASALLE, P.J., CHAMBERS, TAYLOR and HOM, JJ., concur.

leads.caseName: U.S. Bank Natl. Assn. v. Ford
leads.court: Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the State of New York
leads.text:
U.S. Bank Natl. Assn. v Ford 
 2026 NY Slip Op 06343 
 October 28, 2026 
 Appellate Division, Second Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 U.S. Bank National Association, etc., appellant, 
 v 
 Fernando Ford, respondent, et al., defendants. 

 Supreme Court of the State of New York, Appellate Division, Second Judicial Department 
 Decided on October 28, 2026 
 2023-11212, (Index No. 513868/17) 
 Francesca E. Connolly, J.P. 
 Valerie Brathwaite Nelson 
 Barry E. Warhit 
 James P. McCormack, JJ. 

 McCalla Raymer Leibert Pierce, LLC, New York, NY (Brian P. Scibetta of counsel), for appellant. 
 David M. Harrison, Brooklyn, NY, for respondent. 

 [*1] 
 DECISION & ORDER 
 In an action to foreclose a mortgage, the plaintiff appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Kings County (Larry D. Martin, J.), dated May 23, 2023. The order, insofar as appealed from, granted that branch of the cross-motion of the defendant Fernando Ford which was for leave to renew his prior cross-motion pursuant to CPLR 3211(a)(5) to dismiss the complaint insofar as asserted against him as time-barred, which had been denied in a decision and order of this Court dated September 14, 2022, and upon renewal, granted that defendant's prior cross-motion pursuant to CPLR 3211(a)(5) to dismiss the complaint insofar as asserted against him as time-barred. 
 ORDERED that the order is affirmed insofar as appealed from, with costs. 
 In 2006, the defendant Fernando Ford (hereinafter the defendant), executed a mortgage on certain real property located in Brooklyn, securing a note in the amount of $476,000. In 2007, U.S. Bank, National Association, as trustee for the MLMI Surf Trust Series 2006-BC5 (hereinafter U.S. Bank MLMI), commenced an action against the defendant, among others, to foreclose the mortgage, in which U.S. Bank MLMI elected to call due the entire amount secured by the mortgage (hereinafter the 2007 action). The 2007 action was voluntarily discontinued in April 2008. In 2008, U.S. Bank MLMI commenced a second foreclosure action (hereinafter the 2008 action) and elected to call due the entire amount secured by the mortgage. The 2008 action was voluntarily discontinued in June 2013. 
 In 2017, the plaintiff commenced this mortgage foreclosure action against the defendant, among others. The defendant interposed an answer, in which he asserted various affirmative defenses, including the expiration of the statute of limitations. The plaintiff moved, inter alia, for summary judgment on the complaint insofar as asserted against the defendant and for an order of reference, and the defendant cross-moved pursuant to CPLR 3211(a)(5) to dismiss the complaint insofar as asserted against him as time-barred. By order dated March 14, 2019 (hereinafter the March 2019 order), the Supreme Court granted the defendant's cross-motion and denied the plaintiff's motion, in effect, as academic. On appeal by the plaintiff, this Court, in a decision and order dated September 14, 2022, among other things, reversed the March 2019 order, determining that the voluntary discontinuances of the 2007 action and the 2008 action constituted affirmative acts of revocation of the acceleration of the debt within the six-year limitations period and, thus, that the defendant had failed to establish that this action was untimely, and remitted the matter to the Supreme Court for a determination of the plaintiff's motion on the merits ( see U.S. Bank N.A. v Ford , 208 AD3d 1199, 1201 ). 
 Following the enactment of the Foreclosure Abuse Prevention Act (FAPA) (L 2022, ch 821 [eff Dec. 30, 2022]), the defendant cross-moved, inter alia, for leave to renew his prior cross-motion pursuant to CPLR 3211(a)(5) to dismiss the complaint insofar as asserted against him as time-barred. In support, the defendant argued that FAPA constituted a change in the law that would alter the prior determination and that the voluntary discontinuances of the 2007 action and the 2008 action failed to revive or reset the statute of limitations ( see id. § 203[h]). In an order dated May 23, 2023, the Supreme Court, among other things, granted that branch of the defendant's motion which was for leave to renew, and upon renewal, granted the defendant's prior cross-motion. The plaintiff appeals. 
 A motion for leave to renew is the appropriate vehicle for seeking relief from a prior order based on a change in the law ( see U.S. Bank Trust, N.A. v Miele , 243 AD3d 718 , 719; Opalinski v City of New York , 205 AD3d 917 , 919). "A motion for leave to renew pursuant to CPLR 2221(e)(2) based upon a change in the law that would change the prior determination must be made, absent circumstances set forth in CPLR 5015, before the time to appeal the final judgment has expired" ( Ditech Fin., LLC v Naidu , 244 AD3d 1067 , 1068 [alteration and internal quotation marks omitted]; see Wilmington Sav. Fund Socy., FSB v Sposato , 244 AD3d 790 , 792). Contrary to the plaintiff's contention, as a judgment of foreclosure and sale had not yet been entered in this action, that branch of the defendant's motion which was for leave to renew was not untimely ( see Ditech Fin., LLC v Naidu , 244 AD3d at 1069). 
 An action to foreclose a mortgage is governed by a six-year statute of limitations ( see CPLR 213[4]). Even if the mortgage is payable in installments, once a mortgage debt is accelerated, the entire amount is due and the statute of limitations begins to run on the entire debt ( see Citimortgage, Inc. v Gunn , 234 AD3d 922 , 923; Pryce v U.S. Bank, N.A. , 226 AD3d 711 , 712). The entire mortgage debt will be deemed to have been accelerated, as relevant here, by the commencement of a mortgage foreclosure action in which the complaint seeks payment of the full outstanding loan balance ( see Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v Mayer , 244 AD3d 686 , 688; U.S. Bank N.A. v Connor , 204 AD3d 861, 863 ). CPLR 203(h), as amended by FAPA (L 2022, ch 821, § 4), provides that "[o]nce a cause of action upon an instrument described in [CPLR 213(4)] has accrued, no party may, in form or effect, unilaterally waive, postpone, cancel, toll, revive, or reset the accrual thereof, or otherwise purport to effect a unilateral extension of the limitations period prescribed by law to commence an action and to interpose the claim, unless expressly prescribed by statute." 
 Moreover, as relevant to this appeal, FAPA amended CPLR 3217(e) to provide that "[i]n any action on an instrument described under [CPLR 213(4)], the voluntary discontinuance of such action, whether on motion, order, stipulation or by notice, shall not, in form or effect, waive, postpone, cancel, toll, extend, revive or reset the limitations period to commence an action and to interpose a claim, unless expressly prescribed by statute" ( see L 2022, ch 821, § 8; see also 97 Lyman Ave., LLC v MTGLQ Invs., L.P. , 233 AD3d 1038 , 1041). Here, it is undisputed that U.S. Bank MLMI elected to call due the entire balance of the mortgage debt in the complaint in the 2007 action, the instant action was commenced more than six years later, and the voluntary discontinuances of the 2007 action and the 2008 action did not serve to reset or revive the statute of limitations ( see CPLR 203[h]; 3217[e]; FV-1, Inc. v Palaguachi , 234 AD3d 818 , 821). 
 The plaintiff contends that the defendant's motion, inter alia, for leave to renew was procedurally improper, as the Supreme Court was without authority to vacate or modify the decision and order of this Court dated September 14, 2022. The plaintiff's contention is without merit. 
 An appellate court's resolution of an issue on a prior appeal constitutes the law of the case and is binding on the Supreme Court, as well as on the appellate court ( see US Bank, N.A. v Kandra , 244 AD3d 902 , 904; New York Tile Wholesale Corp. v Thomas Fatato Realty Corp. , 205 AD3d 727 , 727). The doctrine of the law of the case operates to foreclose reexamination of the issue absent a showing of new factual circumstances, additional relevant evidence, or a change in the law that would warrant reconsideration of the issue ( see U.S. Bank Trust, N.A. v Miele , 243 AD3d at 720; Frankson v Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp. , 67 AD3d 213, 218 ). 
 Here, on the prior appeal, while this Court determined that the defendant had failed to establish that the action was barred by the six-year statute of limitations, the defendant [*2] demonstrated a subsequent change in the law that would warrant reconsideration of the issue of whether the action was untimely ( see U.S. Bank Trust, N.A. v Miele , 243 AD3d at 720). Consequently, that branch of the defendant's motion which was for leave to renew, based on a change in the law, was not improper and was properly considered by the Supreme Court. 
 The plaintiff's contentions challenging FAPA's retroactive application and constitutionality are without merit ( see Van Dyke v U.S. Bank, N.A. , 45 NY3d 461 ; Article 13 LLC v Ponce De Leon Fed. Bank , 45 NY3d 441 ; Citimortgage, Inc. v Gunn , 234 AD3d at 924; FV-1, Inc. v Palaguachi , 234 AD3d at 822; Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v Dagrin , 233 AD3d 1065 , 1067). 
 Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly granted that branch of the defendant's motion which was for leave to renew his prior cross-motion pursuant to CPLR 3211(a)(5) to dismiss the complaint insofar as asserted against him as time-barred and upon renewal, granted the defendant's prior cross-motion. 
 CONNOLLY, J.P., BRATHWAITE NELSON, WARHIT and MCCORMACK, JJ., concur. 
 ENTER: 
 Darrell M. Joseph 
 Clerk of the Court

leads.caseName: Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. v. Boyd
leads.court: Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the State of New York
leads.text:
Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. v Boyd 
 2026 NY Slip Op 06347 
 October 28, 2026 
 Appellate Division, Second Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 Wells Fargo Bank, N.A., respondent, 
 v 
 Lorna Boyd, appellant, et al., defendants. 

 Supreme Court of the State of New York, Appellate Division, Second Judicial Department 
 Decided on October 28, 2026 
 2023-10370, (Index No. 700862/13) 
 Francesca E. Connolly, J.P. 
 Valerie Brathwaite Nelson 
 Barry E. Warhit 
 James P. McCormack, JJ. 

 Gunilla Perez-Faringer, White Plains, NY, for appellant. 
 Frenkel Lambert Weiss Weisman & Gordon, LLP (Reed Smith LLP, New York, NY [Michael V. Margarella and Andrew B. Messite], of counsel), for respondent. 

 [*1] 
 DECISION & ORDER 
 In an action to foreclose a mortgage, the defendant Lorna Boyd appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Queens County (Timothy J. Dufficy, J.), entered June 21, 2023. The order denied the motion of the defendant Lorna Boyd, and the separate motion of the defendant Lorna Boyd and nonparty Dario Charles, in effect, to vacate an order and judgment of foreclosure and sale (one paper) of the same court entered October 17, 2017, upon the failure of the defendant Lorna Boyd to answer the complaint and to set aside the foreclosure sale of the subject property, and pursuant to CPLR 3211(a)(8) to dismiss the complaint insofar as asserted against the defendant Lorna Boyd for lack of personal jurisdiction. 
 ORDERED that the order is affirmed, with costs. 
 In March 2013, the plaintiff commenced this mortgage foreclosure action against the defendant Lorna Boyd (hereinafter the defendant), among others. The defendant failed to timely answer the complaint. In October 2014, the plaintiff moved, inter alia, for leave to enter a default judgment against the defendant and for an order of reference. The defendant requested an adjournment of the return date of the motion, and the defendant and the plaintiff entered into a stipulation adjourning the motion. In an order dated September 28, 2016, the Supreme Court, among other things, granted the plaintiff's unopposed motion and appointed a referee to compute the amount due to the plaintiff. 
 In December 2016, the plaintiff moved to confirm the referee's report and for a judgment of foreclosure and sale. The defendant opposed the motion. In December 2016, the defendant attempted to serve an answer, which the plaintiff rejected as untimely. In January 2017, the defendant moved pursuant to CPLR 3211(a)(8) to dismiss the complaint insofar as asserted against her for lack of personal jurisdiction. In an order dated April 17, 2017, the Supreme Court granted the plaintiff's motion to confirm the referee's report and for a judgment of foreclosure and sale, and in an order dated May 16, 2017, the court denied the defendant's motion to dismiss the complaint insofar as asserted against her. 
 An order and judgment of foreclosure and sale was entered on October 17, 2017, and the property was sold to a third party at a foreclosure sale held on April 9, 2019. 
 Thereafter, in 2022, the defendant moved, and the defendant and nonparty Dario Charles separately moved, in effect, to vacate the order and judgment of foreclosure and sale and to set aside the foreclosure sale, and pursuant to CPLR 3211(a)(8) to dismiss the complaint insofar as asserted against the defendant for lack of personal jurisdiction. In an order entered June 21, 2023, the Supreme Court denied the motions. The defendant appeals. 
 The order dated May 16, 2017, from which the defendant did not appeal, was the law of the case with respect to the arguments raised by the defendant regarding lack of personal jurisdiction ( see Citimortgage, Inc. v Pierce , 203 AD3d 878, 880 ). Although this Court is not bound by the Supreme Court's prior determination pursuant to the doctrine of law of the case and we may consider the defendant's contentions, the defendant's contentions regarding lack of personal jurisdiction are without merit ( see 23-35 Bridge St., LLC v Excel Auto. Tech Ctr., Inc. , 245 AD3d 870 , 871; Citimortgage, Inc. v Pierce , 203 AD3d at 880 ). The defendant waived the defense of lack of personal jurisdiction by actively litigating the action before the Supreme Court without first asserting an objection to jurisdiction ( see Bank of N.Y. Mellon v Gaston , 241 AD3d 1242 , 1245; BAC Home Loans Servicing, L.P. v Davis , 241 AD3d 1231 , 1232; U.S. Bank Trust N.A. v Gordon , 236 AD3d 705 , 706-707). 
 The defendant's remaining contentions are not properly before this Court. 
 Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly denied the defendant's motion, and the separate motion of the defendant and Charles, in effect, to vacate the order and judgment of foreclosure and sale and to set aside the foreclosure sale, and pursuant to CPLR 3211(a)(8) to dismiss the complaint insofar as asserted against the defendant for lack of personal jurisdiction. 
 CONNOLLY, J.P., BRATHWAITE NELSON, WARHIT and MCCORMACK, JJ., concur. 
 ENTER: 
 Darrell M. Joseph 
 Clerk of the Court

leads.caseName: Wilmington Sav. Fund Socy., FSB v. Leder
leads.court: Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the State of New York
leads.text:
Wilmington Sav. Fund Socy., FSB v Leder 
 2026 NY Slip Op 06349 
 October 28, 2026 
 Appellate Division, Second Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 Wilmington Savings Fund Society, FSB, etc., respondent, 
 v 
 Eric Leder, etc., appellant, et al., defendants. 

 Supreme Court of the State of New York, Appellate Division, Second Judicial Department 
 Decided on October 28, 2026 
 2023-10584, (Index No. 617481/20) 
 Lara J. Genovesi, J.P. 
 Deborah A. Dowling 
 Lillian Wan 
 Susan Quirk, JJ. 

 Irwin Popkin, Melville, NY, for appellant. 
 Hinshaw & Culbertson LLP, New York, NY (Sarah J. Greenberg of counsel), for respondent. 

 [*1] 
 DECISION & ORDER 
 In an action to foreclose a mortgage, the defendant Eric Leder appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Suffolk County (Robert F. Quinlan, J.), dated September 14, 2023. The order, insofar as appealed from, granted those branches of the plaintiff's renewed motion which were for summary judgment on the complaint insofar as asserted against that defendant and for an order of reference, and denied that defendant's cross-motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against him. 
 ORDERED that the order is affirmed insofar as appealed from, with costs. 
 In October 2020, the plaintiff commenced the instant action against, among others, the defendant Eric Leder (hereinafter the defendant). The defendant served an answer raising various affirmative defenses, including the plaintiff's failure to comply with the pre-litigation notice requirements of RPAPL 1304 and paragraph 22 of the mortgage agreement. 
 In August 2023, the plaintiff made a renewed motion, inter alia, for summary judgment on the complaint insofar as asserted against the defendant and for an order of reference. The defendant opposed the renewed motion and cross-moved for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against him. In an order dated September 14, 2023, the Supreme Court, among other things, granted those branches of the plaintiff's renewed motion and denied the defendant's cross-motion. The defendant appeals. 
 RPAPL 1304(1) provides that "at least ninety days before a lender, an assignee or a mortgage loan servicer commences legal action against the borrower, . . . including mortgage foreclosure, such lender, assignee or mortgage loan servicer shall give notice to the borrower." RPAPL 1304(2) requires that "[t]he notices required by this section shall be sent by the lender, assignee or mortgage loan servicer in a separate envelope from any other mailing or notice." Here, included in the envelope with the RPAPL 1304 notice was a second notice providing information of additional rights the borrower might have in connection with certain bankruptcy proceedings. Since the information concerning a debtor's rights in bankruptcy was relevant to avoiding foreclosure and was not false or misleading, the inclusion of this information with the 90-day notice [*2] did not violate the "separate envelope" requirement of RPAPL 1304(2) ( see Bank of Am., N.A. v Kessler , 39 NY3d 317 , 328; Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v Clark , 246 AD3d 1029 ; Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. v Smart , 234 AD3d 1016 , 1018; Bank of Am., N.A. v Gonzalez , 219 AD3d 433, 435 ). 
 Additionally, the loan servicer was authorized to provide the 90-day notice pursuant to RPAPL 1304 and the notice of default required under the terms of the mortgage agreement in the manner that it did. A limited power of attorney authorized the loan servicer, Select Portfolio Services, Inc. (hereinafter SPS), as the attorney-in-fact of the "Owner Trustee," i.e., the plaintiff, to act "in the Trust's name, place and stead" and "for the Owner Trustee's benefit," in connection with certain "enumerated transactions." These "enumerated transactions" included, with respect to the foreclosure of the subject mortgage, "the preparation and filing of notices of default," and "the preparation and execution of such other documents and performance [of] such other actions as may be necessary under the terms of the Mortgage, Deed of Trust or state law to expeditiously complete said transactions." Contrary to the defendant's contention, in sending out the statutorily required 90-day notice pursuant to RPAPL 1304 and contractually required notice of default pursuant to the mortgage agreement, SPS was acting "in the Trust's name, place and stead," which it named in the notice, and "for the Owner Trustee's benefit," as authorized by the limited power of attorney. Moreover, contrary to the defendant's contention, there is no requirement in the limited power of attorney that the notices sent thereunder by SPS expressly name the "Owner Trustee"/plaintiff. 
 The parties' remaining contentions are either without merit or improperly raised for the first time on this appeal. 
 GENOVESI, J.P., DOWLING, WAN and QUIRK, JJ., concur.

 Darrell M. Joseph 
 Clerk of the Court

leads.caseName: SUN BRITE SERVICES, INC. v. KRISTINA GUTIERREZ
leads.text:
FOURTH DIVISION
MCFADDEN, P. J.,
WATKINS and PADGETT, JJ.
NOTICE: Motions for reconsideration must be
received no later than 4:30 pm on the 10th day after
the decision was issued to be deemed timely filed. 
https://www.gaappeals.gov/rules
October 28, 2026
In the Court of Appeals of Georgia
A26A0912. SUN BRITE SERVICES, INC. v. GUTIERREZ et al.
MCFADDEN, Presiding Judge.
Norbert Goodrum, an employee of appellant Sun Brite Services, Inc., struck
and killed a pedestrian while he was driving his personal car. Kristina Gutierrez, the
mother of the pedestrian’s child, and Hillary B. Cranford1, the administrator of his
estate (together, “the plaintiffs”), filed this lawsuit against Goodrum and Sun Brite,
alleging that Sun Brite was vicariously liable for Goodrum’s negligence because
Goodrum was acting in the course and scope of his employment at the time of the fatal
collision. 
1 In the record, Cranford’s first name is spelled as both “Hilary” and
“Hillary.” 
Sun Brite appeals from two interlocutory orders: an order imposing spoliation
sanctions and an order denying its motion for summary judgment. At the hearing on
those motions, the parties argued but did not present evidence. Consequently, the
summary judgment standard for disputes of fact obtained as to both motions. The trial
court did not employ that standard on the spoliation issue. So we vacate the trial
court’s order granting the plaintiffs’ motion for spoliation sanctions. In light of this
holding, we also vacate the order denying Sun Brite’s motion for summary judgment.
We remand the case for further proceedings not inconsistent with this opinion.2 
1. Background
Sun Brite is a commercial and industrial pressure washing company. Jeff
Robison is Sun Brite’s sole owner and CEO, and Goodrum is an employee. 
At the time of the fatal collision, Sun Brite employees drove their personal cars
to the Sun Brite facility; picked up their assigned, printed work order from a job board
at the office; and then retrieved the equipment needed to complete the job, including
a company-owned truck equipped with a pressure washer, which they would drive to
2 Oral argument was held in this case on April 28, 2026, and is archived on the
court’s website. See Court of Appeals of Georgia, Oral Argument, Case No.
A26A0912 (April 28, 2026), available at https://vimeo.com/1188466885.
2
the job site. Sun Brite employees communicated internally using Slack, “a cloud-based
team communication platform.” https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slack_(software)
(retrieved September 16, 2026), and by text messages and telephone calls. 
 Some of Sun Brite’s clients are shopping centers, which must be cleaned when
they are closed at night, so Robison allows his employees flexibility in their hours; as
long as his employees complete the job by 6 or 7 in the morning, they may begin the
work when they prefer. 
Goodrum worked as a senior technician for Sun Brite. He was a night-shift
employee, but some evidence showed that some days in the weeks before the collision,
he began work earlier than the typical night-shift start time of between 9 p.m. and 10
p.m. If a particular job allowed Goodrum to begin work earlier than ususal, Robinson
would inform him by text message or phone call. 
On the night of the fatal collision, October 25, 2021, Goodrum was driving his
personal car from his residence to the Sun Brite facility in order to pick up a pressure-
washing truck to use at a job site. He was wearing a Sun Brite uniform and had a safety
vest in a backpack in his car. He did not see the pedestrian in the road, and struck him,
killing him. 
3
On December 17, 2021, Gutierrez sent Sun Brite a letter, requesting that it 
maintain all records relating to the injuries and death of [the pedestrian].
This request includes all communications with Norbert Goodrum and all
scheduling documents for Norbert Goodrum’s employment for the two
weeks before and after this collision, all photographs, videos, reports,
and any other documentation relating to this collision, and Norbert
Goodrum’s employment status on the date of the collision. 
After the plaintiffs filed this lawsuit, Sun Brite filed a motion for summary
judgment and the plaintiffs filed a motion for spoliation sanctions. The trial court held
a hearing on the motions, at which the parties argued but did not present evidence,
and then entered an order denying Sun Brite’s motion for summary judgment and
granting the plaintiffs’ motion for spoliation sanctions. We granted Sun Brite’s
application for interlocutory appeal, and this appeal followed. 
2. Spoliation
“Spoliation refers to the destruction or failure to preserve evidence that is
necessary to contemplated or pending litigation. AMLI Residential Properties v. Ga.
Power Co., 293 Ga. App. 358, 361 (1) (667 SE2d 150) (2008) (citation modified). See
also OCGA § 24-14-22. Generally, the trial court 
4
has wide discretion in adjudicating spoliation issues, and such discretion
will not be disturbed absent abuse. Where a trial court makes findings of
fact in ruling on a spoliation claim, this [c]ourt will uphold those findings
if there is any evidence to support them, i.e., unless they are clearly
erroneous. When the trial court imposes a sanction that is inconsistent
with its factual findings, the trial court abuses its discretion.
Cowan Systems v. Collier, 361 Ga. App. 823, 823-824 (865 SE2d 619) (2021) (citation
modified). 
But here, there has not been an evidentiary hearing. So the trial court was
required to construe the evidence “under the standard applicable to a motion for
summary judgment, and as the part[y] opposing the motion, [Sun Brite is] entitled to
have the evidence in the record viewed in the light most favorable to [it] and to have
all reasonable inferences from the evidence drawn in [its] favor.” UPS of Am. v.
Whitlock, 366 Ga. App. 542, 555(2)(a) (883 SE2d 556) (2023) (citation modified).
Absent an evidentiary hearing, the court may not decide credibility issues. Id. at 556-
57(2)(a)(i). 
Sun Brite argues that the trial court applied the wrong legal standard when it
found that spoliation had occurred. We agree.
5
We begin by identifying the evidence plaintiffs claimed they had asked Sun Brite
to preserve but that it had not preserved. About that the plaintiffs were not precise.
See Cowan Systems, 361 Ga. App. at 825 n.2 (reviewing motion for sanctions to
determine what evidence the movant alleged was spoliated); Whitlock, 366 Ga. App.
at 555(2)(a) (“the way in which the plaintiff[ ] raised ... the spoliation claim[ ] against
the defendant[ ] is important to our review of the issue before us”). At one point in
the motion, the plaintiffs alleged that Sun Brite failed to preserve its
“communications” with Goodrum, without defining what they meant by
“communications.” At another point they alleged specifically that Sun Brite had not
preserved text messages and records of telephone calls between Sun Brite employees
and Goodrum “in the week leading up to the collision.” They also alleged that Sun
Brite failed to preserve communications with Goodrum “in the two weeks leading up
to” the collision. They elsewhere focused on Sun Brite’s communications with
Goodrum while he was driving to work on the night of the fatal collision and the calls
and text massages “in the hours leading up to the collision.” As to all of these
communications, however, the plaintiffs alleged that Sun Brite failed to preserve the
evidence because Robison replaced his cellular telephone, an undisputed fact. 
6
From this we conclude that in their motion the plaintiffs contended that the
evidence they requested Sun Brite to retain but that Sun Brite did not preserve is the
text messages and records of telephone calls between Goodrum and Robison as
reflected on Robison’s replaced cellular telephone in the two weeks leading up to the
collision and on the date of the collision itself, or from October 11, 2021, through
October 25, 2021.3 
The trial court found as fact, see In re Estate of Flournoy, 373 Ga. App. 133,
138(2) (907 SE2d 724) (2024), that Sun Brite “spoliated the requested records,”
without specifying which particular records. So we must conclude that the trial court
found that Sun Brite spoliated the “requested records” described above: the text
messages and records of telephone calls between Goodrum and Robison, as reflected
on Robison’s replaced telephone, in the two weeks leading up to the collision and on
the date of the collision itself. 
3 In their appellees’ brief, the plaintiffs also argue about Sun Brite’s failure to
preserve Goodrum’s cellular telephone, Slack messages, and work orders. But they
did not make these arguments in their motion for spoliation sanctions, so these
categories of evidence were not before the trial court when he ruled on the spoliation
sanctions motion.
7
We hold that the evidence supports the trial court’s factual finding of spoliation
only in part. Even when viewing the evidence in Sun Brite’s favor, as the trial court
was required to do given the procedural posture of this case, the evidence is
undisputed that Sun Brite failed to preserve text messages and records of telephone
calls between Goodrum and Robison, as documented on Robison’s replaced
telephone, for the period of October 11, 2021, through October 24, 2021. Robison
testified in his deposition that he and Goodrum would have communicated, including
about job start times, by text message or telephone call in this time period. 
But when viewed in Sun Brite’s favor, the evidence does not suppport a finding
that Sun Brite failed to preserve text messages and records of telephone calls between
Goodrum and Robison on the day of the fatal collision, at least before the collision
occurred.4 Goodrum testified in his deposition that on that day, he did not speak or
text with anyone from Sun Brite before the collision occurred. Robison also testified
in his deposition that he would not have communicated with Goodrum on that day
before the collision occurred. And although Robison also testified in his deposition
4 The evidence is undisputed that Goodrum and Robison communicated by
telephone shortly after the collision, but the plaintiffs did not argue about post-
collision communications in their sanctions motion. 
8
that, most likely, that day Goodrum would have received a text message or a phone
call from him or the operations manager informing him what time to begin work, he
clarified that such information “could have been communicated days before in a
conversation.” The trial court could not make a credibility determination, since it did
not hold an evidentiary hearing, and was required to view this testimony in the light
most favorable to Sun Brite. Properly viewed, the evidence does not show that there
were text messages and records of telephone calls between Goodrum and Robison on
the day of the fatal collision before the collision occurred. “It is axiomatic that in order
for there to be spoliation, the evidence in question must have existed. ...” Sentry Select
Ins. Co. v. Treadwell, 318 Ga. App. 844, 847(2)(c) (734 SE2d 818) (2012). So when
viewed in favor of Sun Brite, the evidence does not support the trial court’s factual
finding that Sun Brite spoliated text messages and records of telephone calls between
Goodrum and Robison on the day of the fatal collision before the collision occurred. 
(b) Sanction
Once the trial court has determined that spoliation occurred, the court should
weigh five factors to determine an appropriate sanction: 
(1) whether the party seeking sanctions was prejudiced as a result of the
destroyed evidence; (2) whether the prejudice could be cured; (3) the
9
practical importance of the evidence; (4) whether the destroying party
acted in good or bad faith; and (5) the potential for abuse if any expert
testimony about the destroyed evidence was not excluded.5
Whitlock, 366 Ga. App. at 555(2)(a) (citation modified). “[W]e will not disturb a trial
court’s imposition of sanc
