leads.text:
NOTICE: This opinion is subject to motions for rehearing under Rule 22 as well
as formal revision before publication in the New Hampshire Reports. Readers
are requested to notify the Reporter, Supreme Court of New Hampshire, One
Charles Doe Drive, Concord, New Hampshire 03301, of any editorial errors in
order that corrections may be made before the opinion goes to press. Errors
may be reported by email at the following address: reporter@courts.state.nh.us.
Opinions are available on the Internet by 9:00 a.m. on the morning of their
release. The direct address of the court’s home page is:
https://www.courts.nh.gov/our-courts/supreme-court.

 THE SUPREME COURT OF NEW HAMPSHIRE

 ___________________________

New Hampshire Lottery and Gaming Commission
Case Nos. 2024-0722
 2024-0723
Citation: Appeal of Win Win Win, LLC, 2026 N.H. 40

 APPEAL OF WIN WIN WIN, LLC, d/b/a CONCORD CASINO & a.
 (New Hampshire Lottery and Gaming Commission)

 Argued: February 10, 2026
 Opinion Issued: October 28, 2026

 Nixon Peabody LLP, of Manchester (Mark T. Knights on the brief), and
Simpson Thacher & Bartlett LLP, of Boston, Massachusetts (Zachary R. Hafer
and Adam M. Katz on the brief, and Adam M. Katz orally), for the petitioners.

 John M. Formella, attorney general, and Anthony J. Galdieri, solicitor
general (Mary A. Triick, senior assistant attorney general, on the brief and
orally), for the New Hampshire Lottery and Gaming Commission.

 PER CURIAM.

 [¶1] In this consolidated appeal, the petitioners, Win Win Win, LLC d/b/a
Concord Casino (WWW) and Anthony M. Sanborn, challenge orders from the
respondent, the New Hampshire Lottery and Gaming Commission
(Commission), rendered in separate but related proceedings. From the first
proceeding, the petitioners appeal the Commission’s orders denying their
 request to extend the deadline to sell WWW to a Commission-approved buyer
pursuant to the terms of a forced-sale order. From the second proceeding, they
appeal the Commission’s order denying a prospective buyer’s applications for
certain gaming licenses for himself and WWW. We affirm.

 I. Background

 [¶2] The record supports the following facts. In 2018, WWW received
licenses to operate a charitable gaming facility. In 2021, the Commission
conducted a regularly scheduled audit of WWW that revealed several instances
of inaccurate or insufficient financial documentation. In 2022, the
Commission conducted a subsequent audit that raised concerns about WWW’s
application for, and use of, an Economic Injury Disaster Loan (EID loan) from
the United States Small Business Administration.

 [¶3] In 2023, the Commission and the Attorney General (AG) conducted a
“suitability review” of Sanborn and WWW to determine if they should remain
involved with charitable gaming in New Hampshire. See RSA 287-D:11, II-III
(2016 & Supp. 2023) (providing that any person or entity holding a facilities or
game operator employer license shall file a written statement every five years,
and the Commission and the AG shall investigate the license holder to
determine if they are suitable to be associated with charitable gaming). After
that review, the Commission and the AG determined that neither Sanborn nor
WWW was suitable to be associated with charitable gaming because there was
credible evidence that Sanborn and WWW unlawfully obtained the EID loan
and that Sanborn used the proceeds from that loan for purchases not
permitted by the loan.

 [¶4] Following that determination, the Commission initiated an
administrative action against WWW to suspend or revoke its licenses. See RSA
287-D:23, III (Supp. 2023) (“The lottery commission may suspend or revoke the
license of any licensee who violates any provision of this chapter or for just
cause shown.”); RSA 287-D:2 (2016) (“The lottery commission, with the
assistance of the attorney general and the chief of police of any city or town
where games of chance are held, shall administer and enforce the provisions of
this chapter.”); see also RSA 287-D:11, III(a) (providing that if the Commission
and the AG determine that the license holder is unsuitable to be associated
with charitable gaming, that person or entity shall not continue to hold a
license). After a hearing, the Commission determined that WWW’s conduct
violated RSA chapter 287-D and issued an order suspending WWW’s licenses
to operate as a gaming facility (the forced-sale order). The order further
provided that if WWW was not sold to a Commission-approved buyer within six
months, then WWW’s license suspension would be converted into a revocation.
The order permitted WWW to request a three-month extension in order to
complete a sale if one was pending at the end of the six-month period.

 2
  [¶5] The petitioners found a willing buyer. Sanborn and the buyer
entered into a purchase and sale agreement for the sale of WWW. The
purchase and sale agreement provided that the buyer was not required to
complete the transaction until he obtained a games operator employer license
and games of chance facility license for WWW. See RSA 287-D:7-:8 (Supp.
2023). The buyer applied to the Commission for those licenses.

 [¶6] As the deadline to complete the sale under the terms of the forced-
sale order approached, the Commission had yet to complete its review of the
license applications. Specifically, the parties were waiting for the Commission
and the AG to determine whether the buyer and WWW were suitable to be
associated with charitable gaming. See RSA 287-D:11, III(a). The petitioners
moved to extend the deadline to sell WWW pursuant to the forced-sale order
until fifteen days after the Commission and the AG completed the suitability
review. The Commission denied the motion but stayed the portion of the
forced-sale order that would convert the suspension of WWW’s licenses into a
revocation (the extension of time order). The stay was effective until thirty days
after the Commission issued a notice of decision on any motion for rehearing
on the extension of time order. The petitioners moved for rehearing.

 [¶7] While that motion was pending, by letter dated October 30, 2024,
the Commission informed the buyer of the results of the suitability review. The
Commission stated that its investigator raised “serious concerns about [the
buyer’s] application and the materials submitted” and that it forwarded its
report on the matter to the AG’s office. The AG’s office reviewed the application
and materials and concluded that “[the buyer] and WWW are unsuitable to be
associated with charitable gaming in New Hampshire” on two grounds: first,
“Mr. Sanborn’s continued involvement with and connection to WWW” after the
closing of the proposed transaction and, second, the buyer’s failure “to
demonstrate the financial capacity” to meet his obligations under the proposed
transaction. The Commission stated in its letter, “in light of our initial
concerns and the Attorney General’s Office’s determination, the Lottery
Commission must issue a denial of the application at this time.” The buyer
and the petitioners unsuccessfully moved for rehearing.

 [¶8] On November 25, 2024, the Commission issued an order in which it
determined that the pending filings regarding the petitioners’ motion for an
extension of time were moot because the petitioners had received the relief they
requested, i.e., WWW’s licenses were not revoked until more than fifteen days
after the Commission and the AG completed the suitability review. The
petitioners filed a motion requesting clarification as to whether the mootness
order was effective immediately — meaning that the Commission could revoke
WWW’s licenses — and requesting that the mootness order be stayed. The
Commission issued an order clarifying that the mootness order was effective
immediately and denying WWW’s request to stay the order. On November 26,

 3
 2024, the Commission issued an order revoking WWW’s games operator
employer license and games of chance facility license. These appeals followed.

 II. Analysis

 [¶9] On appeal, the petitioners challenge the Commission’s orders
denying: (1) the license applications; and (2) their request for an extension of
time to comply with the forced-sale order. We address these challenges in
turn.

 A. License Applications

 [¶10] The petitioners challenge the Commission’s order denying the
license applications. The Commission argues that the petitioners lack
standing. The petitioners counter that they have suffered an injury resulting
from the denial of the license applications sufficient to confer standing. We
hold that the petitioners have standing to appeal the Commission’s order.

 [¶11] Standing implicates the court’s subject matter jurisdiction and it
may be raised at any time in a proceeding. See Appeal of Stonyfield Farm, 159
N.H. 227, 231 (2009). Subject matter jurisdiction is jurisdiction over the
nature of the case and the type of relief sought; it is the extent to which a court
can rule on the conduct of persons or the status of things. Lonergan v. Town
of Sanbornton, 175 N.H. 772, 775 (2023). In other words, it is a tribunal’s
authority to adjudicate the type of controversy involved in the action. Id. A
tribunal lacks power to hear or determine a case that concerns subject matter
over which it has no jurisdiction. Id. Thus, in the absence of subject matter
jurisdiction, a tribunal’s order is void and the appellate tribunal acquires no
jurisdiction over the merits upon appeal. Id.

 [¶12] The Commission’s order denying the license applications was
issued pursuant to RSA 287-D:11, III(a). This appeal is therefore governed by
RSA chapter 541. See RSA 287-D:24 (2016). Accordingly, the requirements to
establish standing to appeal the Commission’s decision are set forth by statute.
See RSA 541:3, :4, :6 (2021). To establish standing to appeal an administrative
agency decision under RSA chapter 541, a party must demonstrate that its
rights may be “directly affected” by the decision, or in other words, that it has
suffered or will suffer an injury in fact. Appeal of Union Tel. Co., 160 N.H. 309,
313 (2010); Appeal of Richards, 134 N.H. 148, 154 (1991); see also RSA 541:3,
:4. To show an injury in fact, the alleged harm cannot be speculative. Appeal
of N.H. Right to Life, 166 N.H. 308, 314 (2014). “Another way of formulating
the injury in fact requirement is that no individual or group of individuals has
standing to appeal when the alleged injury caused by an administrative
agency’s action affects the public in general.” Id. (quotations and brackets
omitted). Similarly, standing to challenge an administrative agency’s action
cannot be based upon a mere interest in a problem. See id.

 4
  [¶13] The issue before the Commission was approval of the license
applications. The buyer filed applications for game operator employer licenses
and games of chance facility licenses for himself and WWW. Accordingly, the
buyer and WWW were directly affected by the decision because they both, as a
direct result of the Commission’s decision, were denied the licenses. Cf.
Stonyfield Farm, 159 N.H. at 231 (explaining that a party lacked standing in an
RSA chapter 541 appeal because it had not suffered an “immediate or direct
injury”); Richards, 134 N.H. at 154-57. Because WWW was directly affected by
the Commission’s order and timely filed a motion for rehearing, WWW has RSA
chapter 541 standing to appeal the Commission’s order. See RSA 541:3
(providing that “any person directly affected” by an order or decision of the
Commission may apply for rehearing within thirty days); RSA 541:4 (providing
that no appeal from any order or decision of the Commission shall be taken
“unless the appellant shall have made application for rehearing as herein
provided”); RSA 541:6.

 [¶14] We also conclude that Sanborn has standing to appeal the
Commission’s decision. Sanborn and the buyer had a signed purchase and
sale agreement for the sale of WWW. That sale was contingent upon the buyer
and WWW receiving the licens

leads.caseName: Dave Armitage, Ardean Armitage v. Brandaan DeGroot, Melissa DeGroot
leads.text:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF THE STATE OF IDAHO

 Docket No. 53115

 DAVE and ARDEAN ARMITAGE, husband )
 and wife, )
 )
 Plaintiffs-Counterdefendants- )
 Respondents, )
 September 2026 Term
 )
 v. )
 Opinion Filed: October 28, 2026
 )
 BRANDAAN and MELISSA DEGROOT, )
 Melanie Gagnepain, Clerk
 husband and wife, )
 )
 Defendants-Counterclaimants- )
 Appellants. )
 _______________________________________ )

 Appeal from the District Court of the Second Judicial District of the State of Idaho,
 Nez Perce County. Michelle Evans, District Judge.

 The district court’s order on the amended motion for reconsideration is affirmed;
 and the district court’s order on reconsideration of attorney fees is affirmed.

 Clark & Feeney, LLP, Lewiston, for Appellants. W. Jeremy Carr appeared,
 submitted on the briefs.

 Ramsden, Marfice, Ealy, & De Smet, LLP, Coeur d’Alene, for Respondents. Jack
 A. Mosby appeared, submitted on the briefs.
 _____________________
BRODY, Chief Justice
 This appeal involves the district court’s decision to reject the application of the merger
doctrine in a real property dispute and its decision to award attorney fees to the sellers under Idaho
Code section 12-120(3). Brandaan and Melissa DeGroot purchased a family cabin and its contents
from Dave and Ardean Armitage. After closing the sale, a dispute arose over payment for the
personal property, and the Armitages sued for breach of contract. Following a bench trial, the
district court entered judgment in favor of the Armitages for $96,538 in damages plus attorney
fees.
 The DeGroots challenge the district court’s denial of their post-trial motion for
reconsideration. They do not challenge the district court’s findings of fact but instead argue that

 1
 the district court erred in refusing to apply the merger doctrine to bar the Armitages’ claim. They
contend that, given the district court’s conclusion that the parties mutually intended to transfer both
the real and personal property in a single transaction for a total amount of $450,000, their promise
to pay the $100,000 for the personal property merged into the warranty deed and was extinguished
at closing. They argue the district court’s legal analysis of the merger doctrine was erroneous and
that the case should be remanded for reconsideration of the issue. The DeGroots also challenge the
district court’s award of attorney fees to the Armitages under Idaho Code section 12-120(3). Their
contention is that any civil action that falls within the ambit of section 12-120(3) must involve a
“commercial transaction.” For the reasons discussed below, we affirm the district court’s decisions.
 I. FACTUAL AND PROCEDURAL BACKGROUND
A. The property and the parties.
 In July 2024, the Armitages agreed to sell their real property in Lenore, Idaho, to the
DeGroots. The ten-acre property included a cabin, a three-bay enclosed shop, a shed, outhouse,
wooded areas, and an open meadow overlooking Dworshak Reservoir (collectively, “Property”).
Dave Armitage and his twin brother, Doug, built the cabin, and the two families owned the property
together for about twenty years. The Armitages became the sole owners of the Property when Doug
passed away. The Armitages and their extended family treated the Property as their getaway spot,
hosting vacations, reunions, and a wedding on the property. Because of their advancing age, and
Dave’s health problems, Ardean decided it was time to sell the Property in the summer of 2024.
B. The transaction.
 On July 4, 2024, Ardean told her neighbors that she and Dave were ready to sell the
Property. The news traveled fast, and the DeGroot family heard about the opportunity the next day.
Three days later the parties shook hands, agreeing on $450,000 cash for the real property and the
personal property on the premises. On July 8, 2024, the DeGroots arrived back at the Property with
two documents they drafted to effectuate the transaction. While the Armitages had reservations
with there being two documents instead of one, they signed both documents.
 The first document, titled “Idaho Residential Real Estate Purchase Agreement” (“Real
Estate Agreement”) addressed the purchase of the single-family home and ten acres of land. The
second document, titled “Idaho General Bill of Sale” (“Personalty Agreement”) addressed the sale
of the personal property. The Real Estate Agreement provided that the Armitages agreed to sell the
real property to the DeGroots for $350,000, cash. The Real Estate Agreement also addressed the

 2
 sale of the personal property on the premises in three different provisions: (1) “the Seller shall
include the following personal property: Separate Agreement,” (2) “the Seller DOES NOT include
the following fixtures: Personal Items and Pictures only,” and (3) “Additional Terms and
Conditions: Seller to Include All contents, furniture, tools, Appliances, 2 Four Wheelers, Boat, and
any/all other Contents of Shop and House.”
 The Personalty Agreement provided a separate purchase price of $100,000 for “[a]ny and
[a]ll contents of all buildings” located on the premises. It also listed two 4-Wheeler recreational
vehicles, a boat, and a trailer, with the “REMAINDER UNKNOWN.” The district court noted in
its findings of fact that neither party performed a complete inventory of the personal property at
signing or by closing. Above the description of the personal property, the Personalty Agreement
stated: “Purchase Conditioned upon Completed Purchase of [Physical Address], by: DEGROOTS,
FROM: ARMITAGE.”
 The district court found that the Armitages intended to sell the real property and the
personal property altogether for $450,000. The district court also found that the DeGroots would
not have purchased the personal property independent of the real property.
C. The disappearances of personal property from the premises.
 After the Real Estate Agreement and Personalty Agreement were signed, the Armitages
promptly packed up the few personal items that the Real Estate Agreement allowed them to retain
and headed back home to Washington. The items they took included a large sign saying, “Doug’s
Den” (the name of Dave’s twin), which Brandaan DeGroot helped them load into their car, as well
as a sauerkraut cutter and some photos. When the Armitages left the Property that day, they
mistakenly left behind Ardean’s customized hiking poles. The remainder of the personal property
in and around the Property were to be transferred to the DeGroots at closing, except for some
fishing poles that were going to be picked up by the Armitages’ nephew, Jared Meske.
 The parties closed their transaction on July 26, 2024. It is not disputed that the Armitages
conveyed title of the Property to the DeGroots, and the DeGroots paid the $350,000 in return. The
warranty deed does not appear to have been presented as an exhibit at trial, and it does not
otherwise appear to be in the record on appeal. The DeGroots never paid the $100,000
contemplated under the Personalty Agreement.
 When the DeGroots arrived at the Property after closing, they discovered some of the items
that they had anticipated being left on the premises were missing. They claimed the items included:

 3
 (1) a radial saw; (2) a trolling motor; (3) a pair of walkie talkies; (4) the large “Doug’s Den” sign;
(5) a white utility trailer and damaged tire; (6) high-power binoculars; (7) various hand tools,
including a mallet and a rake; (8) Ardean’s custom hiking poles; (9) various gas cans; (10) a Sorry
board game; (11) a spotting scope and related stand; (12) an electric constellation finder; (13) a
binocular stand; and (14) a shovel.
 Many of these items were later discovered to be in the possession of Meske who had visited
the property prior to closing to pick up the fishing poles that the Armitages had expressly excluded
from the sale. The binoculars, the Sorry board game, the electric constellation finder, and binocular
stand were allegedly returned prior to closing. The white utility trailer (minus a tire) was returned
after closing and after Meske’s wedding. The district court estimated the value of the missing items
to be, at most, $3,462.
D. The breach of contract complaint and resulting litigation.
 The Armitages filed suit, seeking recovery of the $100,000 contemplated by the Personalty
Agreement. Following the bench trial, the district court ruled in favor of the Armitages on their
breach of contract claim. The district court concluded that the Armitages had substantially
complied with their obligations and that the removal of the personal property did not constitute a
material breach. In its judgment, the district court awarded the $100,000 in damages to the
Armitages; however, it offset the $100,000 award by $3,462 to account for the missing items. The
Armitages have not challenged the offset on appeal.
 Following the issuance of the findings of fact and conclusions of law, the DeGroots filed a
motion for reconsideration. Contrary to the position they took at trial, the DeGroots argued that,
given the district court’s finding that the parties intended the Real Estate Agreement and Personalty
Agreement to constitute a single transaction, the DeGroots’ promise to purchase the personal
property merged with the warranty deed at the time of closing and extinguished their obligation to
pay the $100,000 contemplated in the Personalty Agreement. The district court denied the
DeGroots’ motion.
 The Armitages filed a motion for attorney fees pursuant to Idaho Code section 12-120(3).
The district court initially denied the request for attorney fees, but granted it upon reconsideration.
The Armitages argued that because the Personalty Agreement was titled “Idaho General Bill of
Sale,” it constituted a “bill” under Idaho Code section 12-120(3). Drawing on a Black’s Law
Dictionary definition of “bill of sale,” the district court concluded the Personalty Agreement was

 4
 a “bill” as that term is used in the statute and granted the Armitages attorney fees. The DeGroots
timely appealed.
 II. STANDARDS OF REVIEW
 When deciding a motion for reconsideration, the district court employs the same standard
of review that it used when deciding the original motion that is being reconsidered. Fragnella v.
Petrovich, 153 Idaho 266, 276, 281 P.3d 103, 113 (2012). This Court reviews a trial court’s decision
to grant or deny a motion for reconsideration using the same standard employed by the trial court.
Id.
 Since this Court is reviewing the district court’s decision on the DeGroot’s motion for
reconsideration of the findings of fact and conclusions of law, this Court “is limited to determining
whether the evidence supports the findings of fact and whether the findings of fact support the
conclusions of law.” Burns Concrete, Inc. v. Teton County, 168 Idaho 442, 451, 483 P.3d 985, 994
(2020) (citing Caldwell Land & Cattle, LLC v. Johnson Thermal Sys., Inc., 165 Idaho 787, 795,
452 P.3d 809, 817 (2019)). This Court employs free review over the district court’s conclusions of
law and may determine whether the trial court correctly stated the applicable law and whether the
facts sustain its legal conclusions. Id. (citing Kunz v. Nield, Inc., 162 Idaho 432, 438, 398 P.3d 165,
171 (2017)). Upon review of mixed questions of law and fact, “this [C]ourt will differentiate
among the fact-finding, law-stating, and law-applying functions of the trial courts.” Haight v.
Dales Used Cars, Inc., 139 Idaho 853, (Ct. App. 2003) (citing Staggie v. Idaho Falls Consol.
Hosps., Inc., 110 Idaho 349, 351, 715 P.2d 1019, 1021 (Ct. App. 1986)).
 When reviewing a motion for reconsideration of an award of attorney fees, this Court
reviews the decision under the abuse of discretion standard. Med. Recovery Servs., LLC v. Lopez,
163 Idaho 281, 282–83, 411 P.3d 1182, 1183–84 (2018) (quoting Simono v. House, 160 Idaho 788,
791, 379 P.3d 1058, 1061 (2016)). If the dispute over the award of attorney fees depends upon the
interpretation of a statute, then this C

leads.caseName: Reybel Hernandez v. Barclays Mortgage Trust 2022-RPL1, Mortgage-Backed
leads.court: District Court of Appeal of Florida
leads.text:
Third District Court of Appeal 
State of Florida 

Opinion filed October 28, 2026. 
Not final until disposition of timely filed motion for rehearing. 

________________ 

No. 3D26-0312 
Lower Tribunal No. 23-29033-CA-01 
________________ 

Reybel Hernandez, 
Appellant, 

vs. 

Barclays Mortgage Trust 2022-RPL1, Mortgage-Backed, 
Appellee. 

 An Appeal from a non-final order from the Circuit Court for Miami-Dade 
County, Ariana Fajardo Orshan, Judge. 

 Reybel Hernandez, in proper person. 

 Atlas | Solomon LLP, and Eric M. Levine (Stuart), for appellee. 

Before FERNANDEZ, LINDSEY and LOBREE, JJ. 

 LINDSEY, J. 
 2 
Appellant Reybel Hernandez appeals the trial court’s order denying his 
emergency motion to vacate a foreclosure sale and stay further proceedings, 
overruling his objection to the foreclosure sale, and directing the Clerk of 
Court to issue a certificate of title. 1 Hernandez argues we should reverse 
the trial court’s denial of his motion because: (1) appellee Barclays Mortgage 
Trust 2022-RPL1 failed to file the original note and thus did not establish its 
standing to bring the foreclosure action; (2) Hernandez provided evidence of 
a broken chain of title and fraudulent certification of the note, which the trial 
court did not address in denying his motion and objection; (3) the trial court 
erroneously applied section 702.036 even though Barclays was the 
purchaser of the property; and (4) the trial court erroneously failed to grant a 
stay pending appeal. The trial court did not err. 
We affirm because Hernandez failed to preserve any of his arguments 
for appellate review. Even if Hernandez had preserved his arguments, we 
would still affirm because they do not establish reversible error. 

1 We have jurisdiction. See Fla. R. App. P. 9.030(b)(1)(A); U.S. Bank, N.A. 
v. Vogel, 137 So. 3d 491, 492 n.1 (Fla. 4th DCA 2014) (citing Popescu v. 
Laguna Master Ass’n, 126 So. 3d 449, 450 (Fla. 4th DCA 2013) (explaining 
that an order denying a motion to vacate foreclosure sale is a discrete final 
order). 
 3 
BACKGROUND 
Hernandez executed a promissory note and mortgage in favor of 
Countrywide Home Loans, Inc. in April 2005 and signed a modification in 
December 2014. Barclays brought the underlying foreclosure action against 
Hernandez in December 2023, alleging that it was the holder of the original 
note and mortgage and that Hernandez had defaulted on the modified loan 
in November 2022. 
Barclays attached a “certification of possession” and copy of the note 
to the complaint. According to the certification of possession, Barclays was 
in possession of the note as of November 7, 2023. The copy of the note 
reflected a blank indorsement. Barclays filed the original note and mortgage 
with the trial court in November 2024. The original note reflected the same 
blank indorsement as the copy. 
In October 2025, the trial court entered a final judgment of foreclosure 
in Barclays’ favor. In the final judgment, the court explained that Barclays 
had established its standing via possession of the original note endorsed in 
blank. Hernandez did not appeal the final judgment of foreclosure. However, 
he filed a motion to stay the foreclosure sale and vacate the final judgment. 
 4 
The trial court rendered an order on Hernandez ’s motion on November 17, 
2025, but that order was not included in the appendix.2 
The property at issue was subsequently sold to Barclays at a 
foreclosure sale in January 2026. Hernandez moved to vacate the 
foreclosure sale and stay further proceedings and filed an objection to the 
certificate of sale. In his motion to vacate the fore closure sale, Hernandez 
argued that he had filed “emergency notices and motions” informing the trial 
court of “pending federal proceedings involving the same parties and 
property” and asked the trial court to stay the foreclosure sale prior to the 
foreclosure sale. Hernandez argued that the foreclosure sale took place 
despite the lack of a ruling on these motions. Hernandez asked the trial court 
to vacate the foreclosure sale and enter a stay because “[v]acatur and a stay 
are necessary to preserve the status quo, avoid irreparable harm, and 
prevent conflicting rulings with the pending federal action.” 
Hernandez’s objection to the certificate of sale similarly argued that, at 
the time the certificate of sale issued, there were pending unresolved post -
judgment motions and jurisdictional issues. Hernandez further argued that 

2 The appendix to the answer brief on appeal includes a summary of the trial 
court’s docket, which reflects when the trial court entered its order on 
Hernandez’s motion to vacate final summary judgment and stay the 
foreclosure sale. 
 5 
there were contemporaneous proceedings pending in federal court. 
Hernandez argued issuance of the certificate of sale would cause irreparable 
harm by foreclosing judicial review of the unresolved issues. The trial court 
denied Hernandez’s motion and objection. This appeal timely followed. 
ANALYSIS 
A. Standard of Review 
“We review a trial court’s ruling on a motion to set aside a foreclosure 
sale for a gross abuse of discretion. ” 2275 NE 120 St., LLC v. Sanchez 
Struve Bus. Advisors, LLC, 336 So. 3d 757, 759 (Fla. 3d DCA 2021) (citing 
Vogel, 137 So. 3d at 493). The Florida Supreme Court first applied the gross 
abuse of discretion standard when reviewing trial court rulings on motions to 
vacate defaults. See N. Shore Hosp., Inc. v. Barber , 143 So. 2d 849 , 852 
(Fla. 1962); Coggin v. Barfield, 8 So. 2d 9, 11 (Fla. 1942); Benedict v. W.T. 
Hadlow Co., 42 So. 239, 241 (Fla. 1906); Russ v. Gilbert , 19 Fla. 54, 57 
(1882). Application of this heightened level of deference in such cases 
furthers Florida’s longstanding public policy of liberally granting motions to 
set aside defaults so that cases can be decided on their merits. See M.W. 
v. SPCP Grp. V, LLC, 163 So. 3d 518, 519-20 (Fla. 3d DCA 2015); Allstate 
Floridian Ins. Co. v. Ronco Inventions, LLC , 890 So. 2d 300 , 302 (Fla. 2d 
 6 
DCA 2004) (citing Lindell Motors, Inc. v. Morgan , 727 So. 2d 1112, 1113 
(Fla. 2d DCA 1999)). 
Similarly, when reviewing rulings on motions to set aside foreclosure 
sales, appellate courts apply the gross abuse of discretion standard because 
bidders and buyers at such sales seek to make a profit, and establishing a 
precedent that encourages the easy setting aside of foreclosure sales would 
“destroy the incentive which prompts bidding at [a] sale and thereby work a 
hardship on both debtors and creditors.” Long Beach Mortg. Corp. v. Bebble, 
985 So. 2d 611, 613 (Fla. 4th DCA 2008) (quoting City of Sanford v. Ashton, 
179 So. 765, 767 (Fla. 1938)). Application of the gross abuse of discretion 
standard “ensure[s] a competitive market in the foreclosure sale process. ” 
Id. 
There is no definition of what constitutes a gross abuse of discretion or 
how it differs from an abuse of discretion, though it is , on its face, more 
egregious than the garden variety abuse of discretion standard. See Allstate 
Floridian Ins. Co., 890 So. 2d at 302. A typical abuse of discretion occurs 
when no reasonable person could take the view adopted by the trial court. 
Id. (quoting Canakaris v. Canakaris , 382 So. 2d 1197, 1203 (Fla. 1980) ). 
Thus, it follows that the gross abuse of discretion standard requires an 
appellate court to be as deferential to a trial judge’s decision as possible, 
 7 
“upsetting it very rarely and only with undeniable provocation. ” Bethesda 
Mem’l Hosp., Inc. v. Laska, 977 So. 2d 804, 806 (Fla. 4th DCA 2008). The 
burden this standard imposes on a litigant seeking appellate review is 
“almost insurmountable.” M.W., 163 So. 3d at 519. 
B. Preservation 
As a preliminary matter, Hernandez failed to preserve any of the 
arguments he now raises for appellate review. “[T]o be preserved for further 
review by a higher court, an issue must be presented to the lower court and 
the specific legal argument or ground to be argued on appeal or review 
must be part of that presentation if it is to be considered preserved .” 
Homeowner’s Choice Prop. & Cas. Ins. Co. v. Oakes, 431 So. 3d 1005, 1013 
(Fla. 4th DCA 2026) (emphasis added) (quoting Sunset Harbour Condo. 
Ass’n v. Robbins, 914 So. 2d 925, 928 (Fla. 2005)). Arguments that are not 
preserved are waived. Id. (quoting State v. Clark , 373 So. 3d 1128, 1131 
(Fla. 2023)). 
In the proceedings below, Hernandez argued that the foreclosure sale 
should be vacated and the trial court proceedings stayed because there were 
pending federal proceedings involving the same parties and property and it 
was necessary to preserve the status quo, avoid irreparable harm, and 
prevent conflicting rulings with the federal court. In contrast, Hernandez ’s 
 8 
arguments on appeal are that the trial court erred by denying his motion 
because: (1) Barclays did not establish its standing to foreclose because it 
failed to file the original note; (2) Hernandez provided evidence of a broken 
chain of title 3; (3) Barclays was the purchaser of the property, and thus 
section 702.036, Florida Statutes, did not apply; and (4) the trial court should 
have granted Hernandez ’s request for a stay in light of the lack of original 
note, broken chain of title, and inapplicability of section 702.036. Because 
Hernandez did not raise these specific arguments in his motion or objection 
below, they were not preserved for appeal and are waived. See Oakes, 431 
So. 3d at 1013 (quoting Robbins, 914 So. 2d at 928). 
C. Merits 
Even if Hernandez had preserved these arguments for appeal, we 
would still affirm because the arguments raised do not establish a gross 
abuse of discretion on the part of the trial court. First, Hernandez’s claim 
that Barclays failed to provide the original note in the proceedings below is 

3 Hernandez also argues he provided evidence that Barclays’ certification of 
the note was fraudulent or misleading. Beyond making this conclusory 
assertion, Hernandez offers no argument as to why the certification was 
fraudulent. “Claims for which an appellant has not presented any argument, 
or for which he provides only conclusory argument, are insufficiently 
presented for review and are waived.” Hammond v. State, 34 So. 3d 58, 59 
(Fla. 4th DCA 2010) (first citing Doorbal v. State , 983 So. 2d 464, 482 -83 
(Fla. 2008); and then citing Shere v. State , 742 So. 2d 215, 217 n.6 (Fla. 
1999)). 
 9 
refuted by the appendix, which reflects that Barclays filed the original note in 
November 2024. By attaching a certification and copy of the note to the 
complaint and filing the original note prior to the entry of the judgment of 
foreclosure, Barclays satisfied the requirements of Florida law. See Fla. R. 
Civ. P. 1.115(c) (“If the claimant is in possession of the original promissory 
note, the claimant must file under penalty of perjury a certification 
contemporaneously with the filing of the claim for relief for foreclosure that 
the claimant is in possession of the original promissory note. . . . The original 
note and the allonges must be filed with the court before the entry of any 
judgment of foreclosure or judgment on the note.”). 
Second, as to Hernandez’s argument that he presented evidence of a 
broken chain of title, Florida law states that a litigant does not need to be the 
note holder and the note owner to have standing to bring a foreclosure 
action. Aquasol Condo. Ass’n, Inc. v. HSBC Bank USA, Nat’l Ass’n, 312 So. 
3d 105, 110 (Fla. 3d DCA 2018) . “[S]tanding may be established from a 
plaintiff’s status as the note holder, regardless of any recorded 
assignments.” Roif v. JP Morgan Chase Bank , 283 So. 3d 383 , 385 (Fla. 
3d DCA 2019) (emphasis added) (quoting McLean v. JP Morgan Chase 
Bank Nat ’l Ass ’n, 79 So. 3d 170, 173 (Fla. 4th DCA 2012) ). Assuming 
Hernandez is correct that he presented evidence that the chain of title was 
 10 
broken, such evidence is immaterial because Barclays est

leads.caseName: Arkansas State Highway Commission v. Lewis
leads.text:
Cite as 2026 Ark. App. 517
 ARKANSAS COURT OF APPEALS
 DIVISIONS I & IV
 No. CV-25-110

ARKANSAS STATE HIGHWAY Opinion Delivered October 28, 2026
COMMISSION
 APPELLANT APPEAL FROM THE FAULKNER
 COUNTY CIRCUIT COURT
V. [NO. 23CV-15-754]

 HONORABLE SUSAN K. WEAVER,
 WILLIAM LEWIS AND CODY LEWIS, JUDGE
 CO-TRUSTEES OF THE WILLIAM
 MAJOR LEWIS TRUST U/T/D
 12/21/2000
 APPELLEES AFFIRMED

 MIKE MURPHY, Judge
 This is an eminent-domain appeal from a $3 million jury verdict entered in the

Faulkner County Circuit Court in favor of the property owners, appellees William Major

Lewis and Cody Lewis, as co-trustees of the William Major Lewis Trust (hereinafter “the

Lewises”) against the appellant Arkansas State Highway Commission. The case concerned a

condemnation and taking of portions of land owned by the trust. On appeal, the Highway

Commission argues that (1) the court erred when it allowed testimony regarding roads and

roundabouts the Lewises claimed they had to build due to the taking; (2) substantial evidence

does not support the verdict; and (3) the amount and manner in which attorney’s fees were

awarded was improper. We affirm.
  I. Facts and Procedural History

 On August 7, 2015, the Highway Commission condemned portions of two tracts

owned by the Lewises, taking a right-of-way and controlling access across both. The taking

eliminated the tracts’ direct, unrestricted frontage access to Dave Ward Drive, which the

Lewises and their tenant had used to reach the property before the taking. After the taking,

the Lewises were limited to an unpaved, unimproved road on the east side and an access

point on the old Amity Road on the west side of tract 1. The Highway Commission deposited

$417,825 into the registry of the court as its estimate of just compensation.

 The case proceeded through several years of appraisal work and discovery before its

first pretrial hearing. On April 9, 2018, the circuit court heard the parties’ cross-motions in

limine and, as relevant here, granted the Lewises’ motion to admit evidence of the cost of

constructing replacement roads and roundabouts to restore access to Dave Ward Drive. The

court simultaneously denied the Highway Commission’s motion to exclude that evidence. It

admitted proof that the Lewises spent roughly $4–$4.5 million constructing a relocated

Amity Road and an east-west connector road, which the City of Conway required before it

would authorize any road restoring access to the Dave Ward Drive-fronting remainder. The

court found that the Lewises could not use the cost-to-cure or betterment evidence directly

as the measure of damages but could otherwise present evidence of the roads and their cost

at trial.

 2
  The Highway Commission renewed its motion in limine on May 2, 2024, again

seeking to exclude the Lewises’ cost-to-cure evidence. The circuit court again denied the

motion, and the case proceeded to a jury trial beginning June 4.

 At trial, the Lewises’ appraiser, Diana Thompson, opined that the total amount of

just compensation for both tracts was $3.8869 million using a comparable-sales approach

with adjustments for size, location, and time and, for tract 1, an income-capitalization

approach reflecting the lost rental income when the Lewises’ tenant relocated. Trustee Cody

Lewis gave lay-opinion testimony that the market value of tract 1 was $16 a square foot (about

$14 million) before the taking and $10 a square foot after the taking (about $8.564 million).

Lewis testified that the market value of tract 2 was $14 a square foot (about $4.592 million)

before the taking and $8 a square foot (about $2.411 million) after the taking. He explained

that the City of Conway required the Lewises to build a relocated Amity Road and

connecting drive at a cost of several million dollars before they could make commercial use

of the property abutting Dave Ward Drive. They additionally had to use seven acres from

their remaining land for the construction. Audie Alumbaugh, the Lewises’ accountant,

echoed this testimony. At the close of the Lewises’ case, the circuit court denied the Highway

Commission’s motion for a directed verdict, explaining that the Highway Commission’s

objections went “to the credibility and weight for the jury to give” the evidence.

 The Highway Commission’s appraiser, Cheslyn Bartlett, testified that access

remained to both tracts after the taking and opined that total just compensation was

$417,825. To arrive at this figure, she used a comparable-sales approach only with no

 3
 severance-damage component. The Highway Commission renewed its motion for a directed

verdict at the close of all the evidence; the court again denied it, and the case went to the

jury with instructions that it could consider restoration or cost-to-cure evidence “only as an

aid in arriving at the amount of just compensation” and that such costs “are not the measure

of damages.” The jury returned a verdict of $3 million.

 On June 20, 2024, postverdict but before entry of the final judgment, the Lewises

moved for prejudgment interest at “a proper rate,” attorney’s fees, costs, and appraiser’s fees,

relying on Arkansas Code Annotated section 27-67-317(b) (Repl. 2022), and Wilson v. City

of Fayetteville, 310 Ark. 154, 838 S.W.2d 366 (1992). The motion included the Lewises’

contingency-fee agreement, counsel’s affidavit and itemized billing records, a second

attorney’s affidavit opining that the rate, time, and fees claimed were reasonable, and a CPA’s

affidavit opining that a reasonable rate of return on a moderately invested portfolio ran from

7.7 percent to 8.2 percent, compounded annually. The Highway Commission responded on

July 30, making several arguments; it did not, however, contest the reasonableness of the

rate, hours billed, or requested amount.

 On August 12, the circuit court entered judgment on the jury’s verdict, awarding the

Lewises the roughly $2.582 million balance remaining after the Highway Commission’s

deposit plus interest at 8 percent, compounded annually, accruing from August 7, 2015, the

date of the taking. The court separately awarded $123,195.68 in attorney’s fees, costs, and

 4
 appraiser’s fees plus interest at 8 percent, compounded annually, accruing from the date of

the judgment. From this, the Highway Commission timely appealed.1

 II. Evidence of Road Building

 The Highway Commission first argues that the court abused its discretion by

admitting evidence that the Lewises built roads and roundabouts after the taking. We review

a circuit court’s decision to admit or exclude evidence for abuse of discretion. Dovers v.

Stephenson Oil Co., 81 Ark. App. 92, 98 S.W.3d 462 (2003).

 Cost-to-cure evidence has long been admissible in Arkansas condemnation cases as

an aid to determining the diminution in market value a taking caused and as evidence of a

landowner’s efforts to mitigate that diminution. Ark. State Highway Comm’n v. Ptak, 236 Ark.

105, 364 S.W.2d 794 (1963); Ark. State Highway Comm’n v. Dean, 244 Ark. 405, 425 S.W.2d

306 (1968). The controlling authority is Arkansas State Highway Commission v. Speck, 230 Ark.

712, 324 S.W.2d 796 (1959). In Speck, a controlled-access taking left a farm without direct

access to a severed tract, and our supreme court approved evidence of the cost to build a

replacement road and bridge restoring that access as “a proper element to consider” in

valuing the remainder. Id. at 718, 324 S.W.2d at 799.

 We measure just compensation as of the date of taking, comparing the value of the

property immediately before the taking with its value immediately after, as though the

condemnor’s project were then complete. Ark. State Highway Comm’n v. Littlefield, 247 Ark.

 1
 The Lewises filed a notice of cross-appeal but explicitly abandoned it in their
response brief.

 5
 686, 447 S.W.2d 146 (1969). That rule fixes the valuation date; it does not require every

item of cost-to-cure evidence to be contemporaneous with the taking. Speck contemplated

this. In Speck, the supreme court explained that the jury determines “the type of

improvement that will more nearly restore the property to its original status,” with such

“prospective expenditures” serving “only [as] an aid in determining the difference in the

before and after value of the property.” Speck, 230 Ark. at 720, 324 S.W.2d at 800. The

timing of construction accordingly bears on the weight of cost-to-cure evidence and is not a

categorical bar to its admission.

 That is the finding the court made on this record twice. The Highway Department’s

taking extinguished the Lewises’ direct frontage access to Dave Ward Drive, the property’s

“most prime” access. The roads the Lewises built were the means of restoring functional

access to the part of the property fronting the highway. Cody Lewis testified that if the

Lewises were “going to use this property at all,” they had no choice but to build the road the

City designed.

 Whether that testimony—and the City’s demand—in fact flowed from the taking or

instead reflected development costs the Lewises would have borne regardless of it was

squarely contested. At the 2024 hearing on the Highway Commission’s renewed motion in

limine, its counsel read into the record Thompson’s 2018 deposition testimony. When asked

directly whether the Lewises would still have had to put in a road had the Commission’s

project never happened, she answered yes. The circuit court heard that argument and denied

the motion anyway for the reasons it had already given in 2018. At trial, the Commission

 6
 put the same proposition to Thompson again, and her answer was more qualified than the

deposition excerpt, standing alone, suggests. She agreed that, because the property had no

internal roads and a preexisting ditch already blocked travel between its northern and

southern portions, part of the Lewises’ development plans “would have needed” some road

work regardless of the taking, but she maintained throughout that the taking of the Dave

Ward Drive frontage was what “took away [the Lewises’] ability to commercially develop it

the way [they] wanted to” since, absent the taking, “[t]hey would have had frontage off of

Dave Ward Drive.” The Commission pressed its contrary theory directly to the jury in closing

argument: “[T]hey would have needed a road anyway. . . . How else are you going to get up

there?” The jury heard both sides of that dispute and was entitled to resolve it either way.

The fact that the $3,000,000 verdict came in below Thompson’s own $3,886,900 opinion

of total just compensation is consistent with a jury that weighed the Commission’s causation

argument and discounted for it, not one that disregarded it. Resolving that kind of causal

dispute is the jury’s task, not ours. See Ark. State Highway Comm’n v. Fowler, 240 Ark. 595,

401 S.W.2d 1 (1966) (affirming a condemnation verdict against a substantial-evidence

challenge where the landowners’ and the Commission’s valuation testimony conflicted).

 The dissent would go further and hold that any relevance of the road-building

evidence was conditioned on a showing, under Ark. R. Evid. 104(b), that a willing buyer

could have determined from regulations or ordinances in force on the date of taking that

this specific cost would follow. That argument is not before us. Neither of the Highway

Commission’s two motions in limine asked the circuit court to apply a Rule 104(b)

 7
 conditional-relevance screen, and neither of its briefs on appeal mentions Rule 104(b). We

do not reverse a circuit court’s decision that fails to apply a framework no party asked it to

apply, and we do not construct an appellant’s argument for it where the appellant has not

made it.

 The Highway Commission’s principal authority, Arkansas State Highway Commission v.

Barker, 326 Ark. 403, 931 S.W.2d 138 (1996), does not require a different result. Barker

reversed a verdict built on a

Cite as 2026 Ark. App. 499
 ARKANSAS COURT OF APPEALS
 DIVISION III
 No. CV-25-506

 BFT RENTAL, LLC Opinion Delivered October 28, 2026

 APPELLANT
 APPEAL FROM THE WASHINGTON
 COUNTY CIRCUIT COURT
 V. [NO. 72CV-23-3442]

 CITY OF FAYETTEVILLE HONORABLE DOUG MARTIN,
 APPELLEE JUDGE

 AFFIRMED

 N. MARK KLAPPENBACH, Chief Judge

 Appellant BFT Rental, LLC (“BFT”), appeals the Washington County Circuit

Court’s order granting a directed verdict in favor of the City of Fayetteville (“the City”) after

BFT failed to appear for trial. On appeal, BFT purports to appeal both the May 13, 2025

order granting the City’s motion for directed verdict and the court’s February 27, 2025 order

granting BFT’s former counsel’s motion to withdraw as counsel of record. We affirm.

 I. Relevant Facts

 The City filed a condemnation action against BFT on November 8, 2023, followed

by a motion for immediate possession on November 13. In its motion for immediate

possession, the City claimed that it was authorized by eminent domain to acquire real

property owned by BFT for a lawful public purpose, the construction of a water-transmission

main. The City further claimed that “[p]ursuant to Ark. Code Ann. § 18-15-303, Plaintiff
 may present an advance deposit of money to this Court for the purpose of making just

compensation when the amount thereof has been assessed to obtain an immediate right of

entry and possession in real property prior to trial if determination of the question in

controversy in the proceedings is likely to delay progress of the work.” The City asserted that

it had deposited $112,180 into the registry of the court to compensate BFT for the taking.

 BFT answered the complaint on November 15, and the court entered an order of

possession in favor of the City on November 16. BFT filed an unopposed motion to

withdraw the $112,180 deposit on November 28, which was granted by the court on

December 14. BFT’s original counsel filed a motion to withdraw as attorney of record on

March 28, 2024, which the court granted on April 1. Attorney Tona DeMers filed an entry

of appearance on behalf of BFT on July 2.

 On September 23, 2024, the court issued a “Jury Trial Setting and Scheduling” order,

which set a one-day jury trial “in the second out position” for April 30, 2025, and outlined

other discovery deadlines, including the naming of expert witnesses and filing of dispositive

motions.

 On January 31, 2025, Tona DeMers moved to withdraw as attorney of record for

BFT. The City responded to the withdrawal motion on February 3, and although it did not

object to counsel’s withdrawal, it did object to the continuance because the “action was filed

on November 8, 2023, and trial [was] now less than three (3) months away. The City’s expert

and lay witnesses [had] made arrangements to attend the scheduled trial on the date set by

the Court, and the City [was] prepared to proceed.” The City further stated that DeMers

 2
 was “Defendant’s second attorney of record to request withdrawal during the pendency of

this action. . . . [It] object[ed] to any continuance of the trial in this matter based upon her

withdrawal or Defendant’s retention of its third attorney of record.” DeMers replied on

behalf of BFT, arguing that April 30, 2025, was the first trial setting; the trial was a “second-

out setting,” meaning there was no guarantee it would go to trial that day; and there would

be no prejudice created by the court’s grant of a continuance so that BFT could retain new

counsel.

 The court granted the motion to withdraw on February 27 but not the continuance.

Following the February 27 order, the City designated expert witnesses, named exhibits and

witnesses, and filed a motion in limine and jury instructions. The motion in limine was

served on BFT’s registered agent six days before trial. BFT did not respond.

 The matter proceeded to an April 30 jury trial, at which BFT failed to appear. The

City moved for—and the court orally granted—a directed verdict affirming the City’s

ownership of the easement and awarding just compensation to BFT in the amount of

$112,180. On May 7, a new attorney, S. Lance Cox, filed an entry of appearance on behalf

of BFT. Two days later, BFT filed a motion for new trial and brief in support.

 In its motion, BFT moved for “a new trial pursuant to Rule 59 or, alternatively, Rule

60 of the Arkansas Rules of Civil Procedure.” BFT argued that the court’s February 27 order

granting withdrawal but denying the request for continuance was an “abuse of discretion

and reversible error in a case in which there had been no prior continuances, and in which

the Plaintiff would suffer no prejudice by a continuance.” BFT contended that doing so was

 3
 contrary to Arkansas Rule of Civil Procedure 59(a)(1). Alternatively, BFT argued that the

court should modify or vacate the judgment as permitted by Rule 60 of the Arkansas Rules

of Civil Procedure.

 The court entered its written order granting the City’s motion for directed verdict on

May 13, finding that because BFT did not appear at trial and did not submit a witness list or

an exhibit list, it “failed to carry its burden in establishing an entitlement to additional

compensation beyond that which was deposited by Plaintiff . . . [and] a reasonable jury would

not have a sufficient evidentiary basis to award Defendant just compensation in excess of

that previously deposited by the [City].”

 The City responded in opposition to BFT’s motion for new trial on May 14, and BFT

replied on May 27. The court did not rule on the motion, and on June 16, BFT filed its

notice of appeal, which designated the “Court’s Order Granting Motion to Withdraw, file-

marked February 27, 2025, and the Court’s subsequently entered Order Granting Plaintiff

City of Fayetteville’s Motion for Directed Verdict, file-marked May 13, 2025.”

 II. Discussion

 BFT sets forth a singular point on appeal—that the circuit court’s May 13, 2025 order

granting the City’s directed-verdict motion and its subsequent denial of appellant’s motion

for new trial should be reversed. However, BFT also purports to challenge the February 27,

2025 order in which the court granted counsel’s motion to withdraw and denied its motion

for continuance. BFT failed to preserve its challenges to the circuit court’s February 27 order

by failing to raise them before filing its motion for new trial.

 4
  Generally, we are precluded from reaching issues on appeal that are first raised in a

motion for new trial. See, e.g., Tate-Smith v. Cupples, 355 Ark. 230, 244, 134 S.W.3d 535, 543

(2003); Nash v. Nash, 2019 Ark. App. 173, at 12, 574 S.W.3d 171, 179. “[A]n objection first

made in a motion for new trial is not timely.” Tate-Smith, 355 Ark. at 244, 134 S.W.3d at

543. The Arkansas Supreme Court has explained that this reasoning “is to discourage

‘sandbagging’ on the part of lawyers who might otherwise take a chance on a favorable result

and subsequently raise [an issue] if the gamble did not pay off.” Lee v. Daniel, 350 Ark. 466,

476–77, 91 S.W.3d 464, 470 (2002) (quoting Selph v. State, 264 Ark. 197, 204, 570 S.W.2d

256, 260–61 (1978)). A party may not wait for the outcome of the case before deciding to

bring an error to the court’s attention. See, e.g., Jones v. Double “D” Props., Inc., 352 Ark. 39,

49, 98 S.W.3d 405, 410 (2003). For that reason, we are precluded from reaching the circuit

court’s grant of BFT’s motion to withdraw and denial of its motion for continuance—issues

that were first raised in its motion for new trial—on appeal.

 Here, despite the court’s February 27 order denying BFT’s request for continuance

and the appellant’s own admission that it retained new counsel in mid-March, BFT lodged

no objection to the court’s order until more than two months later, following the outcome

of the trial at which it failed to appear. To the contrary, BFT first objected to the February

order denying the request for a continuance and granting the motion to withdraw in its

motion for new trial, which was deemed denied. In so doing, BFT failed to preserve its

claims, and we therefore decline to address them on appeal.

 5
  BFT’s final contention is that the circuit court erred in denying the motion for new

trial. However, we have likewise held that a contemporaneous objection is required when a

new trial is sought on the basis of an irregularity under Arkansas Rule of Civil Procedure

59(a)(1), as BFT argues here. See Nash, supra. BFT cites the same conduct—that the circuit

court abused its discretion in granting its motion to withdraw and denying its motion for

continuance—in support of its argument that the court erred in denying its motion for new

trial. For the same reasons noted above, BFT has failed to preserve its argument. Moreover,

BFT has failed to demonstrate how the court’s actions constituted an abuse of discretion or

resulted in prejudice. BFT likewise fails to demonstrate how the court abused its discretion

in denying alternative relief pursuant to Rule 60.

 Finally, BFT does not advance any argument specifically addressing why the order

granting directed verdict in the City’s favor was erroneous.1

 Affirmed.

 ABRAMSON and VIRDEN, JJ., agree.

 Cox Law Firm, PLLC, by: S. Lance Cox, for appellant.

 Kit Williams, Blake Pennington, and Hannah Hungate, for appellee.

 1
 For further discussion, see BFT Rental, LLC v. City of Fayetteville, 2026 Ark. App. 526
(per curiam), issued this date.

 6

leads.caseName: Renaissance Midtown W. LLC v. Lividini & Co., LLC
leads.court: Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the State of New York
leads.text:
Renaissance Midtown W. LLC v Lividini & Co., LLC 
 2026 NY Slip Op 06265 
 October 27, 2026 
 Appellate Division, First Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 Renaissance Midtown West LLC, Plaintiff-Appellant, 
 v 
 Lividini & Company, LLC, et al., Defendants-Respondents. 

 Decided and Entered: October 27, 2026 
 Index No. 659242/24|Appeal No. 7380|Case No. 2025-06285| 
 Before: Webber, J.P., Kapnick, Shulman, Pitt-Burke, Hagler, JJ. 

 Berliner & Pilson, Great Neck (Richard J. Pilson of counsel), for appellant. 
 Tarter Krinsky & Drogin LLP, New York (David H. Wander of counsel), for respondents. 

 [*1] 
 Order, Supreme Court, New York County (Lyle E. Frank, J.), entered July 24, 2025, which granted defendants' motion to dismiss the amended complaint, unanimously affirmed, without costs. 
 The amended complaint was properly dismissed for lack of notice under paragraph 17(1) of the parties' lease. Paragraph 17(1) contains a conditional limitation permitting the landlord to terminate the lease for defaults other than nonpayment of rent— including "if the demised premises becomes vacant or deserted"— by serving a five-day notice to cure on the tenant "specifying the nature of said default." If the tenant fails to commence cure efforts within that period in good faith, "then Owner may serve a written three (3) days' notice of cancellation of th[e] lease upon Tenant," terminating the lease, and the tenant "shall remain liable as hereinafter provided." 
 The amended complaint specifically alleged that the tenant rendered the premises vacant while the lease remained in effect. This triggered the tenant's right to notice under paragraph 17(1) before plaintiff's reentry and reletting of the premises following the tenant's purportedly ineffective surrender ( see Holy Props. v Cole Prods. , 87 NY2d 130, 133-134 [1995]). 
 It does not avail plaintiff to argue that it was not intending to terminate the lease under this section but merely to collect unpaid rent owed for the balance of the lease term. The allegations that the tenant returned the keys without objection, following which plaintiff executed a new lease with a new tenant, are at odds with the continuation of the landlord-tenant relationship ( see e.g. Bay Plaza Estates v New York Univ. , 257 AD2d 472, 473 [1st Dept 1999]). In any event, both the lease and case law require notice to the tenant in advance of plaintiff's reentry and reletting of the premises ( see Holy Props. , 87 NY2d at 133-134 ). 
 Plaintiff's claims for unpaid amounts due under paragraphs 17(2) of the lease and 66 of the rider are also unavailing, as both provisions apply only when the tenant remains in possession of the premises. Paragraph 17(2) applies if "the notice provided for in [paragraph 17(1)] shall have been given, and the term shall expire as aforesaid; or if Tenant shall [be in] default in the payment of rent" or additional rent. The use of "or" excludes paragraph 17(2)'s application to circumstances to which paragraph 17(1) would apply ( see McKinney's Cons Laws of NY, Statutes § 235, Comment n 75). Because the amended complaint alleges that the tenant rendered the premises vacant, paragraph 17(1) applies here rather than paragraph 17(2). 
 [*2] 
 Paragraph 66 of the rider states, "Notwithstanding anything to the contrary in this lease it is agreed that any demand for rent may be made orally and no written notice of any kind shall be necessary as a condition precedent to commencement of a non-payment petition." This provision applies only where the tenant is in possession, as "a summary proceeding cannot be maintained against a tenant who is neither in possession nor claiming possession at the time of the commencement of the proceeding" ( Merrbill Holdings, LLC v Toscano , 59 Misc 3d 129[A] , *1-2, 2018 NY Slip Op 50410[U] [App Term, 2d Dept, 9th & 10th Jud Dists 2018]). 
 Accordingly, the claims in the amended complaint relying on allegations that the tenant's early vacatur in these circumstances did not constitute an effective surrender were properly dismissed under paragraph 17(1), as plaintiff was required to give notice to the tenant of its intention to reenter and relet the premises, which it acknowledges did not occur. Unlike in 622 Third Ave. Co. LLC v Hyatt Leader Ltd. ( 226 AD3d 463 [1st Dept 2024]), upon which plaintiff relies, the complaint contains no allegations that plaintiff responded to the tenant's notice of surrender of the premises by informing the tenant that the acceptance "was without prejudice to seeking damages for unpaid rent" ( id. at 464). Plaintiff acknowledges that there was no further communication between the parties after the tenant's counsel gave notice of its vacatur in August 2020 until plaintiff commenced this action in November 2024. 
 The court correctly dismissed the claims for breach of guaranty and for piercing the corporate veil against the tenant's principal. As the court properly determined, plaintiff failed to sufficiently allege the existence of a written and executed guaranty or to provide documentary evidence of the guaranty ( see General Obligations Law § 5-701[a] [2]). Although the lease submitted with the amended complaint contains a standard form guaranty, the form is blank and unexecuted. Plaintiff has not sufficiently alleged that a written and executed guaranty exists, nor has it asserted facts warranting leave to replead. 
 [*3] 
 With respect to the claim seeking to pierce the corporate veil, as an initial matter, the doctrine does not support a separately pleaded claim; "it is an assertion of facts and circumstances which will persuade the court to impose the corporate obligation on its owners" ( Cortlandt St. Recovery Corp. v Bonderman , 31 NY3d 30, 47 [2018]). To invoke the doctrine at the pleadings stage, plaintiff must allege that the tenant's principal "exercised complete domination and control over the corporation and abused the privilege of doing business in the corporate form to perpetrate a wrong or injustice" ( id. at 48 [internal quotation marks omitted]). The amended complaint asserts a bare allegation that the principal failed to maintain a separate bank account from the tenant in order to avoid damages. This allegation does not support plaintiff's contention that the principal dominated and controlled the corporation to perpetrate a wrong resulting in plaintiff's injury. 
 We have considered plaintiff's remaining contentions and find them unavailing. 
 THIS CONSTITUTES THE DECISION AND ORDER OF THE SUPREME COURT, APPELLATE DIVISION, FIRST DEPARTMENT. 
 ENTERED: October 27, 2026

Filed 10/27/26 Masoud v. JPMorgan Chase Bank CA4/1 

NOT TO BE PUBLISHED IN OFFICIAL REPORTS 
California Rules of Court, rule 8.1115(a), prohibits courts and parties from citing or relying on opinions 
not certified for publication or ordered published, except as specified by rule 8.1115(b). This opinion 
has not been certified for publication or or dered published for purposes of rule 8.1115. 
COURT OF APPEAL, FOURTH APPELLATE DISTRICT 
DIVISION ONE 
STATE OF CALIFORNIA 

NORA MASOUD, 
 Plaintiff and Appellant, 
 v. 
JPMORGAN CHASE BANK N.A. et al., 
 Defendants and Respondents. 
D085594 

(San Diego Super. Ct. 
No. 37-2015-00035457-CU-
OR-CTL) 

 APPEAL from a judgment of the Superior Court of San Diego County, 
Michael T. Smyth, Judge. Reversed. 
 Foley Law Center and Michael T. Stoller, for Plaintiff and Appellant. 
 Bryan Cave Leighton Paisner, Glenn Jeffrey Plattner and David James 
Root, for Defendants and Respondents. 

2 
 Nora Masoud appeals the order granting summary judgment for 
JPMorgan Chase and U.S. Bank National Association on her claim of 
wrongful foreclosure, asserting there was no admissible evidence that the 
banks possessed authority to foreclose. We agree, as the banks not only 
failed to lay the foundation for a predecessor bank’s documents necessary 
to establish this authority, but their affiant lacked independent personal 
knowledge about indispensable facts concerning Masoud’s mortgage. Finding 
no other basis for this authority in the current record, the judgment must 
be reversed. 
FACTUAL AND PROCEDURAL BACKGROUND 
A. Masoud’s Mortgage Loan 
Masoud bought a home in San Diego in October 2000 with a loan from 
Washington Mutual Bank, F.A.1 Her loan was secured by a deed of trust and 
an accompanying note giving the holder the right to demand that the trustee 
foreclose on the mortgage were she to default on her payments.2 In July 
2005, Masoud refinanced her loan with WaMu for the third and final time. 
Later in 2005, WaMu decided to securitize some of its mortgage loans 
by executing pooling and servicing agreements (PSAs) to sell them into 
trusts, including the one relevant here: the “WaMu Mortgage Pass-Through 
Certificates Series 2005–AR14” created in October 2005 (AR14 trust). 

1 Multiple Washington Mutual entities were involved in the transactions 
described below. Neither party indicates that the role of any specific 
Washington Mutual entity is relevant to this appeal; and so, we use “WaMu” 
to refer to these entities generally. 
2 Because we decide this appeal on evidentiary grounds, we do not delve 
into the details of deeds of trust or this securitization process we describe 
below. Yvanova v. New Century Mortgage Corp. (2016) 62 Cal.4th 919, 926–
928 (Yvanova) provides helpful background into these areas. 

3 
The trust documents initially identified WaMu as the servicer of the trust 
and LaSalle Bank National Association as its trustee. Eventually, U.S. Bank 
National Association (U.S. Bank) became the trustee and served in that role 
at all relevant times. JPMorgan Chase N.A. (Chase) and U.S. Bank 
(together, the banks) maintain that WaMu transferred Masoud’s mortgage 
loan to the AR14 trust, although no assignment of this interest 
was contemporaneously recorded. 
In September 2008, WaMu failed after the housing market crash. 
The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, as WaMu’s appointed receiver, 
sold substantially all of the failed bank’s assets to Chase. Accordingly, Chase 
maintains that it took over WaMu’s role as servicer of the AR14 trust. 
Around the same time, Chase informed Masoud that it would be servicing 
her loan. 
In February 2011, the banks executed a limited power of attorney 
(POA) that gave Chase authority to take certain actions reserved for the 
trustee of the AR14 trust (i.e., U.S. Bank), including to foreclose on mortgage 
loans in default. Claiming to be acting under this authority, Chase initiated 
foreclosure proceedings on Masoud’s loan in September 2011 after she had 
fallen behind on her payments. That same month, Chase executed and 
recorded two documents: (1) as the successor in interest to WaMu, an 
assignment of the beneficial interests in Masoud’s mortgage loan to U.S. 
Bank as trustee of the AR14 trust (the 2011 assignment), which Washington 
testified was meant to memorialize the earlier transfer of her mortgage to the 
AR14 trust even though the effective date of the assignment was September 
6, 2011, and (2) a notice of default and election to sell the property under 
California’s nonjudicial foreclosure procedures. Masoud’s property was 
eventually sold at a trustee’s sale in October 2018. 

4 
B. The Summary Judgment Proceedings 
Masoud filed her initial complaint in October 2015, and in January 
2019, a judgment of dismissal was entered after the court sustained the 
banks’ demurrer without leave to amend. We reversed and remanded this 
matter so that Masoud could assert a claim of wrongful foreclosure. (Masoud 
v. JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. (May 26, 2020, D075582) [nonpub. opn.] 
(Masoud).) She alleges in what is now the operative complaint, among other 
things, that her mortgage was never transferred to the AR14 trust and 
therefore neither Chase nor U.S. Bank possessed the authority to foreclose. 
The banks moved for summary judgment, claiming there was no triable 
dispute that Masoud’s loan had been transferred to the AR14 trust. They 
supported their claim with two declarations by Dorothy Washington, a 
Chase “authorized signer” who does not indicate she ever worked at WaMu. 
Washington did not describe her job responsibilities or indicate that she 
possessed any knowledge about these kinds of trusts or the procedures any 
bank had used to set them up. Rather, she based her testimony solely on the 
contents of the records Chase maintained in connection with Masoud’s loan—
including records received from WaMu—all of which she claimed met the 
requirements to admit them as business records under Evidence Code section 
1271.3 
The main document Washington relied on is a one-page excerpt from a 
computer printout entitled “legal loan listing” for the AR14 trust (AR14 loan 
listing). This document, which has an entry for Masoud’s loan, appears to 
have been run by WaMu before the AR14 trust closing date and purports to 
identify the loans that someone thought or intended would become part of 

3 Later undesignated statutory references are to the Evidence Code. 

5 
the trust. As Washington describes it, this printout was the “mortgage loan 
schedule” required by the PSA even though the markings on the document do 
not identify it as such. She also testified that the 2011 assignment “merely 
memorialize[d] in a recorded document the fact that the beneficial interest 
in the loan had been transferred from WaMu to the AR-14 trust” in 2005. 
Finally, she claimed that the AR14 trust has always possessed the original 
note for the loan. 
For her part, Masoud contended that a document WaMu submitted 
to the United States Securities and Exchange Commission showed her loan 
had been transferred to a different trust before the AR14 trust was created. 
She also objected to Washington’s declaration testimony for lack of personal 
knowledge and failure to satisfy the business records exception to the 
hearsay rule for any of the documents she testified about. 
The trial court granted the banks’ motion. It started by overruling 
Masoud’s objections to Washington’s declaration, including to find that she 
had “provided sufficient foundation and authentication for the documents 
attached to her declaration.” The court also sustained the defendants’ 
objections to Masoud’s evidence that her loan was transferred to a different 
trust. Crediting Washington’s testimony that Masoud’s loan had been 
transferred to the AR14 trust, the court found there was no triable 
controversy that Chase, through the power of attorney it executed with U.S. 
Bank, was authorized to foreclose on Masoud’s loan. 
DISCUSSION 
In reversing the judgment of dismissal, we observed that “it remains a 
factual question as to which persons or entities held the beneficial interest in 
the deed of trust at the time of the foreclosure.” (Masoud, supra, D075582.) 
Masoud claims this is still an open question because the banks did not proffer 

6 
admissible evidence that the AR14 trust held this interest as required to 
meet their initial burden to show they had authority to foreclose on her 
mortgage.4 She further contends that even if the banks could make the 
required showing, there was enough admissible countervailing evidence 
for her claim to survive summary judgment. The banks disagree in both 
respects. 
“The party moving for summary judgment bears the burden of 
persuasion that there is no triable issue of material fact and that he is 
entitled to judgment as a matter of law.” (Aguilar v. Atlantic Richfield Co. 
(2001) 25 Cal.4th 826, 850.) The moving party “bears an initial burden of 
production to make a prima facie showing of the nonexistence of any triable 
issue of material fact” (id. at p. 849), either that “ ‘one or more elements of’ 
the ‘cause of action’ ” in question “ ‘cannot be established,’ ” or that “ ‘there 
is a complete defense’ thereto’ ” (id. at p. 853). “[I]f he carries his burden 
of production, he causes a shift, and the opposing party is then subjected 
to a burden of production of his own to make a prima facie showing of the 

4 The court’s rulings on Masoud’s objections to Washington’s testimony 
were not addressed in detail in the parties’ briefs. Accordingly, we requested 
supplemental briefing on three questions: “(1) On what basis could 
Washington, as a Chase employee, possess personal knowledge that WaMu 
transferred its interest in Masoud’s loan to the [AR14] trust in 2005, as 
required by Code of Civil Procedure section 437c, subdivision (d)? [¶] (2) 
Similarly, on what basis could Washington satisfy all the elements of 
Evidence Code section 1271 for any WaMu documents created in 2005 ... ? 
[Citations]. [¶] (3) If Masoud’s objections had been sustained, could Chase 
have satisfied its initial burden to make a prima facie showing of the 
nonexistence of a triable issue of material fact?” In addition, the statements 
in Washington’s second declaration merely expound upon the testimony of 
her first declaration, and thus we treat Masoud’s objections as covering both 
declarations. 

7 
existence of a triable issue of material fact.” (Id. at p. 850.) We review an 
order granting a summary judgment motion de novo. (Id. at p. 860.) 
“A beneficiary or trustee under a deed of trust who conducts an illegal, 
fraudulent or willfully oppressive sale of property may be liable to the 
borrower for wrongful foreclosure.” (Yvanova, supra, 62 Cal.4th at p. 929.) 
“A foreclosure initiated by one with no authority to do so is wrongful for 
purposes of such an action.” (Ibid.) Because “only the original beneficiary, its 
assignee or an agent of one of these has the authority to instruct the trustee 
to initiate and complete a nonjudicial foreclosure sale,” the banks bore the 
initial burden to prove that they fit into one of these categories. (Ibid.; accord 
Herrera v. Deutsche Bank National Trust Co. (2011) 196 Cal.App.4th 1366, 
1378 [bank not entitled to summary judgment on wrongful foreclosure claim 
because it failed to show a chain of ownership that would establish it was the 
true beneficiary under the deed of trust].) 
We start with Masoud’s evidentiary objections to the AR14 loan listing 
because this document is the linchpin of the banks’ case. Computer printouts 
“are admissible and are presumed to be an accurate representation of the 
data in the computer,” but if they are “offered for the truth ... they must 
qualify under some hearsay exception, such as [section] 1271.” (Aguimatang 
v. California State Lottery (1991) 234 Cal.App.3d 769, 797.) As noted, the 
trial court—erroneously in Masoud’s vie
