 v.

 UNITED STATES ARMY CORPS OF ENGINEERS, Charleston District;
 LIEUTENANT GENERAL WILLIAM H. GRAHAM, JR., in his official capacity
 as Chief of Engineers; UNITED STATES ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION
 AGENCY; LEE M. ZELDIN, in his official capacity as Administrator of the U.S.
 Environmental Protection Agency; UNITED STATES FISH AND WILDLIFE
 SERVICE; LIEUTENANT COLONEL TODD MAINWARING, in his official
 capacity as Commander of the Charleston District; DANIEL P. DRISCOLL, in his
 official capacity as Secretary of the U.S. Army; DOUG BURGUM, in his official
 capacity as Secretary of the United States Department of the Interior,

 Defendants - Appellees,

 and

 TRACT 1 TIMBER, LLC; SEVEN STICKS, LLC; TRACT 7, LLC; CAINHOY
 LAND AND TIMBER, LLC,

 Intervenors/Defendants - Appellees.

 Appeal from the United States District Court for the District of South Carolina, at
 Charleston. Richard Mark Gergel, District Judge. (2:22-cv-02727-RMG)

 Argued: September 10, 2026 Decided: October 23, 2026
 USCA4 Appeal: 25-1797 Doc: 75 Filed: 10/23/2026 Pg: 2 of 16

 Before AGEE, THACKER, and BERNER, Circuit Judges.

 Affirmed by published opinion. Judge Thacker wrote the opinion in which Judge Agee
 and Judge Berner joined.

 ARGUED: Catherine Moore Wannamaker, SOUTHERN ENVIRONMENTAL LAW
 CENTER, Charleston, South Carolina, for Appellants. Jacob David Ecker, UNITED
 STATES DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE, Washington, D.C.; Michael Rhett DeHart,
 ADAMS & REESE LLP, Charleston, South Carolina, for Appellees. ON BRIEF:
 Christopher, K. DeScherer, Emily C. Wyche, SOUTHERN ENVIRONMENTAL LAW
 CENTER, Charleston, South Carolina, for Appellants. Adam R.F. Gustafson, Principal
 Deputy Assistant Attorney General, Rebecca Jaffe, Kristen Sarna, Environment and
 Natural Resources Division, UNITED STATES DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE,
 Washington, D.C., for Federal Appellees.

 2
 USCA4 Appeal: 25-1797 Doc: 75 Filed: 10/23/2026 Pg: 3 of 16

 THACKER, Circuit Judge:

 The United States Army Corps of Engineers (the “Corps”) issued a permit pursuant

 to Section 404 of the Clean Water Act (“CWA”) for the development of the Cainhoy

 Plantation (“Cainhoy”), a residential and commercial development in Charleston, South

 Carolina, after determining the proposed project was the least environmentally damaging

 practicable alternative (“LEDPA”). South Carolina Coastal Conservation League,

 Charleston Waterkeeper, and South Carolina Wildlife Federation (collectively,

 “Appellants”) allege the Corps’ LEDPA determination was arbitrary and capricious

 because the Corps did not consider on-site alternatives affecting less than the proposed

 181.5 acres of wetlands impact. The district court granted summary judgment in favor of

 the Corps.

 Because we conclude the Corps conducted a thorough and reasoned analysis and

 did not act in an arbitrary or capricious manner, we affirm the district court.

 I.

 Tract 1 Timber, LLC, Seven Sticks, LLC, Tract 7, LLC, and Cainhoy Land and

 Timber, LLC (collectively, “Intervenors”) own approximately 16,000 acres of private land

 in Berkeley County, South Carolina. Cainhoy, the property at issue in this appeal,

 comprises 9,076 acres of the total acreage. Intervenors have used Cainhoy as a pine tree

 timber farm for the last 90 years. In 1996, the city of Charleston, South Carolina annexed

 Cainhoy into the city limits and sought to have Intervenors develop Cainhoy to allow for

 growth in the city.

 3
 USCA4 Appeal: 25-1797 Doc: 75 Filed: 10/23/2026 Pg: 4 of 16

 Today, Cainhoy’s surrounding areas have substantially transformed into residential

 and industrial development. Cainhoy is currently zoned as a Planned Unit Development

 (“PUD”), defined as consisting of “a tract or tracts of land under unified control, planned

 and developed as a whole in a single development stage or phased series of development

 stages according to an approved PUD Master Plan.” J.A. 1024–25. 1

 Though Cainhoy totals over 9,000 acres, including over 2,500 acres of wetlands, the

 proposed Cainhoy development will develop only 3,906 acres, including 181.5 acres of

 wetlands. The remaining acres are to be placed in conservation easements and/or

 restrictive covenants to permanently protect the property. Cainhoy is planned to be a mixed

 use commercial and residential development, eventually containing residences, schools,

 medical and assisted living facilities, and other community services.

 In order to accomplish the goal of developing Cainhoy, Intervenors began applying

 for the required permits in 2012, including a CWA Section 404 permit. A Section 404

 permit was required because the development would affect wetlands on the property. An

 early design of the project called for 1,820.1 acres of wetlands impact. But, “[t]hrough the

 avoidance and minimization process, [Intervenors] expressed [a] desire for a conservation

 minded, environmentally sensitive” development. J.A. 919. To accomplish this, the Corps

 and Intervenors focused on only affecting wetlands necessary for road crossings, feasible

 lot development, and essential storm water ponds. As a result, the wetlands impact was

 1
 Citations to the “J.A.” refer to the Joint Appendix filed by the parties in this appeal.

 4
 USCA4 Appeal: 25-1797 Doc: 75 Filed: 10/23/2026 Pg: 5 of 16

 reduced to 187.9 acres. And, in 2022, Intervenors and the Corps further decreased the

 wetlands impact to 181.5 acres.

 In March 2018, pursuant to Section 404 of the CWA, the Corps provided initial

 notice to the public and invited comments regarding the proposed project. The Corps

 received a significant number of comments and addressed each one, spanning 84 pages, in

 an Environment Assessment (the “EA”). After considering all of the public comments, the

 Corps detailed its decision and findings in the EA, which it issued in 2022.

 The Corps conducted an extensive EA, which included a review of the proposed

 plan, 14 alternative plans, and a no action option. The no action option entailed denying

 Intervenors’ permit and leaving Cainhoy open for future, independent development. To

 help guide its analysis of the alternatives, the Corps first determined the project’s overall

 purpose. The Corps described the project’s purpose as a development plan “to construct a

 mixed use development to include residential, commercial, educational, office and

 government facilities with access to major traffic arteries that has the demographic support,

 zoning, infrastructure and access to schools and hospitals to help meet the needs of the

 growing Charleston, South Carolina metropolitan area.” J.A. 931.

 The Corps’ nine off-site alternative plans were located in the Charleston area.

 Consistent with the purpose of the project, the Corps considered whether each alterative

 satisfied certain criteria in determining whether an off-site alternative was practicable. In

 particular, the Corps evaluated whether the off-site alternatives

 • were located within 50 miles of Charleston, South Carolina;
 • had a commute time of 45 minutes or less;

 5
 USCA4 Appeal: 25-1797 Doc: 75 Filed: 10/23/2026 Pg: 6 of 16

 • contained a minimum of 7,500 acres with 5,000 acres developable uplands 2;
 • were within a ten mile radius of an interstate or four lane major highway;
 • were able to be developed and not currently part of a planned development;
 • had access to utilities infrastructure (available and practicable);
 • were appropriately zoned for mixed-use development.

 Each of the nine off-site alternatives was determined to be impracticable by the Corps

 because none satisfied the required criteria.

 The Corps also considered four on-site alternatives but determined each would have

 a greater impact on wetlands than the proposed plan. Finally, the Corps considered a plan

 proposed by Appellants -- the “Dover plan.” 3 The Dover plan included four versions,

 ranging from no wetlands impact to 13.2 acres of wetlands impact. But no version of the

 Dover plan accounted for the entire Cainhoy property -- roughly 8,000 acres would be left

 undeveloped under each iteration. The Corps concluded this would likely contribute

 significantly to future wetlands impacts because of the possibility of future development

 of the remaining acreage, and because no version contained preservation or conservation

 efforts for the undeveloped land. Moreover, the Corps determined that the Dover plan was

 a “distinctly different project” and therefore did not comply with the project’s overall

 purpose. J.A. 1052.

 2
 Uplands are areas of “high land especially at some distance from the sea.” Upland,
 Merriam-Webster, https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/upland
 [https://perma.cc/7VWP-5CP7] (last visited Oct. 6, 2026).
 3
 Appellants’ proposed plan was referred to as the Dover plan because it was
 prepared by Dover, Kohl, and Partners, an urban planning firm.

 6
 USCA4 Appeal: 25-1797 Doc: 75 Filed: 10/23/2026 Pg: 7 of 16

 Lastly, the Corps considered a no action plan. Under a no action plan, Intervenors’

 permit would be denied, leaving Cainhoy open to smaller parcel development plans. The

 Corps concluded that the no action plan would potentially impact more wetlands, and

 prevent the property from receiving the benefit of Intervenors’ “comprehensive approach

 to a compensatory mitigation plan that protects the most ecologically valuable on-site

 wetlands.” J.A. 1051.

 After a full analysis, the Corps determined that Intervenors’ proposed project was

 the LEDPA and issued a Section 404 permit for it in May 2022. Appellants challenged the

 2022 permit, naming the Corps, the Fish and Wildlife Service, and the Environmental

 Protection Agency (the “EPA”) as defendants. Appellants argued that the Corps acted

 arbitrarily and capriciously in issuing the permit, and raised their challenges pursuant to

 the CWA citizen suit provision and the Administrative Procedure Act (the “APA”).

 The Corps moved to dismiss the CWA citizen suit provision claim, arguing the

 court’s jurisdiction arose pursuant to the APA instead. But the district court denied the

 motion and held that its subject matter jurisdiction derived from the citizen suit provision

 of the CWA. Therefore, the court dismissed the APA claim. In so holding, the district

 court relied on National Wildlife Federation v. Hanson, 859 F.2d 313 (4th Cir. 1988).

 Subsequently, the parties filed cross motions for summary judgment, and the district

 court granted summary judgment in favor of the Corps and Intervenors, dismissing the case

 with prejudice. The district court reaffirmed its conclusion that jurisdiction lay pursuant

 to the CWA, not the APA. And on the merits, the district court held that the Corps’ actions

 7
 USCA4 Appeal: 25-1797 Doc: 75 Filed: 10/23/2026 Pg: 8 of 16

 were neither arbitrary nor capricious because it conducted an extensive analysis of

 numerous alternatives in arriving at its LEDPA determination.

 Appellants timely appealed, arguing that the district court erred in concluding that

 the Corps’ LEDPA determination was not arbitrary or capricious.

 II.

 “We review the district court’s legal conclusions regarding its own subject matter

 jurisdiction de novo.” Flame S.A. v. Freight Bulk Pte. Ltd., 762 F.3d 352, 356 (4th Cir.

 2014) (internal citation omitted). “Our review of a district court’s grant of summary

 judgment is de novo.” Deque Sys. Inc. v. Browserstack, Inc., 177 F.4th 585, 598 (4th Cir.

 2026). “Summary judgment is appropriate when there is no genuine issue of material fact

 and the moving party is entitled to judgment as a matter of law.” Sigley v. ND Fairmont

 LLC, 129 F.4th

leads.caseName: Castillo v. Belkorp AG, LLP
leads.text:
Filed 10/23/26 
CERTIFIED FOR PUBLICATION 
IN THE COURT OF APPEAL OF THE STATE OF CALIFORNIA 
FIFTH APPELLATE DISTRICT 

STEVEN CASTILLO, 

 Plaintiff and Respondent, 

 v. 

BELKORP AG, LLP, 

 Defendant and Appellant. 

F090527 

(Super. Ct. No. CV-25-001186) 

OPINION 
APPEAL from a judgment of the Superior Court of Stanislaus County. John R. 
Mayne, Judge. 
Fisher & Phillips, Alden J. Parker, Yuri Khadka and Erin J. Price for Defendant 
and Appellant. 
Justice Law Corporation, Douglas Han, Christoper K. Petersen and Michael W. 
Jones for Plaintiff and Respondent. 
-ooOoo- 

2. 
This is an employment-related dispute between defendant/appellant Belkorp AG, 
LLC (Belkorp) and plaintiff/respondent Stephen Castillo. Former employee Castillo 
brought purely nonindividual claims under Labor Code section 2698 et seq.,1 the Private 
Attorneys General Act (PAGA), against Belkorp. Belkorp filed a motion to compel 
arbitration, which the trial court denied. In this appeal, Belkorp contends the court erred 
by: (1) failing to adjudicate the merits of its motion to compel arbitration; (2) concluding 
that Castillo could maintain a PAGA action alleging only nonindividual PAGA claims; 
and (3) failing to order the parties to arbitration. We affirm. 
BACKGROUND 
From May 2021, to his termination in late January 2024, Castillo worked for 
Belkorp as a service technician. According to Belkorp’s Director of Human Resources, 
in late December 2020, Castillo completed onboarding documents. Included within the 
onboarding documents was an arbitration agreement that provided: “Any dispute or 
controversy arising out of or relating to the employment, or termination of employment, 
of [Castillo] by [Belkorp], … shall be resolved by binding arbitration.” As to class 
actions or collective actions, the arbitration agreement specifically provided: “[Castillo] 
and [Belkorp] agree to bring any claim or dispute in arbitration on an individual basis 
only, and not as a class or collective action; [Castillo] and [Belkorp] waive any right for a 
dispute or claim to be brought, heard, or decided as a class or collective action, and the 
arbitrator has no power or authority to preside over a class or collective action ( ‘[c]lass 
[a]ction [w]aiver’).” The arbitration agreement did not provide for any exceptions to the 
class action waiver. However, the arbitration agreement did provide that, if the class 
action waiver was found to be unenforceable, then the arbitrator would be “without 
authority to preside over a class or collective action and any class or collective action 
[would have to] be brought in a court of competent jurisdiction.” 
In November 2024, pursuant to section 2699.3, Castillo provided written notice to 
the Labor and Workforce Development Agency (LWDA) of Labor Code violations by 

1 All further statutory references are to the Labor Code unless otherwise noted. 
3. 
Belkorp. The LWDA did not respond to Castillo’s notice within the 65-day statutory 
waiting period of section 2699.3, subdivision (a)(2)(A). As a result, Castillo became 
authorized to pursue civil penalties under PAGA as the proxy or agent of the LWDA. 
(§ 2699.3, subd. (a)(2)(A).) 
In February 2025, Castillo filed a complaint for civil penalties against Belkorp in 
the Stanislaus County Superior Court. The complaint contained a single cause of action 
under PAGA based on various violations of the Labor Code. The complaint expressly 
stated that Castillo brought the action “as an exclusively representative action on behalf 
of other current and former aggrieved employees of [Belkorp] for penalties .…” The 
complaint further emphasized that Castillo sought “only to prosecute his non-individual 
PAGA claims and does not seek to prosecute any individual PAGA claims against 
[Belkorp].” The complaint sought penalties “on behalf of current and former aggrieved 
employees of [Belkorp] and exclusively as a proxy of the State of California,” along with 
attorney fees and costs. 
In July 2025, Belkorp filed a motion to compel arbitration. 
On September 5, 2025, the trial court conducted a hearing and issued a ruling that 
denied the motion to compel. The court noted some procedural irregularities with respect 
to Belkorp’s motion, including a breach of the duty of candor based on Belkorp’s failure 
to advise that Leeper v. Shipt, Inc. (2024) 107 Cal.App.5th 1001, review granted 
April 16, 2025, S289305 (Leeper) had been under review since April 16, 2025. On the 
merits of the motion, the court explained: 
“Review has been granted in Leeper and Rodriguez v. Packers 
Sanitation Services LTD (2025) 109 Cal.App.5th 69, but CRST Expedited, 
Inc. v. Superior Court of Fresno County (2025) 112 Cal.App.5th 872 has 
taken the opposite side of the Leeper decision. The California Supreme 
Court in its order under [California Rules of Court, rule] 8.1115(e)(3) has 
permitted trial courts to use Leeper to show a split of authority. 
“Thus, the Court must weigh the logic of both cases. [Belkorp] 
declined to address CRST in its initial filing or its reply. This decision not 
to cite to controlling authority and not to address it appears to this Court to 
be a concession on the merits.” 
4. 
In September 2025, Belkorp appealed the denial of its motion to compel. 
DISCUSSION 
I. A PAGA ACTION WITH ONLY NONINDIVIDUAL PAGA CLAIMS 
A. Parties’ Arguments 
1. Belkorp 
Belkorp contends the trial court erred by permitting Castillo to pursue only 
nonindividual PAGA claims for several reasons. First, Belkorp argues that Castillo’s 
complaint of necessity includes an individual PAGA claim that is brought on his own 
behalf because PAGA requires an aggrieved employee to bring a claim on his own behalf 
and on behalf of other employees. Belkorp argues that, as explained in Leeper, the 
common meaning of “and” as conjunctive, when combined with the Legislature’s 
decision to use the term and instead of or, means that an employee only has standing to 
bring a PAGA action that consists both of individual and nonindividual PAGA claims. 
Second, Belkorp argues that permitting Castillo to pursue only PAGA claims on 
behalf of other employees is contrary to Viking River Cruises, Inc. v. Moriana (2022) 596 
U.S. 639 (Viking River) and Adolph v. Uber Technologies, Inc. (2023) 14 Cal.5th 1104 
(Adolph). Belkorp argues that these decisions envision and mandate that a PAGA action 
will be divided between individual and nonindividual PAGA claims, with the individual 
PAGA claims going to arbitration and the nonindividual PAGA claims remaining in 
court. 
Third, Belkorp points out that the Legislature amended PAGA effective July 1, 
2024 (the July amendments), yet failed to include amendments that expressly permit a 
PAGA action consisting only of nonindividual PAGA claims. Belkorp argues this means 
that the Legislature did not intend to alter Viking River and Adolph and thus, intended for 
all PAGA actions to include individual and nonindividual PAGA claims. 
Finally, Belkorp acknowledges that CRST Expedited, Inc. v. Superior Court 
(2025) 112 Cal.App.5th 872, review granted September 17, 2025, S292005 (CRST) and 
Galarsa v. Dolgen California, LLC (2025) 115 Cal.App.5th 1, review granted 
5. 
December 17, 2025, S293545 (Galarsa) have held that a plaintiff may bring a PAGA 
action consisting only of nonindividual PAGA claims. However, Belkorp argues that 
these cases are procedurally and factually different from this case and were expressly 
limited to the pre-July 1, 2024 version of PAGA, whereas this case is governed by the 
version of PAGA that became effective on July 1, 2024. Belkorp also notes that the 
July amendments require a plaintiff to have experienced each Labor Code violation 
alleged. Belkorp argues this change requires an aggrieved employee to pursue a PAGA 
action that consists of individual and nonindividual PAGA claims based on Labor Code 
violations that were personally experienced, which is consistent with Viking River and 
Adolph. 
2. Castillo 
Castillo contends the trial court correctly permitted him to pursue only 
nonindividual PAGA claims. In part,2 Castillo argues that our court in CRST and 
Galarsa explained the term and was ambiguous and should be construed as an inclusive 
disjunctive that means either and or or. Castillo argues that CRST and Galarsa have 
already considered and rejected most of Belkorp’s arguments, including its reliance on 
Leeper, and that CRST and Galarsa should continue to be followed. Castillo also argues 
that any factual differences that exist between this case and CRST and Galarsa are 

2 Castillo also argues that Belkorp waived and is estopped through the doctrine of invited 
error from making any challenge to the trial court’s adoption of CRST because Belkorp did not 
address CRST in either its motion to compel arbitration or its reply. We disagree. First, an 
“error is invited when a party purposefully induces the commission of [the] error,” and “requires 
some form of active advocacy for the decision now claimed as error on appeal.” (Khoiny v. 
Dignity Health (2022) 76 Cal.App.5th 390, 419.) Here, there was no active advocacy or 
purposeful inducement by Belkorp for the trial court to follow CRST; there was simply reliance 
on Leeper and a failure to address CRST. Second, courts often find a concession by a party’s 
failure to respond to an opponent’s argument. (E.g., Ross v. Superior Court (2022) 77 
Cal.App.5th 667, 681.) However, this is not an inexorable rule, and courts retain discretion to 
consider the “conceding” party’s new arguments. (People v. Hill (1992) 3 Cal.4th 959, 995, fn. 
3; Griffin v. The Haunted Hotel, Inc. (2015) 242 Cal.App.4th 490, 505.) Here, by relying on 
Leeper during the motion to compel, Belkorp was implicitly urging the court to follow Leeper 
and to reject CRST. Because Leeper and CRST are irreconcilable, and Belkorp continues to rely 
on Leeper in this appeal, we will not find waiver or a concession for purposes of this appeal. 
(Hill, at p. 995, fn. 3; Griffin, at p. 505.) 
6. 
immaterial, and the July amendments do not affect these cases’ conclusion that an 
aggrieved employee who has been duly authorized as the LWDA’s representative may 
bring “a PAGA action that asserts only nonindividual PAGA claims.” (CRST, supra, 112 
Cal.App.5th at p. 913, review granted.) Such actions are sometimes referred to as 
“ ‘headless’ PAGA actions.” (Galarsa, supra, 115 Cal.App.5th at p. 4, review granted.) 
B. Legal Standard 
1. Statutory Interpretation 
In construing a statute, courts must ascertain the intent of the Legislature in order 
to effectuate the statute’s purpose. (Shear Development Co., LLC v. California Coastal 
Com. (2026) 19 Cal.5th 334, 366; Turrieta v. Lyft, Inc. (2024) 16 Cal.5th 664, 687.) 
Courts first examine the statutory language, but consider the entire substance of the 
statutory scheme without considering particular language in isolation. (Shear 
Development, at p. 366; Turrieta, at p. 687.) If the language is clear and unambiguous, 
then courts generally must follow the language’s plain meaning. (Shear Development, at 
p. 366; Turrieta, at p. 687.) However, if the statutory language is ambiguous, meaning 
that the language supports more than one reasonable construction, then courts may 
consider other extrinsic aids, such as the statute’s purpose, legislative history, and public 
policy. (Shear Development, at p. 366; Turrieta, at p. 687.) Appellate courts review 
questions of statutory interpretation de novo (Adolph, supra, 14 Cal.5th at p. 1120). 
2. PAGA 
PAGA was enacted to remedy “ ‘systemic underenforcement’ ” of the Labor 
Code. (Estrada v. Royalty Carpet Mills, Inc. (2024) 15 Cal.5th 582, 598.) In order to 
achieve maximum compliance with the Labor Code, PAGA provides that civil penalties, 
which would otherwise be recovered only by the LWDA, “may, as an alternative, be 
recovered through a civil action brought by an aggrieved employee on behalf of the 
e

IN THE COURT OF CHANCERY OF THE STATE OF DELAWARE

RICHARD F. BURKHART, WILLIAM E. )
KELLY, RICHARD S. LAVERY, THOMAS R. )
PRATT and GERALD GREEN, individually )
and on behalf of others similarly situated, )
 )
 Plaintiffs, )
 )
 v. ) C.A. No. 2018-0691-NAC
 )
GENWORTH FINANCIAL, INC.,
 )
GENWORTH HOLDINGS, INC. GENWORTH
 )
NORTH AMERICA CORPORATION,
 )
GENWORTH FINANCIAL INTERNATIONAL
 )
HOLDINGS, LLC and GENWORTH LIFE
 )
INSURANCE COMPANY,
 )
 Defendants. )

 MEMORANDUM OPINION

 Date Submitted: January 21, 2026
 Date Decided: October 23, 2026

Thomas A. Uebler, Adam J. Waskie, Sarah P. Kaboly, MCCOLLOM D’EMILIO
SMITH UEBLER LLC, Wilmington, Delaware; Edward F. Haber, Michelle H.
Blauner, Patrick J. Vallely, SHAPIRO HABER & URMY LLP; Counsel for Plaintiffs.
Srinivas M. Raju, Kevin Gallagher, Elizabeth J. Freud, RICHARDS, LAYTON &
FINGER, P.A., Wilmington, Delaware; Reid L. Ashinoff, Kenneth J. Pfaehler, T.
Carter White, DENTONS US LLP, New York, New York; John C. Hueston, Marshall
A. Camp, Padraic Foran, Zachary Murray, HUESTON HENNIGAN LLP, Los
Angeles, California; Counsel for Defendants.

COOK, V.C.
  The elderly or individuals with serious health conditions often struggle to do

everyday tasks without assistance or expensive supportive equipment. Long term

care insurance (“LTCI”) mitigates that risk and expense by providing funds to help

pay for assisted living and other supportive care. Given the nature of LTCI,

policyholders typically purchase coverage long before they begin receiving benefits.

Once a policyholder becomes eligible, LTCI benefits payments can last for years. As

a result, LTCI companies must carefully manage claims reserves to ensure they have

funds to pay benefits long into the future. Recent financial pressures caused by rising

claims costs, resistance to premium hikes, and increased longevity have caused many

LTCI companies to restructure their business or exit the market.

 Defendants are a group of affiliated insurance companies that sell various

forms of insurance, including LTCI. In the mid-2010s, Defendants restructured their

LTCI business due to a series of economic and legal factors. Specifically, between

2015 and 2016, Defendants isolated their LTCI business from their other insurance

lines while repatriating it in the U.S. Executing that plan required terminating a

series of inter-entity reinsurance agreements that provided asset-backed financial

guarantees to support the LTCI liabilities. During the restructuring period, the

group’s LTCI underwriter also issued a series of dividends to its parent companies.

Plaintiffs filed this suit alleging that those actions constituted intentional and

constructive fraudulent transfers that violated the Delaware Uniform Fraudulent

Transfer Act (“DUFTA”). This decision addresses Defendants’ Motion for Summary

Judgment, Plaintiffs’ Rule 56(d) Motion, and Defendants’ Motion to Strike Plaintiffs’

 2
 Rule 56(d) Motion. For the reasons discussed herein, the Court grants Defendants’

Motion for Summary Judgment and denies both the Rule 56(d) Motion and Motion to

Strike as moot.

 I. BACKGROUND

 The following background discussion is drawn from the parties’ submissions

on the motion for summary judgment. “At this procedural stage, the court must view

the evidence in the light most favorable to the non-movant.” 1

A. The Parties

 Plaintiffs purport to represent a class of Defendant Genworth Life Insurance

Company (“GLIC”) LTCI policyholders and agents who expect to receive benefits and

commissions payments over the coming decades. 2 As of this decision’s submission

 1 Meteora Cap. Partners, LP v. Roadzen Inc., 2026 WL 2530118, at *1 (Del. Ch. Aug.

27, 2026) (citing Merrill v. Crothall-Am., Inc., 606 A.2d 96, 99 (Del. 1992)).

 2 See Plaintiffs’ Second Amended and Supplemental Class Action Complaint (“SAC”)

¶¶ 2–6, 14 (Dkt. 132). In January 2024, Plaintiffs sought certification of a class consisting of
all (1) beneficiaries of in-force GLIC LTCI policies and (2) agents entitled to future
commission payments based on their sale of GLIC LTCI policies. See Plaintiffs’ Motion for
Class Certification (Dkt. 291); Defendants’ Brief in Opposition to Plaintiffs’ Motion for Class
Certification (Dkt. 295). The Court deferred its ruling on class certification. See Transcript
of 6-13-2024 Oral Argument (Dkt. 347).
 3
 date, no policyholder Plaintiff has made a claim under their GLIC LTCI policy. 3

Similarly, each agent Plaintiff has received all commission payments due. 4

 Defendants Genworth Financial Inc. (“Genworth”), Genworth Holdings, Inc.

(“Holdings”), Genworth Financial International Holdings, LLC (“GFIH”), Genworth

North American Corporation (“Genworth NA”), and GLIC are a group of affiliated

insurance companies. 5 Through Holdings, Genworth indirectly owns and operates

the other Defendants. 6 Before the at-issue transactions, Genworth’s subsidiaries

included non-parties Brookfield Life Assurance Company Limited (“Brookfield”) and

Brookfield Life and Annuity Insurance Company Limited (“BLAIC”). 7 Genworth’s

corporate structure at that time was as follows: 8

 3 E.g., Transmittal Affidavit of Kenneth J. Pfaehler in Support of Defendants’ Motion

for Summary Judgment (“Pfaehler Aff.”), Ex. 9 at 28; Ex. 10 at 71–72 (D.I. 373). See also
Affidavit of Scott Goodman in Support of Defendants’ Motion for Summary Judgment
(“Goodman Aff.”), Ex. 28 (D.I. 377) (representing that GLIC has paid $18,242,015,710 in LTCI
benefits since the challenged transactions).

 4 E.g., Pfaehler Aff., Ex 12 at 46; Ex. 13 at 59–60. See also Goodman Aff., Ex. 28

(representing that GLIC has paid $953,632,281 in LTCI commissions since the challenged
transactions).

 5 See SAC ¶¶ 7–11. All Defendants, except for Genworth NA, are Delaware entities.
See id. ¶¶ 7–8, 10–11. Defendant Genworth NA is organized under Washington law. See id.
¶ 9.

 6 See id.Based on that control, this opinion refers to “Genworth” when referring to
the group as a whole or when discussing group-wide decisions or actions.

 7 See id. ¶¶ 122, 126.

 8 Plaintiffs’ Demonstrative from the January 21, 2026, Summary Judgment Hearing

at 6 (Dkt. 431). The Court includes the demonstrative for illustrative purposes only.
 4
 B. LTCI And Delaware Insurance Regulation

 LTCI covers nursing, assisted living, and other healthcare costs for people who

cannot perform daily tasks without assistance. 9 Genworth sells LTCI through

GLIC. 10 GLIC’s LTCI polices are “[g]uaranteed [r]enewable for [l]ife” so long as

 9 See Linhong Chen & Xiaocang Xu, Effect Evaluation of the Long-Term Care
Insurance (LTCI) System on the Health Care of the Elderly: A Review, 13 J. Multidisciplinary
Healthcare 863, 864 (2020) (“LTCI system . . . refers to an institutional arrangement to share
the nursing expenses incurred by people who cannot take care of themselves due to chronic
diseases or physical and psychological disability[.]”).

 10 See Pfaehler Aff., Ex. 1 at 1.

 5
 policyholders pay their annual premiums. 11 Given LTCI’s nature, 12 companies—

including Genworth—use complex actuarial formulas to project uncertain benefits

payouts over decades. 13 Recent macro effects have raised the risk profile of LTCI as

an insurance product generally, causing several insurance companies to scale down

their LTCI business or exit entirely. 14

 Genworth’s LTCI business is not immune from these headwinds and has

experienced similar financial strain. 15 In response to those pressures, GLIC has

repeatedly sought regulatory approval to raise its LTCI premiums pursuant to its

Multi-Year Rate Action Plan (“MYRAP”). 16

 11 E.g., id. at 21.

 12 Because LTCI helps cover costs associated with a loss of daily function and long-

term care, individuals often purchase coverage long before they receive benefits. See, e.g.,
Pfaehler Aff., Ex. 8. Once a policyholder becomes eligible, they typically receive LTCI
benefits for several years. See Jeffrey R. Brown & Amy Finkelstein, The Private Market for
Long-Term Care Insurance in the United States: A Review of the Evidence, 76 J. Risk & Ins.
5 (2009). Therefore, LTCI companies must carefully balance the premiums they receive in
the short term with the benefits they expect to pay out in the long term. See id.

 13 See Pfaehler Aff., Ex. 38 at 8–11; Ex. 39 at 9–12.

 14 See Pfaehler Aff., Ex. 39 at 10 (“Since 2000, all major determinants of premium

adequacy and product profitability had been deteriorating. Overall claim experience had
deteriorated substantially, and carriers were exiting the market. LTC[I] products were
materially underpriced and certain monoline LTC[I] companies were shown to be
undercapitalized. Insolvencies followed.”). See also Chen & Xu, supra note 9.

 15 See, e.g., Transmittal Affidavit of Thomas A. Uebler, Esquire to Plaintiffs’
Answering Brief in Opposition to Defendants’ Motion for Summary Judgment (“Uebler Aff.”),
Ex. 7 at 2 (D.I. 401) (“GLIC Margins Largely Eroded From Higher Expected Claims Cost.
Future Rate Actions Needed To Offset Higher Claim Cost & Support Positive Margins.”).

 16 See, e.g., id. at 4, 21. GLIC can increase the premiums LTCI policyholders pay when

actuarily justified, subject to state regulatory approval. See Pfaehler Aff., Ex. 1 (LTCI policy
disclosing GLIC’s ability to seek regulatory approval to raise premiums).
 6
  The Delaware Department of Insurance (“Department”), led by the Delaware

Insurance Commissioner (“Commissioner”), has broad statutory authorization to

regulate the insurance industry. 17 The Department regulates GLIC as a Delaware

domiciled insurance company. That regulation includes (1) testing GLIC’s cash flow

to monitor its capitalization; 18 (2) directing GLIC to answer questions concerning its

operations; 19 and (3) reviewing GLIC’s annual actuarial memorandum and audited

financials. 20 Once every five years, the Department audits GLIC’s “affairs,

transactions, accounts, records, documents, [] assets . . . and any other fact relevant

to its business methods, management, and its dealings with policyholders[.]” 21 The

Commissioner has broad authority to impose penalties, order corrective action, or

even take GLIC under supervision if its responses or finances are unsatisfactory. 22

 The Department also has authority over mergers among insurers.

Importantly, advance approval from the Commissioner is required before a proposed

merger involving a Delaware insurer can be consummated. The statute sets out

 17 See 18 Del. C. §§ 301–334, 526, 1108, 4930, 5005, 5006, 5901 et seq.

 18 See Goodman Aff., Exs. 18–22 (evidencing the ongoing regulatory dialogue between

GLIC and the Department).

 19 See, e.g., Goodman Aff., Ex. 4; Ex. 17.

 20 18 Del. Admin. C. §§ 301-2.0, 301-5.0. Similarly, the Department reviews GLIC’s
quarterly financials. See Goodman Aff. ¶ 8. In so doing, the Department considers GLIC’s
risk-based capital reports, which indicate whether the company holds sufficient capital based
on its risk profile. See 18 Del. C. § 5802; Goodman Aff., Ex. 5, Ex. 7.

 21 18 Del. Admin. C. § 101-3.1; see 18 Del. C. § 318.

 22 E.g., 18 Del. C. §§ 329, 5803–5806, 5905.

 7
 certain requirements, including filing the contemplated merger agreement and plan

with the Commissioner, notice to the stockholders of the insurers involved, and a

hearing. 23 Only after these statutory requirements are met may such a merger be

approved. Further, the Commissioner is not required to approve a proposed merger

if they find that the proposed transaction is one or more of the following:

 (1) Is contrary to law.

Appeal from the Order Entered September 30, 2025 
In the Court of Common Pleas of Bucks County Civil Division at No(s): 
2023-07605 

BEFORE: PANELLA, P.J.E., NICHOLS, J., and NEUMAN, J. 
MEMORANDUM BY NEUMAN, J.: FILED OCTOBER 23, 2026 
 Appellants, Katherine L. Frescatore and Robert Frescatore (her 
husband), appeal from the trial court’s entry of summary judgment in favor 
of Appellees, Loria Joint Venture, Giuseppe Loria, Michael Loria, Ermir Madani, 
Dave Marques, Arber Mullai, and Il Fiolo D’Olio, LLC.1 We affirm the entry of 
summary judgment in favor of Appellees but order the parties and trial court 
to amend the complaint and caption to fix an incorrect designation. 
____________________________________________ 
1 As discussed infra, Il Fiolo D’Olio, LLC was improperly designated in the 
Frescatores’ complaint as La Voglia, La Voglia Group, and La Voglia Italian 
Restaurant. However, it appears the complaint and caption were never 
amended to correct the designation. Further, as explained herein, John Doe 
A through Z are not legal parties to this action. 
J-A17044-26 
- 2 - 
 We glean the following pertinent background from our examination of 
the record. On December 4, 2023, the Frescatores filed a complaint sounding 
in negligence against Loria Joint Venture, John Doe A through Z, La Voglia, La 
Voglia Group, La Voglia Italian Restaurant, Giuseppe Loria, Michael Loria, 
Ermir Madani, Dave Marques, and Arber Mullai, after Mrs. Frescatore slipped 
and fell on snow or ice while walking to her husband’s car upon leaving La 
Voglia Italian Restaurant on December 20, 2021. 
 On February 7, 2024, Loria Joint Venture, Giuseppe Loria, and Michael 
Loria (collectively “Loria Appellees”) filed an answer with new matter and 
cross-claim against all other defendants.2, 3 On February 12, 2024, the 
Frescatores filed a reply to the Loria Appellees’ new matter. 
 On May 1, 2024, the Loria Appellees filed a motion to compel against 
the Frescatores. The Loria Appellees alleged they served the Frescatores with 
requests for interrogatories and production of documents on February 7, 
2024. According to the Loria Appellees, the Frescatores should have 
responded by no later than March 7, 2024, but failed to do so. On March 19, 
2024, the Loria Appellees advised the Frescatores their discovery responses 
____________________________________________ 
2 The record indicates some of the Loria Appellees are the commercial 
landlords for the property where La Voglia Italian Restaurant is located. See, 
e.g., Madani Appellees’ Answer, 5/17/24, at ¶¶ 57-67; Loria Appellees’ 
Response, 5/28/24, at ¶ 59; Madani Appellees’ Stipulation of Facts, 7/30/25, 
at ¶ 6. 

3 In the Loria Appellees’ cross-claim, they alleged — if the Frescatores’ 
allegations are proven — the other defendants are solely liable, jointly or 
severally liable along with them, and/or liable over them for indemnity and/or 
contribution pursuant to common law and contract. 
J-A17044-26 
- 3 - 
were overdue, but said they received no response. Consequently, the Loria 
Appellees asked the trial court to direct the Frescatores to provide discovery 
responses within twenty days. On May 6, 2024, the trial court issued a notice 
that the Loria Appellees’ motion to compel was not being acted upon by the 
court due to certain deficiencies with the motion. 
 On May 17, 2024, Ermir Madani, Dave Marques, Arber Mullai, and Il 
Fiolo D’Olio, LLC (collectively “Madani Appellees”) filed an answer with new 
matter and cross-claims.4 Therein, inter alia, they indicated Il Fiolo D’Olio, 
LLC was incorrectly identified as La Voglia, La Voglia Italian Restaurant, and 
La Voglia Group. See Madani Appellees’ Answer, 5/17/24, at 2 (stating Il Fiolo 
D’Olio, LLC was incorrectly identified as La Voglia and La Voglia Italian 
Restaurant); id. at ¶¶ 5-7 (denying La Voglia and La Voglia Italian Restaurant 
are jural entities, and denying the Frescatores’ allegations identifying La Voglia 
Group); see also Madani Appellees’ Praecipe to Attach Exhibit A, 5/23/24, at 
2 (indicating Il Fiolo D’Olio, LLC was incorrectly identified as La Voglia, La 
Voglia Italian Restaurant, and La Voglia Group).5 
____________________________________________ 
4 The record indicates the Madani Appellees operate La Voglia Italian 
Restaurant and are the commercial tenants of the Loria Appellees. See, e.g., 
Madani Appellees’ Answer, 5/17/24, at ¶¶ 57-67; Loria Appellees’ Response, 
5/28/24, at ¶ 59; Madani Appellees’ Stipulation of Facts, 7/30/25, at ¶ 6. 

5 In the Madani Appellees’ cross-claims, they claimed that — if they are found 
liable for the Frescatores’ injuries — the Frescatores’ injuries were caused by 
the acts and/or omissions of the other defendants, such that the other 
defendants are solely liable or liable over the Madani Appellees by way of 
contribution and/or indemnity. The Madani Appellees additionally asserted, 
(Footnote Continued Next Page) 
J-A17044-26 
- 4 - 
 On May 23, 2024, the Frescatores filed a reply to the new matter raised 
by the Madani Appellees. On May 28, 2024, the Loria Appellees filed a 
response to the cross-claims of the Madani Appellees. 
On May 29, 2024, the Loria Appellees re-filed their motion to compel, 
indicating they still had not received discovery responses from the 
Frescatores. On June 3, 2024, the trial court issued an order, directing the 
Fresactores to provide responses to the Loria Appellees’ discovery requests 
within twenty days or warning they may suffer sanctions upon further 
application. In the alternative, the trial court stated the Frescatores may file 
for a hearing within ten days. 
On December 26, 2024, the Madani Appellees filed a motion to compel, 
claiming they served the Frescatores with discovery on June 5, 2024. After 
the Frescatores failed to respond, the Madani Appellees said their counsel e-
mailed the Frescatores’ counsel, who asked for a thirty-day extension on July 
16, 2024. When the Frescatores again failed to answer discovery, the Madani 
Appellees’ counsel said they e-mailed the Frescatores’ counsel and requested 
the overdue discovery by December 13, 2024. According to the Madani 
Appellees, the Frescatores failed to comply. 
 On January 1, 2025, the trial court issued a case management order, 
stating the court administrator would consider the matter as ready for 
____________________________________________ 
pursuant to their commercial lease with the Loria Appellees, the Loria 
Appellees were responsible for common area maintenance and owe the 
Madani Appellees defense and indemnity. 
J-A17044-26 
- 5 - 
arbitration or trial on June 4, 2025. On February 6, 2025, the Madani 
Appellees re-filed their motion to compel. On February 18, 2025, the trial 
court granted the Madani Appellees’ motion to compel, ordering the 
Frescatores to respond to the Madani Appellees’ discovery requests within 
twenty days or risk sanctions upon further application. 
 On March 13, 2025, the Madani Appellees filed another motion to 
compel. They relayed that, in violation of the trial court’s February 18, 2025 
order, the Frescatores did not respond to their discovery requests. On March 
21, 2025, the trial court directed the Frescatores to provide responses to the 
Madani Appellees’ discovery within twenty days. It warned “[f]ailure to 
comply shall result in [the Frescatores’] preclusion from presenting evidence.” 
Order, 3/21/25. 
 On April 14, 2025, the Madani Appellees moved for sanctions, stating 
the Frescatores still had not provided responses to their discovery requests 
and asking the court to preclude the Frescatores from offering any evidence, 
witnesses, and testimony at arbitration and trial. On April 25, 2025, the trial 
court granted the Madani Appellees’ request for sanctions, and ordered that 
the Frescatores were precluded from offering evidence, witnesses, and 
testimony at arbitration and trial. 
 On May 7, 2025, the Frescatores filed a motion for reconsideration. 
They stated the suit was filed on December 4, 2023, and “[i]n the initial weeks 
and months[,] several attorneys at counsels [sic] law firm left to form a new 
firm, [and] there was some confusion about which files about which files [sic] 
J-A17044-26 
- 6 - 
were going to the new firm and which were remaining.” Frescatores’ Motion 
for Reconsideration, 5/7/25, at ¶ 3. They contended, “[a]s a result of this 
confusion, [the Frescatores’] counsel was unable to reach [them] to answer 
the discovery in a timely manner, yet it was being answered du [sic] to the 
intital [sic] discovery motion.” Id. at ¶ 4. They said, upon receiving the order 
for sanctions, they served their discovery responses on “Defendants”; 
however, based on the exhibit attached in support, the Frescatores answered 
the Loria Appellees’ discovery requests, instead of the Madani Appellees’ 
discovery requests. Id. at ¶ 6; see also id. at Exhibit C (attaching discovery 
responses to the Loria Appellees’ discovery requests, not the Madani 
Appellees’ discovery requests, and showing they were served on the Loria 
Appellees’ counsel, not the Madani Appellees’ counsel). The Frescatores, thus, 
sought reconsideration of the trial court’s order issuing sanctions. 
 The Madani Appellees filed a reply in opposition to the Frescatores’ 
motion for reconsideration. Among other things, they pointed out the 
Frescatores still had not provided responses to their discovery requests. 
 On June 6, 2025, the trial court denied the Frescatores’ motion for 
reconsideration. On June 17, 2025, the Frescatores filed a motion to modify 
the trial court’s April 25, 2025 order. Therein, among other things, they 
argued their late discovery responses have not caused prejudice, and that 
attorneys’ fees would have been a sufficient sanction under the circumstances. 
They requested oral argument, asserting no oral argument had been granted 
to date on these matters. 
J-A17044-26 
- 7 - 
 On July 1, 2025, the trial court scheduled the matter for trial in the 
August trial term. On July 2, 2025, the Loria Appellees filed a reply to the 
Frescatores’ motion for modification. Among other things, they argued the 
motion for modification should not be considered and/or should be denied, as 
it represents an improper second attempt to seek reconsideration. They also 
denied they were not prejudiced, stating they received no discovery responses 
until five days after the preclusion order. On July 3, 2025, the Madani 
Appellees likewise filed a reply in opposition to the Frescatores’ motion for 
modification. They maintained, among other things, that the Frescatores’ 
modification motion was nothing more than a second motion for 
reconsideration, and that the Frescatores still had not answered the Madani 
Appellees’ discovery requests. They also asserted the Frescatores’ refusal to 
cooperate in discovery stalled the discovery process, and prevented the 
Madani Appellees from fully investigating Appellees’ claims, conducting 
depositions, and evaluating the case to determine the need for expert 
witnesses. 
 On July 3, 2025, the Loria Appellees filed a motion for summary 
judgment. They argued there is no evidence the Loria Appellees were 
negligent and, additionally, that the Frescatores are precluded from 
introducing any evidence at trial. On July 7, 2025, the Madani Appellees also 
filed a motion for summary judgment, in which they argued the Frescatores 
cannot establish a prima facie case against them due to the trial court’s order

BEFORE: HONORABLE PATRICIA A. McCULLOUGH, Judge 
 HONORABLE STACY WALLACE, Judge 
 HONORABLE STELLA M. TSAI, Judge 

OPINION 
BY JUDGE McCULLOUGH FILED: October 23, 2026 
 In these consolidated cases, 1 Edward M. Frimel, et al . ( Appellants) 
appeal from the orders entered in the Clinton County Court of Common Pleas (trial 
court) on May 15, 2025 , denying their motion for partial summary judgment and 
granting the motion for summary judgment filed by Wag-Myr Woodlands, Inc. 
(Appellee). On appeal, Appellants challenge the trial court’s determination that the 
equitable defenses of laches and equitable estoppel bar this action brought by Greene 
Township (Township) seeking to enforce compliance with road grading and width 
provisions included in the Township ’s Subdivision and Land Development 
Ordinance (SALDO).2 We affirm. 

1 The Township filed two separate lawsuits in the trial court at Docket Nos. 280-2022 and 
611-2022. Although t he trial court did not formally consolidate the cases, it entered parallel 
determinations at both docket numbers. ( Reproduced Record (R.R.) at 517.) This Court entered 
an order consolidating the appeals on February 4, 2026. 

2 Appellants were intervenors before the trial court. The Township did not file a notice of 
appeal, and is therefore considered an appellee in this matter. (R.R. at 513. ) The Township has 
filed a brief in this Court stating that it joins Appellants’ brief in its entirety. (Township’s Br., at 
1.) 
2 

I. Background 
 The relevant facts and procedural history of this case are as follows. 
Appellee is a developer that constructed a 35-lot subdivision in the Township, and 
Appellants are property owners who reside in that development. Appellee purchased 
the original approximate 700-acre tract in 1993, and thereafter subdivided the land 
at 16 points in time from 1995 through 2015. (R.R. at 4-5.) 
 On March 21, 2022 , seven years after the final subdivision, the 
Township filed a complaint at Docket No. 280-2022 against Appellee, alleging that 
the roads within the development , primarily a two-mile private access road named 
Wag-Myr Lane serving all of the subdivisions,3 were not constructed in accordance 
with applicable SALDO4 provisions. The Township maintained that Appellee’s 
failure to comply with relevant standards created dangerous condition s for the 
residents of the development, as the roads did not accommodate safe speeds or allow 
adequate use by emergency vehicles. (R .R. at 8 .) The Township sought a court 
order compelling Appellee to bring the roads into compliance with the SALDO, and 
seeking reimbursement of all costs it incurred relating to the lawsuit. 
 While the action was pending, the Township filed a se cond lawsuit 
based on the same factual allegations on June 15, 202 2, (Docket No. 611 -2022), 
requesting the trial court to fine Appellee $500.00 per day until the roads complied 
with SALDO requirements. (R.R. at 17.) Following discovery, Appellants filed an 
unopposed petition to intervene in both cases, which the trial court granted. 

3 The road is approximately 22 feet wide. (R.R. at 154.) The improvements requested by 
the Township would cost an estimated $1,200,000.00 , and most of the lots in the development 
have been sold. (Appellee’s Br., at 31; Appellants’ Br., at 25.) 

4 The Township enacted a subdivision ordinance in 1975, and adopted the SALDO in 2007. 
(R.R. at 25.) 
3 

 On February 28, 2025, Appellee moved for summary judgment based 
on the affirmative defenses of laches and equitable estoppel , contending t hat the 
Township approved all the subdivisions in the development without conditions 
approximately 20 years before bringing th ese actions. Appellee averred that 
Township Supervisors (Supervisors), and others involved in the approval process , 
are now deceased or have faded memories of the relevant events, resulting in 
prejudice warranting dismissal of the lawsuits. (R.R. at 107.) In support of its 
motion, Appellee attached multiple letters involving t he Supervisors, Township 
meeting minutes, and deposition testimony indicating that the Township approved 
the subdivisions and roads through informal means. These exhibits included: 

• A July 9, 1999 letter from the Supervisors (two of 
whom are now deceased) to Appellee’s then 
representative, William Baistian , also now 
deceased, advising, “the subdivision will not be 
signed until the road is put into Township 
conditions or can be bonded and made to Township 
conditions. . . . The Township will get a 
contractor to come in and put the road to 
conditions.” (R.R. at 117) (emphasis added.) 

• The deposition testimony of Marvin Weaver, the 
only surviving Supervisor named in the July 9, 1999 
letter, advising he sustained a serious brain injury 
impacting his memory in 2023, and was 70 years 
old at the time of his deposition. Mr. Weaver 
testified that , during the time he served as 
Supervisor, he was not familiar with the specific 
requirements of the SALDO . Mr. Weaver 
indicated tha t the Township sometimes issued 
permits under circumstances not “exactly by the 
book,” and that the Supervisors’ “main concern 
about [Appellee’s] roads was that the Township 
would not be responsible for maintenance or 
4 

upkeep of the road or plowing or anything .” 
(R.R. at 139.) Mr. Weaver further testified that he 
did not recall any details regarding the July 9, 1999 
letter the Supervisors sent to Appellee, and that, to 
his knowledge, the Township never sent a 
contractor out to the roads in the development. 
(R.R. at 140.) Mr. Weaver acknowledged that the 
Supervisors would not have approved any of the 
subdivisions if they were not satisfied with the 
road conditions. (R.R. at 141.) 

• A July 16, 2003 letter from Clinton County 
(County) Planning Director Tim Holladay to the 
Supervisors noting that the County Planning 
Commission “appreciated the effort made by 
[Appellee] to plan for the future, and show a 
proposed future ,” recommending “that the 
development proceed in phases starting from the 
existing improved road.” (R.R. at 110) (emphasis 
added.) 

• An October 24, 2003 letter from Mr. Holladay to the 
Supervisors stating in relevant part, “[w]e would 
like to thank [Appellee] and Township 
representatives for attending a site visit on 
October 20th.” (R.R. at 112) (emphasis added.) 

• A July 21, 2004 letter from Mr. Holladay to the 
Supervisors advising “ we understand that the 
Township has agreed that the roads are 
acceptable as constructed ” and recommending 
that the roads meet Township width and surfacing 
standards for future phases as the “build out of the 
property will result in the current roads becoming 
inadequate.” (R.R. at 113) (emphasis added.) 

• Mr. Holladay’s deposition testimony indicating that 
he did not reca ll why he wrote the July 21, 2004 
letter or the specific roads he referenced therein, and 
that he was unfamiliar with Township width and 
5 

surfacing standards . Mr. Holladay additionally 
testified that , during his tenure on the Planning 
Commission, he did not believe that the 
Supervisors were familiar with the requirements 
of the subdivision ordinances . (R.R. at 116 ) 
(emphasis added.) 

• August 3, 2004 minutes of a Supervisors ’ meeting 
at which Mr. Bastian and Mr. Holladay were present 
showing discussion of the road con ditions and 
comment that “that the Township could not be 
forced to take over care of Wag -Myr Woodlands 
roads until conditions would be improved for 
paving construction.” (R.R. at 130.) The motion to 
pass Phase I of the land development upon approval 
by the Department of Environmental Protection 
passed. 

• Minutes from an October 3, 2005 Supervisors 
meeting noting: “[Appellee] presented [the] ten plot 
subdivision to the [] Township Planning 
Commission. After some discussion, Larry Sheats 
motioned to accept the subdivision as presented. 
Ralph Brungart seconded. Motion carried . 
[Appellee] was instructed to now take [the] 
subdivision over to Tim Holladay, Clinton County 
Planning Commission for County stamp. 
[Appellee] agreed [to] take it over [and] gave the 
secretary [a] $500.00 check for the ten 
subdivisions.” (R.R. at 133) (emphasis added.) 

• A report prepared by Appellee’s exp ert Daniel 
Vassallo, P.E., P.L.S., in January of 2025 
explaining that, beginning with the subdivisions in 
1999, [the] Township required language be 
included on all subdivision plats, agreements of 
sale, deeds, and other documents with regard to the 
subdivision, specific reference to the fact that access 
to the parcels was being conveyed with access 
provided by private road, that access is not subject 
6 

to municipal maintenance, and that the municipality 
is not responsible for any road construction, 
maintenance, or improvement at any time in the 
future. (R.R. at 168.) 

• The April 4, 2024 deposition testimony of Lucien 
Snook, who built Wag -Myr Lane, confirming that 
Supervisors Tom Rockey and Ralph Brungart 
repeatedly examined the road during its 
construction and gave him “the okay” to 
continue building . (R.R. at 153 ) (emphasis 
added.)5 
 Appellants filed a motion seeking partial summary judgment, asserting 
that none of the roads within the development were constructed in accordance with 
SALDO standards, and that because the Township granted Appellee no legally 
recognizable waivers or modifications from controlling standards, all of the road 
must be brought into compliance with the SALDO. (R.R. at 239.)6 After extensive 
briefing by the parties and oral argument, the trial court entered its May 15, 2025 
order granting Appellee’s motion for summary judgment and denying Appellants’ 
motion for partial summary judgment . In its opinion, the trial court observed that 
Appellee failed to obtain any waivers from SALDO requirements and that “the 
parties seem to agree that the roads at issue do not comply with relevant 
ordinances.”7 (R.R. at 525.) The court determined , “[h]owever, neither the non-
compliance of the roads nor the lack of written waivers to the requirements of the 

5 Mr. Brungart and Mr. Rockey are now deceased. (R.R. at 525.) 

6 See Section 512. 1(b) of the Pennsylvania Municipalities Planning Code, 53 P.S. § 
512.1(b) (providing that “[a]ll requests for a modification shall be in writing and shall accompany 
and be a part of the application for development”). 

7 The trial court did not identify any specific ordinance provisions Appellee

SIXTH DISTRICT COURT OF APPEAL 
STATE OF FLORIDA 
_____________________________ 

Case No. 6D2025-2286 
Lower Tribunal No. 2024-CA-002200 
_____________________________ 

ROBERT DWAYNE HARRIS, 
Appellant, 
v. 
NATIONSTAR MORTGAGE, LLC, 
Appellee. 
_____________________________ 

Appeal from the Circuit Court for Charlotte County. 
Geoffrey H. Gentile, Judge. 

October 23, 2026 

BROWNLEE, J. 

Appellant Robert Dwayne Harris appeals a final judgment of foreclosure, the 
denial of rehearing from that judgment, and the denial of his motion to enjoin the 
foreclosure sale. Appellee Nationstar Mortgage, LLC, concedes the judgment was 
entered without adequate notice to Appellant and that remand for a new foreclosure 
trial is required. 
“A judgment procured without notice or opportunity to be heard is void.” 
Daley v. Elevate Roofing & Exteriors, Inc., 432 So. 3d 653, 656 (Fla. 6th DCA 2026) 
2 

(citing Curbelo v. Ullman , 571 So. 2d 443, 445 (Fla. 1990)). “Notice to legally 
interested parties so that they can assert their claims is the essence of the procedural 
due process protections provided by the Florida Constitution.” Wyrick v. Wyrick, 51 
Fla. L. Weekly D1849, D1850 (Fla. 6th DCA Sept. 2, 2026) (quoting In re Adoption 
of a Minor Child, 593 So. 2d 185, 189 (Fla. 1991)). Here, Nationstar concedes that, 
although Appellant was served with the foreclosure complaint and filed pleadings in 
response, he did not receive notice of the foreclosure trial until after the trial 
occurred. This deprived Appellant of an opportunity to be heard on his defenses to 
the f oreclosure. Appellant brought this to the attention of the trial court on two 
occasions, including in a motion for rehearing, but the court denied that motion, on 
the merits, in an unelaborated order. 
We now accept Nationstar’s concession of error, reverse to vacate the 
foreclosure judgment, and remand for further proceedings. Our disposition makes it 
unnecessary to address Appellant’s arguments concerning the court’s entry of 
judgment without ruling on his motion to dismiss, his arguments on the merits of his 
defenses, or his arguments surrounding the denial of rehearing. See, e.g., Waterfront 
in Naples Condo. Ass’n v. Reynolds Ventures, Inc., 51 Fla. L. Weekly D1728, D1729 
(Fla. 6th DCA Aug. 21, 2026) (“We therefore address only the dispositive issue and 
remand for a trial on the merits.”); see also O’Hair v. O’Hair , 396 So. 3d 630, 634 
(Fla. 6th DCA 2024) (citing Akers v. City of Miami Beach, 745 So. 2d 532, 532 (Fla. 
3 

3d DCA 1999), for the proposition that “appellate courts ‘should not ordinarily 
decide issues not ruled on by the trial court in the first instance’”). 
As to the denial of Appellant’s motion to enjoin the foreclosure sale, we affirm 
because the motion became moot before it was heard, by virtue of the sale taking 
place. See Dolgencorp, Inc. v. Winn- Dixie Stores, Inc., 2 So. 3d 325, 327– 28 (Fla. 
4th DCA 2008) (“Generally, injunctive relief is available to prevent a threatened 
harm but is not available to redress harm which has already occurred.” (quoting 
Speer v. Evangelisto, 662 So. 2d 1340, 1341–42 (Fla. 2d DCA 1995))). Even so, our 
reversal of the foreclosure judgment provides grounds for the parties to seek an order 
in the lower court vacating the foreclosure sale. See Fla. R. Civ. P. 1.540(b)(5). 
Accordingly, we affirm the denial of injunctive relief but reverse the final 
judgment of foreclosure and remand for further proceedings consistent with this 
opinion. 
AFFIRMED in part; REVERSED in part; and REMANDED. 
TRAVER, C.J., and NARDELLA, J., concur. 

Robert Dwayne Harris, Punta Gorda, pro se. 

Zachary Ullman, of Aldridge | Pite, LLP, Delray Beach, for Appellee. 

NOT FINAL UNTIL TIME EXPIRES TO FILE MOTION FOR REHEARING 
AND DISPOSITION THEREOF IF TIMELY FILED
