If this opinion indicates that it is “FOR PUBLICATION,” it is subject to 
revision until final publication in the Michigan Appeals Reports. 

-1- 
S T A T E O F M I C H I G A N 

C O U R T O F A P P E A L S 

THOMAS WILLIAMS, 

 Plaintiff-Appellant, 

UNPUBLISHED 
October 22, 2026 
8:55 AM 
v No. 375121 
Sanilac Circuit Court 
CREEKSIDE HURON SHORES, LLC, and 
CREEKSIDE COMMUNITIES, LLC, 

LC No. 23-040295-NO 
 Defendants-Appellees. 

Before: PATEL, P.J., and M. J. KELLY and GARRETT, JJ. 

PER CURIAM. 
 Plaintiff, Thomas Williams, fell on three occasions while walking from his vehicle to his 
manufactured home located on a lot he leased from defendant Creekside Huron Shores, LLC 
(Huron Shores). He filed this action against Huron Shores and defendant Creekside Communities, 
LLC (Creekside), the company that Huron Shores retained to maintain its property , alleging 
common-law negligence and violation of MCL 554.139 and MCL 125.536. Williams appeals by 
right the trial court’s order granting summary disposition in favor of Huron Shores and Creekside. 
He also challenges the trial court’s order denying his motion for reconsideration. Because genuine 
issues of material fact exist regarding Williams’s common-law negligence claims, we reverse the 
trial court’s orders in part and remand for further proceedings. 
I. FACTUAL BACKGROUND 
 Williams lived in a manufactured home on a lot he leased from Huron Shores in its 
manufactured housing community. The lot included a walkway that led from the community 
sidewalk to Williams ’s home situated on the lot. The walkway abutted the sidewalk in a “T” 
formation. The walkway was not level with the community sidewalk, which Williams asserted 
had sunk below the level of the walkway, creating a trip hazard. According to Williams, the 
sidewalk had sunk before he moved onto the lot. Williams estimated the height differential 
between the sidewalk and walkway to be approximately two inches on one side of the walkway 
and one inch on the other side. 
-2- 
Williams’s first fall occurred on June 21, 2023. He went to the store to buy groceries and 
tripped on the raised walkway after he returned and attempted to carry the groceries to his home. 
He fell to the ground and treated his injuries with ice and heat that night. The following day, he 
drove himself to the hospital because he was in severe pain when he awoke. He was advised to 
follow up with his doctors. Williams tripped on the raised edge of the walkway a second time on 
July 17, 2023. He fell to the ground and landed on his right wrist. Four days later, he tripped and 
fell a third time because of the same condition. 
 Williams filed a complaint against Huron Shores. Thereafter, he filed an amended 
complaint adding as a defendant Creekside, the maintenance company Huron Shores hired to 
maintain the manufactured housing community. Williams asserted negligence claims against both 
defendants. He alleged that Huron Shores failed to maintain the sidewalk in a careful and prudent 
manner, contrary to MCL 554.139, MCL 125.536, and the common law . Against Creekside, 
Williams alleged that it failed to maintain the community sidewalks in a reasonable and 
nonnegligent manner in accordance with its contract with Huron Shores. 
 Defendants moved for summary disposition, arguing that MCL 125.536 was inapplicable 
because it applied to dwellings, and Williams ’s falls did not occur in a dwelling. Defendants 
maintained that MCL 554.139 was also inapplicable because Williams ’s one -year lease had 
expired by the time he fell , and he remained on the premises as a month -to-month tenant. 
Defendants asserted that, as stated in the lease agreement, Williams assumed the responsibilities 
set forth in MCL 554.139 after expiration of the lease, including maintaining and repairing the 
intersection of the sidewalk and walkway. Regarding Williams’s common-law claims, defendants 
asserted that the height differential between the sidewalk and walkway was less than one inch as 
established by their expert, Dr. Justin Waxman, and photos that Williams took after he fell. 
Defendants argued that the duty to repair the sidewalk should not be greater than that of 
municipalities “which are clearly more funded.” They maintained that, under MCL 691.1402a, a 
municipality is entitled to governmental immunity if a height differential is less than two inches, 
and Williams has not established a vertical discontinuity of two inches or more. 
 Williams did not respond to defendants ’ motion, which the trial court granted after 
dispensing with oral argument. The court determined that MCL 125.536 was inapplicable because 
it does not apply to private dwellings in a city, village, or township with a population less than 
100,000. Regarding MCL 554.139, the court noted that Williams failed to specify in his amended 
complaint whether he alleged violation of MCL 554.139(1)(a) or (b). The court determined that 
MCL 554.139(1)(b) was inapplicable because that section does not apply to sidewalks located in 
common areas. The court also determined that the sidewalk was not unfit for its intended use as 
stated in MCL 554.139(1)(a) because the purpose of a sidewalk is for walking on it and providing 
access to the areas connected to it. The court noted that “[t]he statute does not require a lessor to 
maintain a sidewalk in ideal condition or in the most accessible condition possible, but merely 
requires the lessor to maintain the sidewalk in a condition that renders it fit for use as a sidewalk.” 
The court concluded that the vertical height discontinuity was approximately 1.4 inches and did 
not render the sidewalk unfit for its intended use. The court also reasoned that Williams had failed 
to respond to defendants’ motion and provide documentary evidence establishing a genuine issue 
for trial as required under MCR 2.116(G)(4). 
 The trial court next addressed Williams’s common-law negligence claims, stating: 
-3- 
 The Defendants argue that the Plaintiff cannot show a breach of a duty owed 
to him as an invitee. Furthermore, the Defendants argue that a private landowner 
should not be held to a higher standard than a municipality for purposes of a vertical 
height discontinuity (less than 1.5” in this case vs. 2.0” for a municipality) related 
to a sidewalk. MCL 600.1402a. The Defendants’ arguments —especially those 
related to MCL 600.1402a—are persuasive to this Court. 
Further, the court again recognized that Williams had failed to respond to defendants’ motion. The 
court therefore granted the motion under MCR 2.116(C)(10) and dismissed Williams’s claims with 
prejudice. 
 Williams moved for reconsideration. He argued that he failed to respond to defendants’ 
motion for summary disposition because he erroneously believed the hearing on the motion had 
been adjourned. Substantively, he conceded that MCL 125.536 and MCL 554.139 (1)(b) were 
inapplicable but argued that defendants failed to maintain the sidewalk in a condition fit for its 
intended purpose as set forth in MCL 554.139(1)(a). He maintained that the height differential 
was a factual issue because his photos indicated a difference of approximately two inches , which 
was greater than the height differential asserted by Dr. Waxman. Williams denied that the lease 
agreement delegated to him, as a holdover tenant, the duty to keep his premises in reasonable 
repair, but asserted that even if it did, he fell because of a problem with the community sidewalk 
in the common area and not because of a condition on his premises. Regarding his common-law 
claims, Williams asserted that the two -inch rule applicable to municipalities did not apply to 
private landowners. 
 The trial court denied the motion. The court noted that it did not enter the order granting 
defendants’ motion for summary disposition until after Williams’s response to the motion was due, 
but Williams failed to file a response. The court indicated that it then decided the matter based on 
the evidence that had been presented and based in part on Williams’s failure to respond to 
defendants’ motion. The court stated that Williams did not seek reconsideration of the court’s 
decision but instead wished to respond to defendants’ motion “through the use of a motion for 
reconsideration.” Accordingly, the court denied Williams’s motion. This appeal followed. 
II. STANDARDS OF REVIEW 
 We review de novo a trial court’s decision on a motion for summary disposition. Houston 
v Mint Group, LLC, 335 Mich App 545, 557; 968 NW2d 9 (2021). When deciding a motion under 
MCR 2.116(C)(10), the trial court must consider the affidavits, deposition testimony, and other 
documentary evidence that the parties submit. Anderson v Transdev Servs, Inc , 341 Mich App 
501, 506; 991 NW2d 230 (2022). Summary disposition is appropriate if the evidence, viewed in 
the light most favorable to the nonmoving party, establishes that there is no genuine issue of 
material fact for trial. Id. at 507. “A genuine issue of material fact exists when the record, giving 
the benefit of reasonable doubt to the opposing party, leaves open an issue upon which reasonable 
minds might differ. ” Id. (quotation marks and citation omitted). We review for an abuse of 
discretion a trial court’s decision on a motion for reconsideration . Farm Bureau Ins Co v TNT 
Equip, Inc, 328 Mich App 667, 672; 939 NW2d 738 (2019). “A trial court abuses its discretion if 
it chooses an outcome outside the range of principled outcomes.” Id. 
-4- 
III. ANALYSIS 
A. MCL 554.139(1)(a) 
 Williams argues the trial court erred by determining that no material factual dispute exists 
regarding whether Huron Shores failed to maintain the sidewalk in a condition that rendered it fit 
for its intended use under MCL 554.139(1)(a). “MCL 554.139 provides a specific protection to 
lessees and licensees of residential property in addition to any protection provided by the common 
law.” Allison v AEW Capital Mgt, LLP, 481 Mich 419, 425; 751 NW2d 8 (2008). “The statutory 
protection under MCL 554.139(1) arises from the existence of a residential lease and consequently 
becomes a statutorily mandated term of such lease.”1 Id. MCL 554.139 states, in relevant part: 
(1) In every lease or license of residential premises, the lessor or licensor covenants: 
(a) That the premises and all common areas are fit for the use intended by the 
parties. 
Our Supreme Court has recognized that a “common area” is “ ‘the portion of demised premises 
used in common by tenants over which landlord retains control ( e.g. hallways, stairs) and hence 
for whose condition he is liable, as contrasted with areas of which tenant has exclusive 
possession.’ ” Allison, 481 Mich at 427 , quoting Black’s Law Dictionary (6 th ed), p 275. The 
parties do not dispute that the sidewalk at issue in this case was a common area. 
 Under MCL 554.139(1)(a), a lessor has a duty to maintain a common area in a condition 
“ ‘fit for the use intended by the parties.’ ” Id. at 429, quoting MCL 554.139(1)(a). “The statute 
does not require any level of fitness beyond what is necessary to allow tenants to use the [common 
area] as the parties intended.” Id. at 431. The statute also does not require a lessor to maintain a 
common area “in an ideal condition .” Id. at 430. “[T]he appropriate inquiry under MCL 
554.139(1)(a) remains whether the common area in question is fit (i.e., adapted, suited, or 
appropriate) for the use intended by the parties. ” Bowerman v Red Oak Mgt Co, Inc , ___ Mich 
___ ; ___ NW3d ___ (2026) (Docket No. 167718); slip op at 18. 
 The parties ostensibly intended the sidewalk at issue to be used for walking and providing 
access to the walkway located on Williams’s lot. The fact that the sidewalk had sunk to a degree, 
creating a height differential between the sidewalk and walkway, d id not render it unfit for this 
use. As the trial court recognized, Williams had used the sidewalk without inci

leads.caseName: Bank of America v. Hambrick
leads.text:
2026 IL App (3d) 250524-U 
No. 3-25-0524 
Order filed October 22, 2026 
NOTICE: This order was filed under Illinois Supreme Court Rule 23 and is not 
precedential except in the limited circumstances allowed under Rule 23(e)(1). 

IN THE 
APPELLATE COURT OF ILLINOIS 
THIRD DISTRICT 

BANK OF AMERICA, N.A., Plaintiff-Appellee, 
v. 
EDWARD HAMBRICK, Defendant-Appellant 
Appeal from the Circuit Court of Will County. 
Honorable Jeffrey J. Tuminello, Judge, Presiding. 
No. 25-SC-2908 

JUSTICE DA VENPORT delivered the judgment of the court. 
Justices Holdridge and Anderson concurred in the judgment. 
ORDER 
¶ 1 Held: The circuit court properly denied defendant’s petition for relief from judgment. The 
court did not err when it denied defendant’s request for a nunc pro tunc correction 
of the record. Defendant forfeited his claims that his constitutional rights to due 
process and free access to the courts were violated. Affirmed. 

¶ 2 Plaintiff, Bank of America, N.A., sued defendant, Edward Hambrick, to recover an unpaid 
credit card balance. The circuit court entered a default judgment in plaintiff’s favor, and it later 
denied defendant’s petition to vacate the judgment under section 2- 1401 of the Code of Civil 
Procedure (Code) (735 ILCS 5/2-1401 (West 2024)). 

- 2 - 
¶ 3 Defendant appeals, contending the circuit court abused its discretion in denying his petition 
and erroneously denied his request for a nunc pro tunc “correction of the record.” He also contends 
the circuit clerk violated his constitutional rights to due process and free access to the courts. We 
affirm. 
¶ 4 I. BACKGROUND 
¶ 5 A. Prejudgment Proceedings 
¶ 6 In April 2025, plaintiff filed a small claims action against defendant, alleging defendant 
had failed to pay a $2,592.43 balance that was due on his credit card account. The circuit clerk, at 
plaintiff’s request, issued a summons with a return date of June 13, 2025, the same day. 
¶ 7 Defendant was served with the summons and complaint on May 3, 2025. Later that month, 
he mailed the circuit clerk two documents titled (1) “non-negotiable notice of acceptance and 
request for performance from accommodation parties [sureties] ‘Andrea Lynn Chasteen’ ‘et al.’ ”; 
and (2) “non-negotiable notice and demand for cross-claim against attorney for plaintiff ‘et al.’ ”
1 
The “non-negotiable notice of acceptance” was file-stamped on May 27, 2025. In both documents, 
defendant stated he was “here by special appearance.” 
¶ 8 On June 13, 2025, the parties appeared before the circuit court. Defendant identified 
himself and stated he was “appearing today by special appearance, not general appearance” and 
that he “reserve[d] all [his] rights under UCC 1-308 without prejudice.” Defendant asked the court 
to “close the account” and discharge the matter. The court ordered defendant to file an appearance 
by July 11, 2025, and continued the matter to July 29, 2025, for a bench trial. The court tendered 
a copy of the order to defendant and warned him that the failure to file an appearance as ordered 

1The titles of these documents, as well as other documents defendant submitted throughout these 
proceedings, were typed in all caps typeface. We have reproduced them in lowercase typeface to aid 
readability. 

- 3 - 
would likely result in a default judgment on the trial date. Defendant did not file an appearance as 
ordered. 
¶ 9 On July 11, 2025, plaintiff moved for a default judgment, which was scheduled for 
presentment on July 21, 2025. Plaintiff sent notice of the hearing to defendant. 
¶ 10 Thereafter, defendant mailed the circuit clerk a “special and limited appearance objecting 
to jurisdiction,” an accompanying memorandum, and several other documents. The documents 
were dated July 11, 2026, and file-stamped on July 16, 2025. In his “special appearance” mailing, 
defendant asserted the court lacked both subject-matter and personal jurisdiction. Defendant also 
stated he did not tender any filing fees with his submission, “as payment would constitute a 
voluntary submission to jurisdiction.” 
¶ 11 On July 21, 2025, plaintiff presented its motion for default judgment. Defendant did not 
appear. The court continued the matter to July 29, 2025, for a hearing on the motion, directing 
plaintiff to give notice of the order to defendant. The next day, plaintiff sent notice as directed. 
¶ 12 On July 28, 2025, plaintiff filed a new motion for default judgment, noting defendant had 
not filed his appearance as of July 22, 2025.
2 Plaintiff included an alternative request for dismissal 
without prejudice because the witness who could substantiate the complaint’s allegations had been 
“assigned to cover other legal matters” for plaintiff. 
¶ 13 On July 29, 2025, the matter was called for trial and a hearing on plaintiff’s default motion. 
Plaintiff appeared, and defendant did not. Accordingly, no trial was held, and the court entered a 
default judgment against defendant, awarding plaintiff $2,592.43 plus $384.96 in costs. 
¶ 14 B. Postjudgment Proceedings 

2Plaintiff filed a notice of hearing on July 22, 2025, stating that its new default motion would be 
presented on July 29, 2025. The motion file-stamped until July 28, 2025. 

- 4 - 
¶ 15 On August 28, 2025, defendant used the court’s electronic filing system for the first time. 
He filed an appearance, signed “without prejudice,” along with a fee-waiver application. The court 
granted the fee waiver. 
¶ 16 On September 18, 2025, defendant electronically filed a “Motion to Vacate Default 
Judgment.” He stated his motion was brought under section 2-1301(e) of the Code (735 ILCS 5/2-
1301(e) (West 2024)) and, “in the alternative,” section 2- 1401 of the Code (735 ILCS 5/2 -1401 
(West 2024)). 
¶ 17 In the section 2-1401 portion of his motion, defendant seemingly asserted the court lacked 
jurisdiction over him. He also stated, without alleging any specific facts, as follows: 
“Plaintiff’s counsel acted as a debt collector and is subject to the Fair Debt Collection 
Practices Act ([‘]FDCPA[’]) [citation]. Their conduct—including misrepresentation of the 
amount and character of the debt, initiated suit in an improper venue, and using unfair 
litigation p ractices—violated [sections] 807, 808, and 811 of the FDCPA. The U.S. 
Supreme Court in Heintz v. Jenkins, 514 U.S. 291 (2005), confirmed that attorneys engaged 
in debt collection are bound by the FDCPA. These violations provide an independent 
meritorious defense and further justify vacating the default judgment.” 
Defendant did not address his failure to appear at the July 11, 2025, hearing on plaintiff’s motion 
for default or his failure to appear on the July 29, 2025, trial date. 
¶ 18 As part of his petition, defendant also requested a “nunc pro tunc order to correct the docket 
and record so that it reflects the true and accurate history of [his] filings.” Defendant listed several 
documents that he had mailed to the circuit clerk but were not filed or that were filed but he 
believed were stamped with an incorrect date. Defendant attached the documents, proof that he 

- 5 - 
had mailed the documents, and correspondence from the circuit clerk stating the reason some of 
the documents were being returned to him without being filed. These included the following: 
(1) his May 2025 mailing with a May, 27, 2025, file stamp ( supra ¶ 7), which, according 
to a return receipt, was actually received by the clerk on May 23, 2025; 
(2) a “non-negotiable notice of special appearance demanding dismissal of plaintiff’s suit 
with prejudice for failure to state a claim for which relief may be granted and notice for 
cross-claim against attorney for plaintiff for cause”, mailed on June 4, 2025; 
(3) a “non-negotiable notice of acceptance,” mailed on June 4, 2025; 
(4) a “notice of inquiry to the clerk of court respecting failure to file form 1066 and form 
1120 to account for taxes mandated to be paid on qualified mortgages and foreclosed 
property acquired by real estate mortgage investment conduits on ‘startup day,’ ” mailed 
on June 4, 2025; 
(5) his July 2025 mailings, file -stamped on July 16, 2025 ( supra ¶ 10), which “were 
returned without docket entry”; 
(6) a “notice to the clerk of court for record correction,” mailed on August 15, 2025, and 
returned to defendant on August 27, 2025; 
(7) a “special and limited appearance in equity only” and “notice of motion to vacate 
default judgment” (combined into one document), mailed on August 15, 2025, and returned 
to defendant on August 27, 2025; and 
(8) a “notice of fault and dishonor,” mailed on August 15, 2025, and returned to defendant 
on August 27, 2025. 
¶ 19 At the hearing on the motion to vacate, the parties’ arguments initially focused on whether 
section 2-1301 was applicable, as defendant’s motion was filed on September 18, 2025, more than 

- 6 - 
30 days after the default judgment was entered. Defendant asserted he had previously submitted a 
motion to vacate within 30 days of the default judgment, which was rejected by the clerk. Neither 
plaintiff nor defendant raised any argument with respect to the section 2- 1401 portion of 
defendant’s motion. 
¶ 20 The court denied the motion, and this appeal followed. 
¶ 21 II. ANALYSIS 
¶ 22 Preliminarily, we note that while the “Motion to Vacate Default Judgment” requested relief 
under sections 2-1301(e) and 2-1401 of the Code, defendant raises no section 2-1301(e) argument 
on appeal. We therefore limit our analysis to whether the court properly denied the section 2-1401 
portion of defendant’s motion. Relatedly, because proceedings under section 2- 1401 are initiated 
by the filing of a petition (see 735 ILCS 5/2- 1401(a) (West 2024)), we will refer to defendant’s 
“motion” as a petition throughout our analysis. 
¶ 23 A. The Court Properly Denied Defendant’s Section 2-1401 Petition 
¶ 24 Defendant first contends the circuit court abused its discretion when it denied his section 
2-1401 petition. Section 2-1401 of the Code allows a party to petition the court to vacate a final 
judgment more than 30 days old. 735 ILCS 5/2-1401 (West 2024). When seeking relief under this 
section, the party must set forth specific factual allegations establishing (1) the existence of a 
meritorious defense or claim, (2) due diligence in presenting the defense or claim to the circuit 
court in the original action, and (3) due diligence in filing the petition. Warren County Soil and 
Water Conservation District v. Walters, 2015 IL 117783, ¶ 51. “The quantum of proof necessary 
to sustain a section 2- 1401 petition is a preponderance of the evidence.” Id. When, as here, a 
defendant raises a fact-based challenge in a 2-1401 petition, we review the court’s decision for an 
abuse of discretion. Id. 

- 7 - 
¶ 25 Defendant’s petition failed to set forth any specific factual allegations to support the 
existence of a meritorious defense. In his petition, defendant asserted he had meritorious defenses 
under sections 807, 808, and 811 of the Federal Debt Collection Practices Act (15 U.S.C. §§ 1692e, 
1692f, 1692i). Even assuming defendant’s purported meritorious defenses under the Fair Debt 
Collection Practices Act “would defeat *** plaintiff’s claim in the underlying action” (Erickson v. 
Mitrione, 2025 IL App (4th) 250297, ¶ 23 (internal quotation marks omitted)), defendant’s petition 
failed to set forth any specific facts to establish those defenses. Indeed, defendant failed to state 
any facts establishing that plaintiff used false, deceptive, or misleading representations in 
connection with collecting the debt (id. § 1692e); used unfair or unconscionable means to collect 
or attempt to collect the debt (id. § 1692f); or brought the action in an improper venue (id. § 1692i). 
¶ 26 Moreover, defendant’s petition failed to set forth any facts to establish he acted diligently 
in the original action. “Due diligence requires the section 2 -1401 petitioner to have a reasonable 
e
